title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
section: 8.8 The typical workflow in both APIs
text:
8.8 The typical workflow in both APIs
The Context API is a layer over the framework, so the first chapter’s five steps can be written in either. The script does both on the same hundred toy scores as A first release, drawn by the same seeded generator. So the scales can be compared with the ones you saw there. The first two steps are the privacy unit and the budget. The framework states the first as a distance and a metric, and the second as a distance and a measure.
d_in = 1  # neighbouring datasets differ by at most one row...
input_metric = dp.symmetric_distance()  # ...counted as additions and removals
input_domain = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float))  # a vector of floats, NaN allowed
d_out = EPSILON  # the distributions of two releases differ by at most epsilon...
privacy_measure = dp.max_divergence()  # ...measured by the max divergence, which is pure DP
unit: d_in=1 input metric=SymmetricDistance()  (Context API: (SymmetricDistance(), 1))
loss: d_out=1.0 output measure=MaxDivergence  (Context API: (MaxDivergence, 1.0))
input domain: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64))
The pairs that dp.unit_of and dp.loss_of returned in the first chapter are these same objects. The framework also asks for the input domain up front, which the context inferred from the list you handed it. The domain allows NaN because a list of floats may contain one. The third step, the public bounds and the imputed value, is identical in both. The fourth step is to mediate access, and here the framework shows what a context is made of.
compositor = dp.c.make_adaptive_composition(
    input_domain=input_domain,
    input_metric=input_metric,
    output_measure=privacy_measure,
    d_in=d_in,
    d_mids=[d_out / QUERIES] * QUERIES,  # the shares of the budget, one per query
)
queryable = compositor(data)  # a measurement; invoking it on the data gives the queryable that answers queries
compositor: type=Measurement map(1)=1.0
queryable: type=Queryable
context accountant: type=Measurement d_mids=[0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333]
An adaptive composition is itself a measurement. Its privacy map at d_in is the sum of the shares, because the budgets of sequential releases add up. That is the composition property that the full edition’s chapter on properties proves. Invoking the composition on the data does not release anything. It returns a queryable, an object that holds the data and answers measurements submitted to it, one share at a time. The composition is adaptive because each measurement may depend on the answers before it. The context’s accountant field is this same object, and its d_mids are the same three shares. The fifth step submits the queries, and each is built by hand.
count = dp.t.make_count(input_domain, input_metric)
count_sensitivity = count.map(d_in)  # adding or removing one row changes a count by 1
count_scale = dp.binary_search_param(
    lambda scale: count >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale), d_in=d_in, d_out=d_out / QUERIES
)
count_measurement = count >> dp.m.then_laplace(count_scale)
dp_count = queryable(count_measurement)
count: sensitivity=1  output metric=AbsoluteDistance(i32)
count at scale 3.0: map(1)=0.33333333333333337 check(1, 1/3)=False
count by search: scale=3.0000000000000004 check(1, 1/3)=True
count scale: framework=3.0000 context=3.0000 equal=True
count: 95% accuracy=9.4457
The count is a transformation whose stability map gives the sensitivity 1, and the Laplace measurement after it needs a scale. You know from theory that the scale is the sensitivity over a third of \(\varepsilon\), which is 3. Typing in 3.0 fails the check, because one over three in floating point lands one rounding step above the share. The binary search returns a scale one rounding step above 3, which passes. It is bit for bit the scale that context.query().count().laplace().param() returned in the first chapter, because the context runs the same search. Submitting the measurement to the queryable spends the first share and returns the noisy count. The mean follows the first chapter’s recipe, with the released count fixing the size.
mean = (
    dp.t.make_impute_constant(input_domain, input_metric, IMPUTED)  # NaN becomes the public midpoint
    >> dp.t.then_clamp(BOUNDS)
    >> dp.t.then_resize(size=dp_count, constant=IMPUTED)  # the released count fixes the size
    >> dp.t.then_mean()
)
mean_scale = dp.binary_search_param(
    lambda scale: mean >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale), d_in=d_in, d_out=d_out / QUERIES
)
dp_mean = queryable(mean >> dp.m.then_laplace(mean_scale))
mean: output domain=AtomDomain(T=f64)  output metric=AbsoluteDistance(f64)
mean at size 100: sensitivity=1.0000
mean scale at size 100: framework=3.0000 context=3.0000 equal=True
mean at size 100: 95% accuracy=8.9872
mean scale at the released count: equal=True
Four transformations chain into one, from a vector of floats with NaN allowed to a single float. The stability of the whole is the maps of the parts composed. At the true size of 100, one row moves the mean by at most 1, so the scale is again 3. The context gives the same scale, both at the true size and at the released count. The scale of the mean changes with the released count, so the page quotes the one at the true size, which is a development-time number on a public toy. A third query takes the last share, and a fourth is refused.
try:
    queryable(count_measurement)
    refusal = "released"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    refusal = f"{err.variant}: {err.message}"
fourth query: FailedFunction: out of queries
The queryable raises the library’s own exception, with the variant FailedFunction and the message “out of queries”. The context wrapped the same refusal in a ValueError about an exhausted allowance. The queryable also refuses a single query whose map exceeds its share, before it touches the data. What the framework version makes plain is that a context is three objects you can build yourself, namely a space, an adaptive composition over that space, and a queryable. So Utilities and the Context API inside follows a query through the context to show where each is used. Finally the releases of one run, read against their error bars.
released (one run):
  laplace scale 5 on 0.0: 12.84  (within 15.0 with probability 0.95)
  hours sum 56,316,146  (true 56,315,594, within 8,628 with probability 0.95)
  count 99  (true 100, within 9.4 with probability 0.95)
  mean scale 3.0303  mean 50.43  (true 50.93)
  third query, a second count 104
The Laplace draw at scale 5 landed within its bar of about 15, and the sum of hours within its bar of about 8,600. The count and the mean landed within theirs. The comparison with the truth is possible only because the LFS sample and the toy scores are public. On real data you would read the error bars, which cost nothing, and release once.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.9 Summary



Table 8.1: The objects and elements of the framework, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




Transformation
A deterministic map from data to data, with an output_metric and a stability map
Its output is not private; chain it with a measurement before anything leaves


Measurement
A randomized map from data to a release, with an output_measure and a privacy map
Its map(d_in) is the guarantee; read it before releasing


trans(x), trans.invoke(x)
Evaluate the function field
Printing a transformation’s output steps outside the guarantee


atom_domain(T, bounds, nan)
One value of type T, optionally bounded, with or without NaN
Noise needs nan=False; a sum needs bounds; the printed form shows nan only when true


vector_domain(domain, size)
Vectors of a domain, optionally of fixed length
A mean needs the size; member tests a value by hand


symmetric_distance()
Additions and removals, with multiplicity
d_in is the records one person can add or remove


absolute_distance(T)
The difference of two numbers
d_in is a sensitivity; it appears midway through a chain


insert_delete, change_one, hamming
Ordered add/remove, replace-one, ordered replace-one
Pick the one that matches how your data can change


max_divergence()
Pure differential privacy; d_out is \(\varepsilon\)
The measure behind loss_of(epsilon=...)


zero_concentrated_divergence()
zCDP; d_out is \(\rho\)
The Gaussian mechanism’s native measure


smoothed_max_divergence(), fixed
Approximate DP; d_out is a privacy profile, or one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair
make_fix_delta turns the curve into the pair


obj.map(d_in), obj.check(d_in, d_out)
The smallest provable d_out; whether a proposed one fits
Let the map produce the distance; a hand-typed 3.0 fails by one rounding step


trans >> meas
A measurement whose map composes the two maps
Domains and metrics must match; then_ constructors match them for you


binary_search_param
The largest scale whose chain passes check
What the Context API runs for param()


make_adaptive_composition
A measurement whose invocation returns a queryable
A context is this, over a space, plus the queryable

title: 9  Transformations
text:
9.1 Constructors and chains
Every query of the previous parts began with the data and ended with noise, and in between stood a chain of steps that cast, imputed, clamped, resized and aggregated. In OpenDP each of those steps is a transformation, a function from data to data that comes with a promise about how much its output can change when its input changes. A framework to understand differential privacy introduced that promise as the stability map. This chapter builds the transformations themselves, from the preprocessing steps to the sum, the mean and the scores behind a quantile, and shows how the promise travels down a chain.
The idea that holds the chapter together is that a chain is only as good as the match between its links. Each transformation has an input space and an output space, and the output space of one must be exactly the input space of the next. That match is what makes the stability of a chain the product of the stabilities of its parts. It is also why so many constructors exist, because each one takes the data one provable step closer to the shape an aggregator needs. By the end you will be able to build a sum, a mean or a median’s scores from the framework alone and read off the sensitivity for your privacy unit. You will also recognize the error OpenDP raises when two spaces do not match.
The script opendp_transformations.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample. Its vector is the HWUSUAL column, the hours a respondent usually works, without its nulls and without the code 99 for “not applicable”, cast to integers. The sensitivities, scales, accuracies, scores and true values it prints are the same on every run. The released values are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, and neither is a float sum that truncates its input by a random sample. Those appear in one block marked as one run. The short snippets use toy vectors instead and print only what is deterministic.
Every constructor comes in two forms. The make_ form takes the input space first, as a domain and a metric, and then the constructor’s own arguments, so make_clamp(input_domain, input_metric, bounds) is the full call. The then_ form leaves the space out. It returns a partial constructor, and the >> operator fills in the space from whatever stands to its left, either a space written as a tuple or a transformation whose output space is used. The two forms build the same object, and the snippet shows both.
Clamping changes the domain and not the metric. The input domain was the vectors of integers, and the output domain is the vectors of integers between 0 and 10. The metric is still the symmetric distance, which counts the rows you must add or remove to turn one vector into the other. The sum then takes that output space as its input space, which make_sum(*clamp.output_space) says literally, and its own output is a single integer under the absolute distance. Reading output_space after each step is the habit this chapter teaches, because the next constructor must accept exactly that space. When it does not, the chain refuses to build, as Section 9.6 shows.
The number that map returns is the transformation’s stability, the largest change in the output for inputs at most d_in apart, each change measured in its own metric. For the clamp it is 1, because one added row of the input is one added row of the output. For the sum it is 10, because one added row can add at most the larger bound to the total. For the chain it is the product of the two. When the last step of a chain is an aggregator, its stability is what differential privacy calls the sensitivity of the query, which the full edition’s chapter on sensitivity derives for sums, means and histograms. That number is what a measurement needs to calibrate its noise.

title: 9  Transformations
text:
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance()
clamp = dp.t.make_clamp(*space, bounds=(0, 10))
print(clamp([-5, 3, 50]))  # [0, 3, 10]
print(clamp.output_space)  # (VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0, 10], T=i32)), SymmetricDistance())
total = dp.t.make_sum(*clamp.output_space)
chain = space >> dp.t.then_clamp(bounds=(0, 10)) >> dp.t.then_sum()
print(chain([-5, 3, 50]), (clamp >> total)([-5, 3, 50]))  # 13 13
print(chain.output_space)  # (AtomDomain(T=i32), AbsoluteDistance(i32))
print(clamp.map(1), total.map(1), chain.map(1))  # 1 10 10

title: 9  Transformations
text:
9.2 Preprocessing
Preprocessing turns the data into the domain an aggregator accepts, and every aggregator states that domain. The sum wants bounded values, for example, while the mean wants bounded values and a known size. The documentation lists the preprocessing constructors in the order you typically chain them, which is casting, imputing, clamping and resizing, and the subsections below keep that order. All but one of them work row by row, so one added row of the input is one added row of the output and the stability is 1. The exception is the resize.

9.2.1 Casting and imputing
Data read from a file arrive as strings, and make_cast turns a vector of strings into a vector of another type. A string that does not parse becomes a missing value, so the output domain is a vector of options, a type that holds either a value or nothing. No aggregator accepts options, for a reason the documentation states plainly. An aggregator that skipped the missing values would understate the sensitivity of the people with values, and one that propagated them would reveal whether anything was missing. So the missing values have to go first. make_impute_constant replaces each with a value of your choice, and make_drop_null removes the rows. make_cast_default folds the cast and the imputation into one step, with the type’s default standing in, which is 0 for numbers.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
strings = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=str)), dp.symmetric_distance()
cast = strings >> dp.t.then_cast(TOA=int)
print(cast.output_domain)  # VectorDomain(OptionDomain(AtomDomain(T=i32)))
imputed = cast >> dp.t.then_impute_constant(0)
print(imputed(["1", "2", "x"]))  # [1, 2, 0]
print(imputed.output_domain)  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=i32))
by_default = strings >> dp.t.then_cast_default(TOA=int)
print(by_default(["1", "2", "x"]))  # [1, 2, 0]
floats = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float)), dp.symmetric_distance()
print(floats[0])  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64))
uniform = floats >> dp.t.then_impute_uniform_float(bounds=(0.0, 10.0))
print(uniform.output_domain)  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=f64))
print(cast.map(1), imputed.map(1), uniform.map(1))  # 1 1 1
Floats carry their own missing value, the not-a-number value, and the domain says whether it is allowed. The plain atom_domain(T=float) allows it, which the nan=true in the printed domain records. make_impute_constant accepts that domain too, and make_impute_uniform_float replaces each missing float by a uniform draw from the bounds you pass, so that imputed values do not pile up at one point. Both output the domain without nan, which is the one the aggregators want. The stability of every step here is 1, as the last line shows. Preparing microdata does the same preparation on a whole table through Polars, inside the guarantee.


9.2.2 Clamping and resizing
Clamping pins every value into public bounds. A value below the lower bound becomes the lower bound, and a value above the upper becomes the upper. It changes nothing in between, so it costs no accuracy on data that already lie within the bounds, and it is what makes the sum’s sensitivity finite. Without a bound, one person could move a sum by any amount, and no finite noise could hide them. The bounds must come from public knowledge, such as a codebook, never from looking at the data, because a bound read off the data leaks it.
Resizing is the step with a stability of 2. It takes a target size and makes every vector that size: a shorter vector is padded with a constant, and a longer one is cut down by a random sample. It exists because some aggregators, the mean and the variance among them, must know how many rows they divide by, and the number of rows is itself private. The resize writes a size into the domain, which from then on OpenDP treats as public, and that size can be a guess, a released count or public knowledge. The stability follows from one case. Add one row to an input that was shorter than the target. The output gains that row and loses one padded row, so two rows changed for one.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
floats = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
clamp = floats >> dp.t.then_clamp(bounds=(0.0, 10.0))
print(clamp([-5.0, 3.0, 50.0]), clamp.map(1))  # [0.0, 3.0, 10.0] 1
resize = clamp >> dp.t.then_resize(size=5, constant=5.0)
print(resize([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]))  # [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 5.0]
print(resize.output_domain)  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 10.0], T=f64), size=5)
print(resize.map(1))  # 2
The documentation’s resize page shows by simulation what a wrong target does. A target below the true size throws rows away, which widens the spread of the mean that follows. A target above it pads with the constant, which pulls that mean toward it. Neither error appears in an error bar, because the size is treated as true. Nor can the resize warn you, since an error that depended on the true size would leak it. So spend a little budget on a count first, as the previous chapters did, because a count has a sensitivity of 1 and lands close to the truth.


9.2.3 Categories and bins
Categorical data go through three constructors that map between values and indices. make_find replaces each value by its position in a category list, and a value outside the list becomes a missing index, so an imputation follows and gives it the next index. make_find_bin turns a number into the index of the bin it falls in, given the bin edges, and make_index goes the other way, from an index back to a label.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
strings = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=str)), dp.symmetric_distance()
find = strings >> dp.t.then_find(categories=["A", "B", "C"]) >> dp.t.then_impute_constant(3)
print(find(["A", "B", "C", "A", "D"]))  # [0, 1, 2, 0, 3]
floats = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
bins = floats >> dp.t.then_find_bin(edges=[1.0, 2.0, 10.0])
print(bins([0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 15.0]))  # [0, 1, 2, 3]
label = bins >> dp.t.then_index(categories=["low", "mid", "high"], null="other")
print(label([0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 15.0]))  # ['low', 'mid', 'high', 'other']
counts = strings >> dp.t.then_count_by_categories(categories=["A", "B", "C"])
print(counts(["A", "B", "C", "A", "D"]))  # [2, 1, 1, 1]
print(counts.output_metric, counts.map(1))  # L1Distance(i32) 1
The aggregator that goes with them is make_count_by_categories. It counts how often each category occurs and appends a count of everything else, unless you turn that off with null_category=False. Its output is a vector of counts, so its output metric is a vector norm. The default is the \(L_1\) distance, which chains with Laplace noise, and the MO argument switches it to the \(L_2\) distance, which chains with Gaussian noise. Adding one row changes one count by one, so the stability is 1 in either norm.

title: 9  Transformations
text:
9.3 The sum
The sum is the aggregator everything else is built on, and its documentation page is a study in where sensitivity comes from. Start with integers in public bounds and no known size.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
bounded = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 10))), dp.symmetric_distance()
total = bounded >> dp.t.then_sum()
print(total([1, 2, 4]), total.map(1))  # 7 10
sized = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(-10, 10)), size=3), dp.symmetric_distance()
sized_total = sized >> dp.t.then_sum()
print([sized_total.map(d) for d in range(5)])  # [0, 0, 20, 20, 40]
Adding one row changes the sum by at most the larger of the two bounds in absolute value, here 10, and that is what map(1) reports. When the dataset’s size is public, you write it into the domain and the sum uses a tighter bound. Two datasets of the same size cannot differ by one row. The nearest neighbours differ by one row replaced, which is one removal and one addition, a symmetric distance of 2. A replacement changes the sum by at most the width of the bounds, and that is map(2). Odd distances round down, which gives the staircase in the last line. A distance of 1 maps to 0 because no two datasets of the same size are one row apart.
On the survey the same two calls read as follows. The vector is built once with Polars, and the chain clamps the hours into the codebook’s bounds, 0 to 98, and sums them.
def hours_usually_worked(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> list[int]:
    """The `HWUSUAL` column without nulls and without the code 99, as a list of ints."""
    kept = frame.filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL").is_not_null() & (pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99))
    return kept.select(pl.col("HWUSUAL").cast(pl.Int64)).collect()["HWUSUAL"].to_list()
def int_sum(size: int | None = None) -> dp.Transformation:
    """Clamp to the public bounds, then sum; with a size the domain says how many rows there are."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int), size=size), dp.symmetric_distance()
    return space >> dp.t.then_clamp(BOUNDS) >> dp.t.then_sum()
hours vector: 1,496,192 values
true sum: 56,315,594  true mean: 37.6393  true median: 37
int sum: value 56,315,594  map(1)=98  map(36)=3528
sized int sum: map(36)=1764  map(35)=1666
The privacy unit of this survey is one person, who appears at most 36 times, so every map on this page is read at an input distance of 36. Without a size the sensitivity is that many added rows of 98 hours each, which is 3,528 hours. With the size in the domain it is 18 replacements, which is half as much, and an odd distance of 35 rounds down to 17 replacements. The Polars filter that builds the vector runs outside OpenDP, as data preparation this chapter does not protect. Preparing microdata runs the same filter inside the guarantee, and Essential statistics releases this sum through the Context API.
Floats behave differently, for two reasons that the documentation’s sum page sets out. The first is rounding. Adding floats rounds each partial sum to the nearest representable number. So two datasets at distance 2 can have sums that differ by a little more than the width of the bounds, and the stability map adds a term for it.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
metric = dp.symmetric_distance()
sized = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(-10.0, 10.0)), size=1000), metric
print((sized >> dp.t.then_sum()).map(2))  # 20.00000000004426
unsized = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(-10.0, 10.0))), metric
print((unsized >> dp.t.then_sum()).map(1))  # 20.00000009313226
negative = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(-10.0, 0.0))), metric
print((negative >> dp.t.then_sum()).map(1))  # 10.00000009313226
print(dp.t.make_bounded_float_checked_sum(size_limit=100, bounds=(-10.0, 0.0)).map(1))  # 10.00000000000295
With a known size of a thousand rows the term is tiny, in the eleventh decimal place. The second reason appears when the size is unknown. Then the rounding error has no bound, so the float sum first truncates its input to at most \(2^{20}\) rows, a little over a million, by a random sample. Truncation changes the sensitivity analysis, because a neighbouring dataset with one more row may have to drop a random row to stay within the limit. The sensitivity therefore becomes the largest of the magnitudes of the bounds and their width. That doubles it for bounds symmetric about zero, as the second line shows, and changes nothing for bounds of the same sign, as the third line shows. The specialized constructor make_bounded_float_checked_sum lets you set the size limit yourself, and a limit of 100 shrinks the rounding term from the eighth decimal place to the twelfth.
The notebook’s examples are too small to show why the limit matters. The hours vector has 1,496,192 values, more than \(2^{20}\). A plain then_sum on it as floats keeps a random million of them and sums those. The result is about 70% of the true sum, as the one-run block at the end of the chapter shows. Nothing warns you. The privacy guarantee holds, because the sensitivity is right for the truncated computation, but the number answers a different question from the one you asked. The fix is a size limit above any size the data could have, from public knowledge, here four million rows, or the exact size in the domain when it is public.
def float_sum(size_limit: int | None = None) -> dp.Transformation:
    """The float sum: `then_sum` truncates to 2^20 rows; a size limit of your own lifts that."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
    clamped = space >> dp.t.then_clamp(FLOAT_BOUNDS)
    if size_limit is None:
        return clamped >> dp.t.then_sum()
    return clamped >> dp.t.make_bounded_float_checked_sum(size_limit=size_limit, bounds=FLOAT_BOUNDS)
float sum, size limit 2^20=1,048,576: map(36)=3528.0000009127
float sum, size limit 4,000,000: value 56,315,594  map(36)=3528.0000038179
Both sensitivities are 3,528 hours plus a rounding term, and the larger limit buys a larger term, in the sixth decimal place rather than the seventh. The term also depends on the summation algorithm, which the specialized constructors take as the S argument.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
pairwise = dp.t.make_sized_bounded_float_checked_sum(1_000, (0.0, 10.0), S="Pairwise<f64>")
sequential = dp.t.make_sized_bounded_float_checked_sum(1_000, (0.0, 10.0), S="Sequential<f64>")
print(f"{pairwise.map(0):.2e} {sequential.map(0):.2e}")  # 4.43e-11 4.44e-09
pairwise = dp.t.make_sized_bounded_float_checked_sum(1_000_000, (0.0, 10.0), S="Pairwise<f64>")
sequential = dp.t.make_sized_bounded_float_checked_sum(1_000_000, (0.0, 10.0), S="Sequential<f64>")
print(f"{pairwise.map(0):.2e} {sequential.map(0):.2e}")  # 8.85e-08 4.44e-03
The map at distance 0 isolates the rounding term, since two datasets with the same rows in a different order can already sum to different floats. The default is the pairwise sum, which adds the values as a balanced tree, so its term grows a little faster than the number of rows. The sequential sum adds the values one after another, and its term grows with the square of the number of rows. At a million rows the sequential term is 0.0044 against the pairwise 0.0000001. The reason to ask for the sequential analysis is a sum computed elsewhere, because database engines add floats in sequence, and a sensitivity claimed for their result must match how they add. Integer sums have no rounding term, which is one reason to cast hours to integers.
To release the integer sum, chain a Laplace measurement onto the chain. Its scale is the sensitivity over \(\varepsilon\), which the full edition’s chapter on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms derives. Each of the three measurements on this page is calibrated to \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) on its own, and composing them is the job of Combinators. At that budget the scale is 7,056 hours. The error bar is about 21,000 hours on a total of 56 million, which is 0.04%.
sum release: scale=7056  map(36)=0.5000  95% accuracy=21,138.4

title: 9  Transformations
text:
9.4 The mean and the variance
The mean is a sum divided by a size, and make_mean divides by the size in its input domain, not by the length of the data it is given. So the domain must carry a size, and without one the constructor refuses.
mean without a size: dataset size must be known. Either specify size in the input domain or use make_resize
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0.0, 10.0)), size=10), dp.symmetric_distance()
mean = space >> dp.t.then_mean()
print(mean([5.0] * 10), mean.map(2))  # 5.0 1.0000000000000169
print(mean([5.0]))  # 0.5
print(mean.input_domain.member([5.0]))  # False
With ten values between 0 and 10, replacing one value moves the mean by at most the width over the size, which is 1. That is map(2), up to a rounding term. The second print is the warning the documentation attaches to the mean. The mean of a one-element list came out as 0.5, because the division is by the size the domain declares, and nothing checks the data. A transformation assumes its input is a member of its input domain, and member checks that.
On the survey the size is not public, so the chain resizes first. The constant pads a vector that comes out short, and here it is the true median of 37 hours. A real release would resize to a released count, as A first release did, or to a public total. The script resizes to the true size, which is allowed here because the data are public, so nothing is padded.
def mean_chain(size: int, constant: float) -> dp.Transformation:
    """Clamp, resize to a known size (padding with the constant), then the mean over that size."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
    return space >> dp.t.then_clamp(FLOAT_BOUNDS) >> dp.t.then_resize(size=size, constant=constant) >> dp.t.then_mean()
mean chain: value 37.6393  map(36)=0.0023580
mean release: scale=0.0047160  map(36)=0.5000  95% accuracy=0.0141
Read the map against the sized sum. The sized sum’s map was 18 replacements of 98 hours, and dividing that by the size gives 0.0012. The mean’s map is twice that, because the resize in front of it is 2-stable. The input distance of 36 becomes an output distance of 72, which the mean reads as twice as many replacements. That is the price of not knowing the size, and it is paid once per chain. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the Laplace scale is 0.0047 hours, and the error bar is 0.014 hours.
The documentation’s mean page also shows the alternative, which it calls the plug-in approach: release a sum and a count separately and divide. The division is post-processing, so it costs nothing beyond the two releases, by the property that the full edition’s chapter on properties proves. The resize page compares the two by simulation and finds the resized mean tighter at the same budget, because its numerator and denominator agree on how many rows there are. The variance takes the same preprocessing and the same kind of map. On the resized chain then_variance gives 137.63 hours squared, with a stability of 0.2311 at distance 36, and a Laplace measurement would release it exactly as the mean.
variance chain: value 137.6290  map(36)=0.2311

title: 9  Transformations
text:
9.5 Quantile scores
A quantile is not a sum, and noise alone cannot release it. The documentation’s quantile page opens with the reason. Take a dataset in which half the values sit at the lower bound and half at the upper. Its median jumps from the middle of the range to the upper bound when one value is added, so the median’s sensitivity is half the range, and Laplace noise at that scale would drown it. Instead OpenDP scores every candidate quantile by how far it is from the truth and lets a selection mechanism pick one. That is the exponential mechanism of the full edition’s chapter on selection, and make_quantile_score_candidates computes the scores.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance()
median = space >> dp.t.then_quantile_score_candidates(candidates=[0, 25, 50, 75, 100], alpha=0.5)
print(median([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90]))  # [9, 5, 0, 5, 9]
print(median.output_metric, median.map(1))  # LInfDistance(T=u64) 1
quartile = space >> dp.t.then_quantile_score_candidates(candidates=[0, 25, 50, 75, 100], alpha=0.25)
print(quartile([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90]), quartile.map(1))  # [9, 1, 8, 19, 27] 3
The score of a candidate for the median is the difference between the number of values below it and the number above it, in absolute value. In the snippet the candidate in the middle has four values on either side and scores zero, while the lowest candidate has all nine above it. The lowest score marks the best candidate, which is why the selection in the next chapter is told to pick the minimum. For another quantile the two counts get weights. The quarter quantile weights the values below by three and the values above by one, so that the score is zero where a quarter of the data lie below. Its stability rises to 3, because one added row can move a weighted count by that much. The output metric is the \(L_\infty\) distance, since one row moves every candidate’s score at once, and that is the metric the noisy max measurement expects.
On the survey the candidates are every whole number of hours from 0 to 98.
def median_scores() -> dp.Transformation:
    """One score per candidate: how far it is from being the median; the lowest score is the best candidate."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance()
    return space >> dp.t.then_quantile_score_candidates(candidates=CANDIDATES, alpha=0.5)


def median_measurement(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Noisy max over the scores releases an index; `negate` makes the lowest score the one most likely to win."""
    return median_scores() >> dp.m.then_noisy_max(dp.max_divergence(), scale=scale, negate=True)
median scores: lowest 15,190 at 37 hours, next 89,573 at 36  map(36)=36
median release: scale=144  map(36)=0.5000  score gap=74,383  gap/scale=517
The lowest score is at 37 hours, the true median. The next best candidate is one hour less and scores worse by 74,383. The scores’ stability at distance 36 is 36. The measurement that turns scores into a quantile is the noisy max of Measurements. It adds noise to every score and reports the index of the best one. Its privacy map under the max divergence is twice the stability over the scale, so a scale of 144 gives \(\varepsilon = 0.5\). The released index names a candidate, which is post-processing. The gap between the two best scores is over five hundred times the scale, so the released median is 37 on essentially every run. The bundled make_private_quantile of the next chapter chains these same steps. Its scale is doubled before it reaches the noisy max for the median, so a private quantile at scale 72 is this chain at scale 144.

title: 9  Transformations
text:
9.6 Reading a chain
Two methods read a chain’s promise. map gives the stability, or the privacy loss once a measurement ends the chain, and check asks whether the promise at a given input distance stays within a bound. The sum chain’s map at 36 is 3,528, so check(36, 3528) is true and check(36, 3527) is false. Both cost nothing and touch no data. The context of the first chapter runs check in a loop to find the largest scale that fits a budget, and Utilities and the Context API inside shows that search.
int sum chain: check(36, 3528)=True  check(36, 3527)=False
The other thing to read is a refusal. The rule every chain obeys is that the output space of one step is the input space of the next, and >> checks it when the chain is built. The sum below is built on the vectors bounded by 0 and 100, then chained after a clamp to 0 and 98.
try:
    _ = clamped >> dp.t.make_sum(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 100))), dp.symmetric_distance())
    mismatch = "built"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    mismatch = f"{err.variant}: {err.message}"
mismatched chain: DomainMismatch: Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
    output_domain: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0, 98], T=i32))
    input_domain:  VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0, 100], T=i32))
The message names both spaces. The fix is to build the sum from the clamp’s output space, as make_sum(*clamped.output_space), or to use the then_ form, which does so for you. A metric mismatch reads the same way: an ordered sum needs the insert-delete distance, so it refuses to follow a clamp under the symmetric distance, and make_ordered_random between the two converts the metric. The third kind of refusal is a constructor whose input domain lacks what it needs, as the mean showed for a missing size and the sum shows for missing bounds.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance()
clamp = space >> dp.t.then_clamp(bounds=(0, 10))
try:
    clamp >> dp.t.make_bounded_int_ordered_sum(bounds=(0, 10))
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(err.variant)  # MetricMismatch
try:
    space >> dp.t.then_sum()
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(err.message)  # `input_domain` must be bounded. Use `make_clamp` to bound data.
Every refusal happens at construction, before any data are touched. Finally, the releases of one run, read against their error bars.
released (one run):
  sum 56,307,689  (true 56,315,594, within 21,138 with probability 0.95)
  float sum truncated to 2^20 rows 39,467,741  (true 56,315,594; about 70% of it)
  mean 37.6367  (true 37.6393, within 0.0141 with probability 0.95)
  median 37  (true 37)
The sum and the mean landed within their bars, as they should about 19 times in 20. The truncated float sum is not a noisy release but a wrong computation, short by 30% with no noise added, and no error bar covers it. The median is exact, as the gap between its scores said it would be.

Casacuberta, Shoemate, Vadhan and Wagaman, “Widespread Underestimation of Sensitivity in Differentially Private Libraries and How to Fix It” (2022): the rounding term and the truncation of the float sum.
Smith, “Privacy-Preserving Statistical Estimation with Optimal Convergence Rates” (2011): the quantile scores and their sensitivity.

The full edition’s chapters on sensitivity, the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, post-processing and composition and selection derive the results this chapter states.

title: 10  Measurements
text:
10.1 Additive noise
A transformation moves data to data and promises how far its output can move. A measurement is the step that ends the chain. It takes data and returns a random release, and its promise is a bound on how much the distribution of that release can change when one person’s data changes. The previous chapter, Transformations, built the deterministic half of a query. This chapter builds the random half, which is where the privacy guarantee actually comes from.
OpenDP ships a small catalogue of measurements, and every one of them is read the same way. Its input domain says what it accepts, and its input metric says how two inputs are compared. Its output measure says in which currency the privacy is counted, and its privacy map turns a distance between inputs into a bound in that currency. Once you can read those four things, you can calibrate any mechanism in the library and compare two mechanisms honestly. The chapter goes through the catalogue in the documentation’s order. It starts with the additive noise mechanisms and the canonical noise mechanism. Then come the thresholded mechanisms, which release counts for keys the data chose, and the approximate Laplace projection. It ends with the noisy max family, the private quantile built on it, and randomized response.
The script opendp_measurements.py builds every mechanism on this page on OpenDP 0.16.0 and prints its metric, its measure and its map. Two of them run on the Labour Force Survey (LFS): a thresholded count of the ILOSTAT categories and a private median of HWUSUAL. The rest take the documentation’s toy inputs. Every map, check, threshold, score and error message is the same on every run. The released values are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so they appear in one block marked as one run at the end.
The simplest measurement adds a random draw to a number. OpenDP offers two draws, and the choice between them is a choice of currency. The constructor make_laplace adds Laplace noise and counts privacy in the budget \(\varepsilon\) of pure differential privacy (DP), under the output measure MaxDivergence. The constructor make_gaussian adds Gaussian noise and counts privacy in the budget \(\rho\) of zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), under ZeroConcentratedDivergence. Both are built on the same space, so the input domain and the input metric do not decide which you get.
The map of the Laplace mechanism is the sensitivity divided by the scale, so a unit sensitivity at unit scale costs \(\varepsilon = 1\). The map of the Gaussian mechanism is the squared sensitivity over twice the squared scale, which at the same inputs gives \(\rho = 0.5\). The check method compares the map with a budget. A sensitivity of 2 does not fit within the budget that a sensitivity of 1 fits.
What the two currencies promise is different. Pure DP with parameter \(\varepsilon\) says that one person changes the probability of any release by a factor of at most \(e^\varepsilon\). Zero-concentrated DP with parameter \(\rho\) bounds the privacy loss on average and in its tails at once, which suits the Gaussian’s thin tails. Combinators converts a \(\rho\) into an \(\varepsilon\) with a slack \(\delta\). Assessing utility and choosing the noise weighs the two for a release. The full edition’s chapter on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms derives both maps.

title: 10  Measurements
text:
def scalar_mechanisms(scale: float) -> tuple[dp.Measurement, dp.Measurement]:
    """Laplace and Gaussian noise on one float; the input space is the same, the output measures differ."""
    space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
    laplace = space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=scale)  # output measure: MaxDivergence, read as epsilon
    gaussian = space >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=scale)  # output measure: ZeroConcentratedDivergence, read as rho
    return laplace, gaussian

laplace float: map(1.0)=1.0 measure=MaxDivergence
gaussian float: map(1.0)=0.5 measure=ZeroConcentratedDivergence
laplace float: check(1.0, 1.0)=True check(2.0, 1.0)=False


10.1.1 Integers, floats and vectors
The same constructors accept integers. On an integer domain, make_laplace draws from the discrete Laplace distribution and make_gaussian from the discrete Gaussian, so the release is an integer too. The maps are unchanged, and the sensitivity is an integer as well.
laplace int: map(1)=1.0 output type=int
gaussian int: map(1)=0.5
A vector input changes the metric. Laplace noise on a vector wants a bound on the L1 distance between two inputs, which is the sum of the absolute differences. That is because its map adds up the cost of every coordinate. Gaussian noise on a vector wants a bound on the L2 distance, the square root of the summed squares, because its cost adds up in squares. The constructor refuses a space whose metric does not match.
def vector_mechanisms(scale: float) -> tuple[dp.Measurement, dp.Measurement]:
    """The same two mechanisms on a vector of floats: Laplace wants an L1 bound, Gaussian an L2 bound."""
    domain = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False))
    laplace = (domain, dp.l1_distance(T=float)) >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=scale)
    gaussian = (domain, dp.l2_distance(T=float)) >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=scale)
    return laplace, gaussian
The maps read as before. Doubling the L2 sensitivity quadruples \(\rho\), which is the squared sensitivity showing through, while the Laplace map stays linear. Passing a plain float to a vector mechanism is a type error, and the message says what was expected.
laplace vector: metric=L1Distance(f64) map(1.0)=1.0
gaussian vector: metric=L2Distance(f64) map(1.0)=0.5
gaussian vector: map(2.0)=2.0 map(4.0)=8.0
laplace vector on a scalar: Expected type is Vec<f64> but input data is not a list.
gaussian on an L1 space: No match for concrete type L1Distance<f64>. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/451.


10.1.2 Why OpenDP rounds, and the parameter k
Floating-point noise is a known source of broken implementations. A computer cannot sample a continuous distribution, and the gaps between floats leak which input was used. OpenDP avoids the problem by never sampling a continuous draw. A float input is turned into an exact rational, integer noise is added to its numerator by the discrete distribution, and the result is rounded back to a float. That is the same as sampling true continuous noise and then rounding, which is post-processing, so the analysis stays exact.
The grid of that rational is \(2^k\), where the integer k is a parameter of the constructor. The default k is the smallest exponent a 64-bit float can express, so the grid is exact and costs nothing. A coarser grid samples faster. But rounding the input to the grid can move two neighbouring inputs apart by up to one extra grid step, so the map adds that step to the sensitivity. The script shows the penalty. At the default there is none, while a grid of a half adds a half to every map, even at zero sensitivity.
laplace k=-1074: map(0.0)=0.0 map(1.0)=1.0
laplace k=-1: map(0.0)=0.5 map(1.0)=1.5
laplace k=0: map(0.0)=1.0 map(1.0)=2.0
laplace k=1: map(0.0)=2.0 map(1.0)=3.0
laplace k on integers: k is only valid for domains over floats
Integers need no grid, so the constructor rejects k on an integer domain. Leave k alone unless a vector release is too slow, and if you change it, read the map again. The full edition explains the discrete distributions and why they are safe in its chapter on discrete mechanisms.


10.1.3 The geometric mechanism and make_noise
The constructor make_geometric is the Laplace mechanism restricted to integers, with one extra option. Passing bounds makes the sampler run in constant time, which closes a timing side channel, and it clamps the release into the bounds. On floats the constructor fails, because the geometric distribution has no float version.
geometric = int_space >> dp.m.then_geometric(scale=1.0)
bounded = int_space >> dp.m.then_geometric(scale=1.0, bounds=(0, 10))  # runs in constant time; clamps the output
geometric: map(1)=1.0 measure=MaxDivergence
geometric bounds (0, 10): map(1)=1.0
geometric on floats: No match for concrete type f64. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/451.
Finally, make_noise is the general constructor behind the two. You name the output measure, and the library picks the distribution that goes with it: Laplace for the max divergence and Gaussian for zero-concentrated divergence. It is the constructor to reach for in code that lets the caller choose the currency.
noise_pure = space >> dp.m.then_noise(dp.max_divergence(), scale=1.0)  # the Laplace mechanism
noise_zcdp = space >> dp.m.then_noise(dp.zero_concentrated_divergence(), scale=1.0)  # the Gaussian mechanism
make_noise MaxDivergence: map(1.0)=1.0 measure=MaxDivergence
make_noise ZeroConcentratedDivergence: map(1.0)=0.5 measure=ZeroConcentratedDivergence

title: 10  Measurements
text:
10.2 Canonical noise
The mechanisms above take a scale and tell you what it costs. The canonical noise mechanism works the other way round. You state the sensitivity and the budget, and it draws from the distribution that spends exactly that budget. Approximate DP relaxes the pure guarantee with a slack \(\delta\), the probability with which the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) may fail. For that guarantee the canonical distribution is the Tulap distribution, a discrete Laplace draw plus a uniform one. It is the noise that leaves the most powerful hypothesis test possible at a given budget. So it is the mechanism to use when a release feeds a statistical test or a confidence interval rather than a table.
def canonical_mechanism(d_in: float, epsilon: float, delta: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Canonical noise on one float, calibrated so that inputs at most d_in apart cost exactly (epsilon, delta)."""
    space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
    return space >> dp.m.then_canonical_noise(d_in=d_in, d_out=(epsilon, delta))
The map is a step rather than a line, because the calibration is fixed at construction. For any sensitivity up to the one you declared it returns the pair you declared. Above that sensitivity it refuses, since the mechanism was never calibrated for it. The check method behaves accordingly.
canonical noise: measure=Approximate(MaxDivergence)
canonical noise: map(1.0)=(1.0, 1e-07) map(0.5)=(1.0, 1e-07)
canonical noise: check(1.0, (1.0, 1e-07))=True check(1.0, (0.9, 1e-07))=False
canonical noise map(2.0): d_in from the map (2) must be in [0, 1]
The installed version supports only a scalar float input and only an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) budget. In the Context API the same mechanism is query.canonical_noise(). Passing binomial_size to it returns an object with confidence intervals and p-values for a binomially distributed count, which the documentation’s notebook walks through on a count of married people.

title: 10  Measurements
text:
10.3 Thresholded noise
A histogram over keys that come from the data has a problem that noise alone does not fix. If a category appears in the release at all, then someone in the data belongs to it. When that someone is one person, the key itself is the leak. The thresholded noise mechanisms release a dictionary of noisy counts and keep only the keys whose noisy count clears a threshold. A key with many contributors survives on either of two neighbouring datasets, so its presence says nothing about any one person. A key with one contributor survives only if its noise is huge, and the probability of that is what the slack \(\delta\) pays for. Grouping used this mechanism through Polars without naming it. This is what runs underneath.
The input domain is a map from keys to counts, and the input metric is a triple. The first entry bounds how many keys one person can touch. The second bounds the total change across all keys, in L1 for Laplace and in L2 for Gaussian. The third bounds the change to any one key.
def threshold_mechanisms(scale: float, threshold: float) -> tuple[dp.Measurement, dp.Measurement]:
    """Laplace and Gaussian noise on a dictionary of float counts, releasing only the keys whose noisy count passes."""
    domain = dp.map_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=str), dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False))
    laplace = dp.m.make_laplace_threshold(
        domain, dp.l01inf_distance(dp.absolute_distance(T=float)), scale=scale, threshold=threshold
    )
    gaussian = dp.m.make_gaussian_threshold(
        domain, dp.l02inf_distance(dp.absolute_distance(T=float)), scale=scale, threshold=threshold
    )
    return laplace, gaussian
The documentation’s example has a person who touches one key by at most one. At scale 1 the Laplace version prices that at \(\varepsilon = 1\) plus a \(\delta\). The \(\delta\) is the chance that a count one person can create clears the threshold by noise alone. The Gaussian version prices it in \(\rho\) with a far smaller \(\delta\), because its tails fall faster.
laplace threshold: metric=L01InfDistance(AbsoluteDistance(f64)) measure=Approximate(MaxDivergence)
laplace threshold scale 1 threshold 20: map((1, 1.0, 1.0))=(1.0, 2.8014e-09)
gaussian threshold scale 1 threshold 20: map((1, 1.0, 1.0))=(0.5, 1.1102e-16)
gaussian threshold: measure=Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence)
A smaller \(\delta\) is not a smaller cost, because the two maps are in different currencies. The script converts the Gaussian guarantee to approximate DP at the Laplace mechanism’s \(\delta\), with the combinators of Combinators. Then the honest comparison comes out the other way, and the Gaussian’s \(\varepsilon\) is about six times larger. The picture flips when a person touches many keys by a little, which is the case the second line prices. There the L2 bound is much smaller than the L1 bound, and the Gaussian wins.
gaussian threshold as approximate DP at delta=2.8014e-09: epsilon=6.3036
spread (100, 10.0, 0.001): laplace (0.1000, 1.0316e-07) gaussian epsilon=0.0500
Notice that the Laplace map charged a tenth rather than ten over one. A person who touches a hundred keys by at most a thousandth can change the total by at most a tenth. The library knows this, so it tightens the stated L1 bound to that product. Integer counts take the discrete distributions, as in the previous section. The general form is make_noise_threshold, which takes the measure as an argument. The installed version wants that measure wrapped as approximate, which its docstring does not say.
discrete laplace threshold scale 1 threshold 10: map((1, 1, 1))=(1.0, 3.3190e-05)
make_noise_threshold Approximate(MaxDivergence): map((1, 1, 1))=(1.0, 3.3190e-05)
make_noise_threshold MaxDivergence: output_measure must be MaxDivergence or ZeroConcentratedDivergence

10.3.1 Counts of ILOSTAT
The LFS codes each response’s labour status in ILOSTAT, and in this sample only four codes occur. Suppose you did not know which, so the keys must come from the data. The script counts the responses per code with Polars. Then it hands the dictionary to a thresholded Laplace mechanism over integer keys and integer counts.
def ilostat_counts(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dict[int, int]:
    """The number of responses in each ILOSTAT category, keyed by the category: the input of the thresholded count."""
    counts = frame.group_by("ILOSTAT").len().sort("ILOSTAT").collect()
    return {int(key): int(count) for key, count in zip(counts["ILOSTAT"], counts["len"])}


def ilostat_mechanism(scale: float, threshold: int) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Discrete Laplace noise on integer counts keyed by an integer category, with a threshold on the noisy count."""
    domain = dp.map_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.atom_domain(T=int))
    metric = dp.l01inf_distance(dp.absolute_distance(T=int))
    return dp.m.make_laplace_threshold(domain, metric, scale=scale, threshold=threshold)
A person answers at most 36 times. Without further public knowledge the triple is therefore 36 in every entry, since a person could touch that many keys by one each, or one key that many times. The scale is the sensitivity over \(\varepsilon\), which at a budget of 1 is 36. The error bar at that scale is about 108 responses. The threshold is then the only free choice, and it buys \(\delta\). The script prices three thresholds. Then it searches for the smallest one that keeps \(\delta\) under the chapter’s default of one in ten million.
ILOSTAT counts: {1: 1517011, 2: 155661, 3: 1450283, 9: 688977}
ILOSTAT d_in: (36, 36, 36) scale: 36 95% accuracy: 108.3
ILOSTAT threshold 500: map=1.0, delta=4.4835e-05
ILOSTAT threshold 1000: map=1.0, delta=4.1667e-11
ILOSTAT threshold 1500: map=1.0, delta=3.9968e-15
ILOSTAT smallest threshold with delta <= 1e-07: 720
ILOSTAT threshold 10: threshold (10) must not be smaller than l-infinity sensitivity 36
Every \(\delta\) comes from the same tail. It is the chance that the noise lifts a count one person can make alone, which is 36 at most, over the threshold. That chance is then taken over every key the person could create. Raising the threshold shrinks it fast. A threshold below the per-key sensitivity is refused outright, because one person could then create a key with no noise at all. Here the smallest count is in the hundreds of thousands, so a threshold of 720 drops nothing, and all four counts come back within their error bars. The threshold only bites on rare categories, which is exactly where it should. Why it costs a \(\delta\) and not an \(\varepsilon\) is derived in the full edition’s chapter on sensitivity, under partition selection.

title: 10  Measurements
text:
10.4 The approximate Laplace projection
Thresholding is one answer to unknown keys. The approximate Laplace projection is another. Instead of releasing a dictionary, it releases a compressed, hashed sketch of the whole key space. You then query the sketch for any key you like, including keys that never occurred. Nothing is dropped and nothing is listed, so no key leaks, and queries after the release are post-processing. The price is twofold. Answers are rounded to multiples of a parameter alpha, four by default, and two frequent keys can collide in the hash unless the sketch is large enough. Its size grows with two public bounds, total_limit on the sum of all counts and value_limit on any one count. The documentation’s example sets them for a table of first names.
def projection_mechanism(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """A private projection of counts keyed by strings; releases a queryable that answers for any key, known or not."""
    domain = dp.map_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=str), dp.atom_domain(T=int))
    metric = dp.l01inf_distance(dp.absolute_distance(T=int))
    return dp.m.make_alp_queryable(domain, metric, scale=scale, total_limit=50_000, value_limit=1_000)
One trap: here scale is not a noise scale but the privacy loss per unit of sensitivity, so a larger value spends more, not less. The map at unit sensitivity equals the scale, and it grows with the L1 entry of the triple.
alp scale 1: map((1, 1, 1))=1.0 measure=MaxDivergence
alp scale 2: map((1, 1, 1))=2.0
alp scale 1: map((2, 2, 1))=2.0
The documentation finds the scale for a budget with binary_search_chain, which Utilities and the Context API inside covers. On the toy table, the one-run answers at the end of the page land within a few units of the true counts. The name that is not in the table comes back near zero.

title: 10  Measurements
text:
10.5 Noisy max and selection
Not every release is a number. Often the question is which one: which category is largest, which candidate value is the median, which model is best. The noisy max mechanisms take a vector of scores, add noise to each, and release the index of the largest. Their input metric is the L-infinity distance, a bound on how much any single score can change. That is the right bound because the release depends on how the scores compare, not on their sum. As with additive noise, the output measure chooses the distribution: exponential noise under the max divergence, and Gumbel noise under zero-concentrated divergence.
def noisy_max_mechanisms(scale: float) -> tuple[dp.Measurement, dp.Measurement]:
    """Select the index of the largest score: exponential noise under pure DP, Gumbel noise under zCDP."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.linf_distance(T=float)
    exponential = space >> dp.m.then_noisy_max(dp.max_divergence(), scale=scale)
    gumbel = space >> dp.m.then_noisy_max(dp.zero_concentrated_divergence(), scale=scale)
    return exponential, gumbel
The map of the exponential version is twice the sensitivity over the scale, so at a scale of 2 a unit sensitivity costs \(\varepsilon = 1\). The factor of two is there because one person can raise one score and lower another at the same time. If the scores can only move in one direction, you declare the metric monotonic, and the factor goes away. The Gumbel version is the exponential mechanism of the theory, which picks a candidate with probability growing exponentially in its score. Its map is the square of that same ratio, divided by eight. Negating the scores selects the smallest, at no extra cost. The constructor make_noisy_top_k releases the best \(k\) indices in order, for \(k\) times the cost.

The older make_report_noisy_max_gumbel still exists and carries the pure-DP map. But the installed version marks it deprecated and points to make_noisy_max. The exponential mechanism, why selection costs twice what a count costs, and why exponential noise beats Gumbel under pure DP are in the full edition’s chapter on selection.

10.5.1 A private median of HWUSUAL
Selection is how OpenDP releases a quantile. The candidates are a list of possible answers, here every whole number of hours from 1 to 98. The transformation make_quantile_score_candidates from the previous chapter scores each one by how far it is from splitting the data in half. The best candidate has the smallest score, so the chain ends with a noisy max over negated scores. The released index is looked up in the candidate list afterwards, which is post-processing. The constructor make_private_quantile does the three steps in one call.
def hours_of_the_working(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> list[float]:
    """HWUSUAL for the people at work (ILOSTAT 1), keeping 1 to 98 hours: 0 means varying, 99 not applicable."""
    at_work = (pl.col("ILOSTAT") == 1) & pl.col("HWUSUAL").is_between(1, 98)
    return frame.filter(at_work).select("HWUSUAL").collect()["HWUSUAL"].to_list()


def median_by_hand(scale: float) -> tuple[dp.Transformation, dp.Measurement]:
    """The private median from its pieces: score each candidate, then pick an index by noisy max."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
    scores = space >> dp.t.then_quantile_score_candidates(candidates=HOURS, alpha=0.5)
    select = scores >> dp.m.then_noisy_max(dp.max_divergence(), scale=scale, negate=True)  # the smallest score wins
    return scores, select  # the released index is looked up in HOURS afterwards, which is post-processing


def median_mechanism(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The same median in one constructor."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
    return space >> dp.m.then_private_quantile(dp.max_divergence(), candidates=HOURS, alpha=0.5, scale=scale)
The data are the usual hours of the people at work, with the codes for varying and not applicable removed. A row filter keeps a person’s contribution at most 36 rows, so the input distance is still 36 under the symmetric distance. The scores are integers, and each one moves by at most the input distance, so their L-infinity sensitivity is 36.
HWUSUAL at work, 1 to 98 hours: n=1,490,113 true median=37
quantile scores: metric=LInfDistance(T=u64) map(36)=36
best candidate: 37 hours, score 9,111
second candidate: 36 hours, score 95,652
gap in noise scales: 1,202
scores >> noisy max scale 72: map(36)=1.0
make_private_quantile scale 36: map(36)=1.0
make_private_quantile zCDP scale 36: map(36)=0.125
Two scales appear because the one-step constructor doubles the scale you pass. The scores of a median are integers scaled by two, the denominator of one half. So make_private_quantile multiplies the scale by that same two before handing it to noisy max, and the two maps agree at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Read the scores before trusting the release. The best candidate beats the runner-up by over a thousand noise scales, so the mechanism returns 37 hours on practically every run, and the test checks for exactly that. On a smaller dataset the gaps shrink and the release starts to wander among nearby candidates. That wandering is the error you should expect from a private quantile.

title: 10  Measurements
text:
10.6 Randomized response
Every mechanism so far runs on a trusted server that holds the data. Randomized response runs on the respondent’s own device before the answer is sent, so that no server ever sees the truth. That is the local model of DP, in which the privacy unit is one answer. The metric is the discrete distance: two inputs are at distance 1 if they differ and 0 if they do not. OpenDP provides the randomizers only, and leaves the transport and the aggregation to you.
def randomized_response_mechanisms(prob: float) -> tuple[dp.Measurement, dp.Measurement]:
    """Randomized response on one yes/no answer and on one ILOSTAT category, each kept truthful with probability prob."""
    boolean = dp.m.make_randomized_response_bool(prob=prob)
    categorical = dp.m.make_randomized_response(categories=[1, 2, 3, 9], prob=prob)
    return boolean, categorical
The boolean version keeps the true answer with the probability you pass and flips it otherwise. Its map at distance 1 is the logarithm of the odds of telling the truth, so a probability of three quarters costs about 1.1. A probability below one half is refused, because the answer would then be more often false than true. The categorical version keeps the truth with the same probability and otherwise picks one of the other categories uniformly. Its map grows with the logarithm of the number of alternatives, so four ILOSTAT codes cost twice what a yes/no answer costs.
randomized response bool: domain=AtomDomain(T=bool) metric=DiscreteDistance() measure=MaxDivergence
randomized response bool prob 0.75: map(1)=1.0986 ln(0.75/0.25)=1.0986
randomized response bool prob 0.9: map(1)=2.1972
randomized response bool prob 0.4: probability must be within [0.5, 1]
randomized response 4 categories prob 0.75: map(1)=2.1972 ln(3*0.75/0.25)=2.1972
A single randomized answer is close to useless, and that is the point. The answers become useful in aggregate, after a correction for the known flipping rate, which the documentation derives for both versions. The third randomizer, for a bit vector, is the primitive behind RAPPOR, the first large deployment of local DP. The domain bounds how many bits can be set, and each bit is rerandomized with probability f. The map is then twice the weight times the logarithm of the odds of a bit surviving.
def bitvector_mechanism(f: float, max_weight: int) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Randomized response on a bit vector with at most max_weight ones, each bit rerandomized with probability f."""
    return dp.m.make_randomized_response_bitvec(dp.bitvector_domain(max_weight=max_weight), dp.discrete_distance(), f=f)
bit vector f=0.8 max_weight=3: domain=BitVectorDomain(weight=3) map(1)=2.4328 formula=2.4328
The script sends the documentation’s 24-bit vector through the randomizer ten thousand times. Then it runs debias_randomized_response_bitvec over the answers. The three set bits come back near ten thousand and the others near zero, with a spread of a few hundred. That is what the correction can do at that many reports. Local DP buys its trust at a steep price in accuracy, and the full edition’s chapter on trust models quantifies it.
The releases of the run behind this page close the chapter. The additive releases sit within a few units of 100, the thresholded count kept all four codes, the projection answered the unknown name with zero, and both medians are 37.

10.8 References

OpenDP documentation: “Measurements”, “Additive Noise Mechanisms”, “Canonical Noise Mechanism”, “Thresholded Noise Mechanisms”, “Approximate Laplace Projection”, “Report Noisy Max Mechanisms” and “Randomized Response” in the API user guide.
Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (2006): the Laplace mechanism.
Canonne, Kamath and Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (2020): the discrete Gaussian and the discrete Laplace samplers OpenDP uses.
Awan and Vadhan, “Canonical Noise Distributions and Private Hypothesis Tests” (2023): the Tulap distribution.
Rogers, “A Unifying Privacy Analysis Framework for Unknown Domain Algorithms in Differential Privacy” (2023): the thresholded mechanisms’ maps.
Aumüller, Lebeda and Pagh, “Differentially Private Sparse Vectors with Low Error, Optimal Space, and Fast Access” (2021): the approximate Laplace projection.
McKenna and Sheldon, “Permute-and-Flip: A New Mechanism for Differentially Private Selection” (2020): the exponential-noise noisy max.

Warner, “Randomized Response: A Survey Technique for Eliminating Evasive Answer Bias” (1965), and Erlingsson, Pihur and Korolova, “RAPPOR: Randomized Aggregatable Privacy-Preserving Ordinal Response” (2014).
The full edition’s chapters on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, selection, sensitivity and partition selection, discrete mechanisms and trust models derive the results this chapter states.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.1 Chaining
The previous two chapters built transformations and measurements one at a time. A real release is never one of them. It is a clamp, then a sum, then noise, then a second query that depends on the first. At the end it is reported as one guarantee of differential privacy (DP). The pieces that join measurements and transformations into bigger ones are the combinators. Each takes one or more objects of the framework and returns a new one, with a privacy map that says what the new object costs. You never add budgets by hand, because the combinator’s map does it, and it refuses to join pieces whose promises do not fit.
The chapter follows the documentation’s Combinators pages in order. Chaining joins a transformation to what comes after it. Composition releases several measurements on the same data, first all at once, then one at a time, then without deciding the budget of each in advance. Measure casting converts a guarantee between privacy measures, so that a Gaussian release can be reported with the privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) and the slack \(\delta\) of approximate DP. Amplification by subsampling reads a smaller guarantee for a sample of a larger population. By the end you will be able to read the privacy map of any chain, say why a context refuses a query, and convert a budget between measures.
The script opendp_combinators.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0. Its toy data are twenty integers from 0 to 10 drawn by a seeded generator. Its toy measurements are a Laplace count and a Laplace sum of the clamped values, as in the documentation. One example runs on the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample, where the number of queries in a composition changes the noise scale of a real sum. The maps, profiles, scales and error messages on this page are the same on every run. The released values are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so they appear in one block marked as one run.
The simplest way to combine two pieces is to run one after the other, and three constructors do that. make_chain_tt joins two transformations. make_chain_mt puts a measurement after a transformation, and make_chain_pm attaches a post-processing function to a measurement. There is no chainer for two measurements, because anything computed after a measurement is post-processing and needs no further accounting. The script builds the clamped sum and its Laplace release with the long forms first.
The outer piece comes first in each call and the inner piece second, as in function composition. Each constructor takes its input space from the output space of the piece before it. The chained transformation has a stability map, which Transformations introduced as the bound on how far the output moves when the input moves by a given distance. Adding or removing one record changes the clamped sum by at most the width of the bounds, so the map at distance 1 is 10. The chained measurement has a privacy map, which Measurements introduced, and it is the stability of the inner part divided by the noise scale. A sum that moves by 10 under Laplace noise of half that scale costs \(\varepsilon = 2\).
The >> operator chooses the right chainer for you, and it takes a then_ constructor on its right so that the input space never has to be repeated. Below is the same measurement in one line.
Post-processing is any computation on a release that does not touch the data again. It costs nothing, because whatever an adversary could learn from the processed value they could have learned from the release itself. The full edition’s chapter on properties proves that. In OpenDP you attach a Python function to a measurement with >>, and the result is a measurement with the same privacy map.
In version 0.16.0 this needs a second feature flag, honest-but-curious, which the script switches on just before the chain and off just after. The reason is that the library cannot inspect a Python function. A post-processor must not read global state, such as the clock, and must not raise an exception whose presence depends on the data. Either would open a channel from the data to the caller that the privacy map does not account for.
A chain only forms when the pieces fit. The output domain of the inner piece must equal the input domain of the outer one, and the same holds for the metrics. The script tries to feed a sum of floats into a Laplace mechanism built for integers, and the library refuses.
The second message comes from a count, whose output is an integer at an integer absolute distance, chained to a Laplace mechanism whose metric measures distances in floats. With a mismatched domain, the outer piece’s proof would cover inputs the inner piece never promised to produce. When you meet one of these errors, read the two lines it prints and insert the cast, clamp or impute step that makes them equal.
The sum and count that the rest of the chapter composes have the error bars below, which Assessing utility and choosing the noise explains how to read.

title: 11  Combinators

def chained_by_hand() -> tuple[dp.Transformation, dp.Measurement]:
    """The clamped sum and its Laplace release, built with the long-form chainers."""
    clamp = INT_SPACE >> dp.t.then_clamp(BOUNDS)
    total = dp.t.make_sum(clamp.output_domain, clamp.output_metric)
    clamped_sum = dp.c.make_chain_tt(total, clamp)  # a transformation: clamp, then sum
    laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(clamped_sum.output_domain, clamped_sum.output_metric, scale=SUM_SCALE)
    noisy_sum = dp.c.make_chain_mt(laplace, clamped_sum)  # a measurement: the chain, then noise
    return clamped_sum, noisy_sum
