title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.2 Non-adaptive composition
Suppose you want both the sum and the count of the toy vector. Running the two measurements on the same data spends both of their budgets, and the question is what the total is. Basic composition says that it is the sum of the parts. A release that is \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP followed by one that is \(\varepsilon_2\)-DP on the same data is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP, which the full edition’s chapter on properties proves. The combinator make_composition builds that rule into one measurement, which runs every part on the data and returns their releases as a list.
both = dp.c.make_composition([shortcut, count])  # one measurement that releases the sum and the count
print(f"composition: map(1)={both.map(1):.1f}  parts: {shortcut.map(1):.1f} + {count.map(1):.1f}")
composition: map(1)=3.0  parts: 2.0 + 1.0
composition output measure: MaxDivergence
The parts must agree on their input domain, their input metric and their output measure. That is because a composition is a statement about one dataset under one notion of neighbours and one way of measuring privacy. The sum and the count share all three. The composition is called non-adaptive because every part is fixed before any data are seen, so no part can depend on another’s answer.
The same combinator composes measurements in other measures, and the rule it applies is the measure’s own. Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) measures privacy by a single parameter \(\rho\), which bounds the Rényi divergence between the output distributions on neighbours at every order. Under zCDP the parameters add just as \(\varepsilon\) does, which the full edition’s chapter on concentrated DP derives. The Gaussian sum at scale 5 has \(\rho = 2\), the Gaussian count at scale 1 has \(\rho = 0.5\), and the composition reports their sum.
zCDP composition: map(1)=2.50  parts: 2.00 + 0.50
mixed measures: All output measures must be the same
The second line shows the check that stops you from mixing measures, because the maps of a Laplace count and of a Gaussian count return numbers that mean different things. Section 11.7 shows the combinators that bring them to a common measure first.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.3 Adaptive composition
Often you do not know the second query until you have seen the first answer. You release a count, and it tells you whether a mean is worth asking for. Composition still holds when each query is chosen after the earlier answers, as long as the budget of each is fixed in advance. The full edition’s chapter on composition proves this adaptive form. The combinator for it is make_adaptive_composition. Its constructor is more verbose than the non-adaptive one, because it cannot read the supporting elements off parts it has not seen yet.
def adaptive_compositor(d_mids: list[float]) -> dp.Measurement:
    """An adaptive compositor over the toy space: one share of pure-DP budget per query, fixed in advance."""
    return dp.c.make_adaptive_composition(
        input_domain=INT_SPACE[0],
        input_metric=INT_SPACE[1],
        output_measure=dp.max_divergence(),
        d_in=1,  # neighbours add or remove one record
        d_mids=d_mids,  # the epsilon each query may spend, in the order the queries arrive
    )
The argument d_in is the distance between neighbouring datasets, here 1 for adding or removing one record. The argument d_mids lists the privacy loss each query may spend, in order, and the privacy map of the compositor is their sum, here 3.
adaptive: map(1)=3.0
Invoking the compositor on the data does not release anything. It returns a queryable, which is a small state machine. It holds the data and the shares that remain, and it accepts a measurement as a query. It checks that the measurement’s map at d_in fits within the next share, and it answers with the measurement’s release. The script submits the sum, then tries the sum again, then submits the count.
queryable = compositor(data)  # the data go in once; what comes back answers measurements
adaptive_sum = queryable(shortcut)  # spends the first share, 2.0
try:
    queryable(shortcut)  # asks 2.0 of the second share, 1.0
    over_share = "answered"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    over_share = str(err.message)
adaptive_count = queryable(count)  # spends the second share, 1.0
second query over its share: insufficient budget for query: 2.0 > 1.0
third query: out of queries
The shares are consumed in order, so a query that asks for more than the next share is refused, and the share is not spent. After the count takes the second share, a third query of any size is refused as well. This is the object a context wraps. When A first release built a context with split_evenly_over=3, the library built an adaptive compositor with three equal shares and kept its queryable. The context’s accountant attribute is that compositor, and its d_mids are the shares. A release() is a submission to the queryable, and the refusal you saw there is the “out of queries” above, translated.
On real data the number of shares decides the noise of every query. The script builds two contexts over the LFS sample, one with the whole budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) on a single query and one split evenly over three. Both ask for the sum of HWUSUAL, the hours usually worked per week, with the code 99 for “not applicable” filtered out. The values are bounded to 0 to 80 hours. A person appears in at most 36 quarters, so the privacy unit is 36 contributions. The sum therefore moves by up to 36 times the upper bound when one person is added or removed.
LFS context over 1: accountant map(36)=1.0 d_mids=[1.0]
LFS HWUSUAL sum over 1: scale=2,881.04 95% accuracy=8,630.8
LFS context over 3: accountant map(36)=1.0 d_mids=[0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333]
LFS HWUSUAL sum over 3: scale=8,643.11 95% accuracy=25,892.4
true HWUSUAL sum: 56,315,594
Both accountants map the privacy unit’s distance to 1, because the shares always add up to the budget you declared. What changes is the scale the context finds for the query, which is the sensitivity over the share. Three shares triple the scale and the error bar. On a sum of about 56 million hours an error bar of 26 thousand is still small. On a small group it would not be. The scale sits slightly above the sensitivity over the share, because the sum of floats carries a rounding term that Transformations explains.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.4 Odometers
Adaptive composition fixes each query’s budget before the first answer. Sometimes even that is too early, because the answer to the first query decides how much the second one deserves. Fully adaptive composition lets the privacy loss of each query be chosen as you go. The object that tracks it is an odometer, a running total of the loss spent so far that stays valid at whatever point you choose to stop. The full edition’s chapter on adaptive composition shows why plugging adaptively chosen parameters into the ordinary theorems fails, and which running totals are valid. For pure DP the sum of the losses spent is one, and that is what OpenDP’s odometer reports.
odometer = dp.c.make_fully_adaptive_composition(
    input_domain=INT_SPACE[0], input_metric=INT_SPACE[1], output_measure=dp.max_divergence()
)
odometer_queryable = odometer(data)
loss_before = odometer_queryable.privacy_loss(1)  # nothing spent yet
odometer_sum = odometer_queryable(shortcut)
loss_after_sum = odometer_queryable.privacy_loss(1)
odometer_count = odometer_queryable(count)
loss_after_count = odometer_queryable.privacy_loss(1)
The constructor takes the same three supporting elements as the adaptive compositor but no d_in and no d_mids, because nothing about the budget is decided yet. What it returns is an Odometer, not a Measurement, and an odometer has no privacy map, because it makes no promise about the total. Invoking it on the data gives an odometer queryable. It answers measurements like the compositor’s queryable did, and it also reports privacy_loss(d_in), the total spent so far at the given input distance.
odometer loss: before=0.0 after sum=2.0 after count=3.0 after another count=4.0
odometer loss at d_in=2 after three queries: 8.0
The total starts at zero, grows by the map of each query as it is answered, and never refuses anything. The last line shows why the argument matters. At distance 2, each Laplace query costs twice as much, so the total doubles. The odometer answers “how much have I spent?” and leaves “may I spend more?” to you. That suits an open-ended exploration, but nothing stops the total from growing past what you may claim. The next combinator adds the stop.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.5 Privacy filters
A privacy filter is an odometer with a cap. It refuses any query that would take the running total past a bound fixed in advance. The total can then never exceed the bound, so the filter is a measurement with an ordinary privacy map. The full edition’s chapter on adaptive composition proves that for pure DP the cap on the sum of the realized losses is a valid guarantee. The combinator make_privacy_filter takes the odometer, the input distance and the cap.
privacy_filter = dp.c.make_privacy_filter(odometer, d_in=1, d_out=2.0)
filter_queryable = privacy_filter(data)
filter_count_1 = filter_queryable(count)
filter_count_2 = filter_queryable(count)
try:
    filter_queryable(count)  # would take the loss to 3.0
    refusal = "answered"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    refusal = str(err.message)
filter: map(1)=2.0
filter third query: filter is now exhausted: pending privacy loss (3.0) would exceed privacy budget (2.0)
filter loss after refusal: filter is exhausted: no more queries can be answered
The filter’s map at distance 1 is the cap, whatever queries later arrive, which is what makes it a measurement. Two counts at a cost of 1 each fit under a cap of 2, and the third is refused with a message that names the pending total and the budget. The installed version then treats the filter as finished. After one refusal, even privacy_loss raises, so read the running total before the query that might exhaust it, not after. Unlike the adaptive compositor, a filter needs no list of shares.
The filter is also what a context wraps when you give it a budget but no split. The script builds a context on the toy data with dp.loss_of(epsilon=2.0) and neither split_evenly_over nor split_by_weights. Its queryable is then an odometer queryable behind a filter, and current_privacy_loss reads the odometer. The script gives its count query an explicit scale, since there is no share for the context to search within.
context without a split: queryable=OdometerQueryable spent=1.0 remaining=1.0

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.6 Chaining and nesting compositors
Compositors and filters are measurements, so the chainers and the compositors apply to them too. Two patterns come up in practice. The first is a transformation before a compositor, which saves repeating the same preprocessing in every query. The script chains the clamped sum in front of an adaptive compositor, so that the compositor’s queries are measurements on the sum, a single integer, rather than on the vector.
sum_compositor = clamped_sum_only >> dp.c.then_adaptive_composition(
    output_measure=dp.max_divergence(),
    d_in=clamped_sum_only.map(1),  # the sum moves by at most 10 when one record changes
    d_mids=[2.0, 1.0],
)
sum_space = clamped_sum_only.output_domain, clamped_sum_only.output_metric
laplace_on_sum = sum_space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=SUM_SCALE)  # a query on the sum, not on the vector
transformation >> compositor: d_in=10 map(1)=3.0
laplace on the sum: map(10)=2.0
The one thing to get right is d_in. The compositor sits after the sum, so its input distance is the sum’s output distance, which is the stability map of the sum at the privacy unit’s distance, here 10. The then_ form takes the domain and metric from the transformation, but it cannot guess the distance, so compute it with map rather than typing it. A query to this compositor is checked at that distance, and a Laplace mechanism of scale 5 on the sum then costs 2, which fits the first share.
The second pattern is a compositor inside a compositor. The inner compositor is a measurement whose map is the sum of its shares, so it can be submitted as a query to an outer one. The answer is the inner queryable.
outer = adaptive_compositor(d_mids=[3.0, 1.0])
inner = adaptive_compositor(d_mids=[2.0, 1.0])  # a measurement costing 3.0: it fits the outer's first share
outer_queryable = outer(data)
inner_queryable = outer_queryable(inner)  # the answer to a compositor query is a queryable
inner_sum = inner_queryable(shortcut)
outer_count = outer_queryable(count)  # the outer's second share, while the inner queryable stays open
inner_count = inner_queryable(count)  # pure DP composes concurrently, so the inner one still answers
nested: outer map(1)=4.0 inner map(1)=3.0
The outer compositor charges 3 for the inner one, whatever the inner one later answers, because 3 is the inner map. The script interleaves the queries. It asks the inner queryable for the sum, the outer one for the count, and the inner one again for the count. That works because pure DP supports concurrent composition, where several queryables spawned from one compositor stay open at the same time. For approximate zCDP and approximate Rényi differential privacy (RDP) the library instead freezes an earlier queryable when a new query arrives, because post-processing has not been proved to hold there while an analyst can still interact with it. The documentation uses nesting to run a zCDP compositor inside an approximate-DP one, after casting the inner compositor’s measure with the combinators of the next section.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.7 Measure casting
Every measurement carries an output measure, and a composition needs all of its parts to carry the same one. A Laplace release is measured in pure DP, a Gaussian release in zCDP, and a report is usually wanted as \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). The casting combinators move a measurement from one measure to another, each by a conversion the full edition derives, so that the pieces can be composed.
The first conversion goes from pure DP to zCDP. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\), which the full edition’s chapter on concentrated DP proves, and make_pureDP_to_zCDP applies it to the map. make_approximate turns a pure-DP measurement into an approximate-DP one with a slack of zero. It can then be composed with measurements that have a real \(\delta\).
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
laplace = space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)
print(dp.c.make_pureDP_to_zCDP(laplace).map(1.0))  # 0.5
print(dp.c.make_approximate(laplace).map(1.0))  # (1.0, 0.0)
The conversion you will use most goes from zCDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), because that is how a Gaussian release is reported. A \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism satisfies approximate DP at every slack at once, with a privacy loss that grows as the slack shrinks. So the honest output of the conversion is not a pair but a curve, the privacy profile, which gives the smallest privacy loss for each slack and the reverse. make_zCDP_to_approxDP returns a measurement whose map is that curve, with the methods epsilon(delta) and delta(epsilon). The script builds a Gaussian mechanism with \(\rho = 0.1\), which the scale \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\) gives at unit sensitivity. It then reads the curve at a slack of one in ten million.
gaussian = FLOAT_SPACE >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=math.sqrt(1 / (2 * rho)))  # rho = 1 / (2 scale^2)
profile_measurement = dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(gaussian)
profile = profile_measurement.map(1.0)  # a curve, not a number
epsilon_at_delta = profile.epsilon(delta=delta)
delta_at_one = profile.delta(epsilon=1.0)
fixed = dp.c.make_fix_delta(profile_measurement, delta=delta)  # the curve at one delta: an (epsilon, delta) pair
gaussian: rho=0.1000
profile at rho=0.1: epsilon(delta=1e-07)=2.3484 delta(epsilon=1)=0.008933
simple conversion: 2.6391  improved conversion: 2.3484
fix_delta: map(1.0)=(2.3484, 1e-07)  measure=Approximate(MaxDivergence)
A budget of \(\rho = 0.1\) is \((2.35, 10^{-7})\)-DP. The third line compares that with the two conversions the full edition states. The simple one is \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho \ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{11.1}\] which gives 2.64 here. The improved conversion of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke minimizes a tighter expression over the Rényi order, and the script’s numerical minimum agrees with OpenDP to four decimals. So the library implements the improved conversion, which matters when you check its numbers against a paper that quotes the simple one. The full edition’s chapter on RDP conversions explains where the simple formula loses.
A curve cannot be composed with a pair, so make_fix_delta evaluates the curve at one \(\delta\) of your choice and returns a measurement whose map is the pair. Its output measure is then the approximate max divergence, the same as make_approximate produces, and the two can meet in a composition. The last casting combinator, make_fixed_approxDP_to_approxDP, goes the other way and turns a fixed pair back into a curve. For a pure-DP release cast with make_approximate, that curve is flat, since the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP at zero slack and therefore at every larger slack too.
approximate: map(1.0)=(1.0, 0.0)  measure=Approximate(MaxDivergence)
fixed to profile: epsilon(delta=1e-07)=1.0 epsilon(delta=0)=1.0
laplace count + gaussian count: map(1)=(6.6709, 1e-07)
The last line is the payoff. The Laplace count, which Section 11.2 could not compose with the Gaussian count, is cast with make_approximate. The Gaussian count is cast to a curve and fixed at the same slack, and make_composition accepts the two. The total privacy loss is large because a Gaussian count with \(\rho = 0.5\) is expensive at so small a slack. Casting makes a composition legal, not cheap. When the Gaussian parts dominate, account the whole release in zCDP and convert once at the end, as the practitioner edition’s release workflow does.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.8 Amplification by subsampling
The last combinator changes what a privacy map promises without changing the computation. Suppose your dataset is a simple random sample from a larger population, and nobody knows who was sampled. Then the release is more private with respect to the population than to the sample, because a person who may not be in the sample is harder to detect. The full edition’s chapter on subsampling derives this amplification and shows why the sampling scheme must match the neighbouring relation. Write \(n\) for the size of the sample and \(N\) for the size of the population. Under pure DP the amplified loss is \[\varepsilon' = \ln\!\Big(1 + \frac{n}{N}\,(e^{\varepsilon} - 1)\Big). \tag{11.2}\] The script prints it beside the library’s map. make_population_amplification needs a measurement whose input domain carries the sample size, because the ratio of the two sizes is part of the guarantee.
def sample_mean() -> dp.Measurement:
    """The Laplace mean of a sample of exactly SAMPLE values in [0, 10]: the domain carries the size."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0.0, 10.0), nan=False), size=SAMPLE), dp.symmetric_distance()
    return space >> dp.t.then_mean() >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=0.5)


def amplified_mean(population_size: int) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The same mean, with its guarantee read for the population the sample was drawn from."""
    dp.enable_features("honest-but-curious")  # the library cannot check that the data are such a sample
    return dp.c.make_population_amplification(sample_mean(), population_size=population_size)
sample mean: map(2)=2.0000
amplified, population 100: map(2)=0.4940  formula=0.4940
amplified, population 1000: map(2)=0.0619  formula=0.0619
amplifying an unsized domain: elements of the vector domain have unknown size
The maps are read at distance 2, because two datasets of the same fixed size differ by a swap of one record, which the symmetric distance counts as one removal and one addition. The mean of ten values in a range of 10 moves by 1 under a swap, and Laplace noise of half that costs \(\varepsilon = 2\). Read for a population of a hundred, the same release costs about 0.49, and for a population of a thousand about 0.06. The formula matches the library’s map, and the gain grows with the population. A measurement on a vector domain without a size is refused, as the last line shows.
The combinator needs the honest-but-curious flag, for the same reason as the Python post-processor. The guarantee is only true if the data really are a uniform sample of a population of the stated size, and if the sample’s membership is unknown to whoever reads the release. The library cannot verify either from the data, so the flag records that the claim rests on your word. Use the unamplified map when the sample was chosen in a way that depends on the people in it, or when the sampled identities are public.

OpenDP documentation: “Combinators”, “Chaining”, “(Non-Adaptive) Composition”, “Adaptive Composition”, “Fully Adaptive Composition and Odometers”, “Privacy Filters”, “Compositor Chaining and Nesting”, “Measure Casting” and “Amplification” in the API user guide.

Whitehouse, Ramdas, Rogers and Wu, “Fully Adaptive Composition in Differential Privacy” (2023): the fully adaptive composition theorem the odometer implements.
Haney, Shoemate, Tian, Vadhan, Vyrros, Xu and Zhang, “Concurrent Composition for Interactive Differential Privacy with Adaptive Privacy-Loss Parameters” (2023): why several queryables may stay open at once.
Bun and Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (2016): zCDP, its composition and the cast from pure DP.
Canonne, Kamath and Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (2020): the improved conversion from zCDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) that the privacy profile implements.
The full edition’s chapters on post-processing and basic composition, composition, concentrated DP, RDP conversions, subsampling and adaptive composition derive the results this chapter states.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.1 Types
Every query in this book so far ended with a call such as .laplace() that named no scale, and the context filled it in. This chapter shows what fills it in. The answer is a handful of utilities that the framework exposes on their own. Type descriptors say what kind of number a chain carries, a binary search turns a budget into a scale, and a serializer turns a measurement into text. The Context API is a thin layer over these utilities and over the combinators of the previous chapter. Once you can see the layer, you can predict what a query will do before you release it. You can also rebuild any part of it by hand when the layer refuses.
The chapter follows the documentation’s pages on typing, parameter search and serialization, then its page on the Context API and its comparison of the two APIs. It ends by taking apart the count query of the first chapter, piece by piece, and finding the same scale of 3. By the end you will be able to read a type error, run the search a context runs, and store a measurement and reload it. You will also be able to say which framework object each line of a Context API program creates.
The script opendp_utilities.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with Polars 1.36.1. Its plain-data queries use the first chapter’s hundred integers from a seeded generator, and its one Polars query counts the rows of the France Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample. The type descriptors, the error messages, the scales the searches find and the privacy maps are the same on every run. The released counts are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so they appear in one block marked as one run.
OpenDP’s core is written in Rust, and Rust has no single integer type. It has signed and unsigned integers of several widths, from 8 bits to 128, and floats of two widths. The library keeps that precision because the constants of a privacy proof depend on it. A sum of 32-bit integers can overflow where a sum of 64-bit integers cannot, and a float’s rounding error depends on how many bits it has. So every domain, metric and measure carries a type descriptor, and the library never casts one type to another on its own. The framework chapter introduced the descriptors as the T= arguments of the constructors. This section says how to write and read them.
A descriptor can be written in three ways, and the snippet shows that they agree. The canonical form is a string such as "i32" or "Vec<f64>". A Python type such as int, float, str or bool is an alias, and list[int] is an alias for a vector. The objects in opendp.typing, such as dp.i32, dp.f64 and dp.Vec[dp.i32], spell the same strings with completion in an editor.
The aliases hide one decision. A Python int means a 32-bit integer and a float a 64-bit float, which the script confirms. The function dp.RuntimeType.infer reads the type off a value in the same way. NumPy’s default integer has 64 bits, so an integer from an array arrives as i64 while a domain built with T=int expects i32, and the two do not meet. The function set_default_int_type changes what the alias means for the rest of the program, which is the clean fix when all your integers have 64 bits.
When the types do not meet, the error reads inferred type is XXX, expected YYY, and the troubleshooting page of the documentation gives it an entry. The script provokes it in the simplest way. It builds a Laplace mechanism on an integer domain with an integer metric, then asks for its privacy map at a sensitivity of 1.5.
The message names the type the library inferred from your argument and the type the metric expects, and the fix is to pass what it expects, here the integer 2. The second pair of lines shows the case you will meet most often. The count query’s input metric is the symmetric distance, whose distances are unsigned integers, so map(1.0) fails and map(1) succeeds. One more cause the documentation names is a scalar \(\varepsilon\) passed to a measurement whose measure expects a pair of \(\varepsilon\) and the slack \(\delta\) of approximate differential privacy. In 0.16.0 that case reads differently, so the script prints it too.
The chapter on limitations and troubleshooting collects the other errors you can meet. The rule for this one is short. Read the expected type, then change your argument, your bounds or your data to match it. Never change the domain to match the argument, because the library chose that type for the proof.

print(dp.atom_domain(T=float))  # AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64)

print(dp.Vec[dp.i32] == dp.RuntimeType.parse(list[int]))  # True

import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

print(dp.RuntimeType.parse(int))  # i32
print(dp.RuntimeType.infer(np.int64(1)))  # i64
dp.set_default_int_type(dp.i64)

print(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)))  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=i64))

laplace_int = int_space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)  # Laplace noise on a 32-bit integer

    laplace_int.map(1.5)  # a float sensitivity, on a metric whose distances are integers
    message = "no error"
except TypeError as err:
    message = first_line(err)

map(2) on an integer metric: 2.0
float d_in on the count: TypeError: inferred type is f64, expected u32
integer d_in on the count: 0.3333

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.2 Parameter search
A measurement has three kinds of parameter. The input distance d_in is the privacy unit’s bound, the output distance d_out is the budget, and the constructor’s own arguments include the noise scale. With every parameter fixed, check(d_in, d_out) answers whether the measurement stays within the budget, as the measurements chapter showed. The answer is monotone. If a scale passes at some budget, every larger scale passes too, and if a budget passes, every larger budget passes. A monotone yes-or-no function has one boundary, and a binary search finds it, so you can solve for any one parameter from the others.
The library wraps the search three ways. The first, dp.binary_search, takes a predicate on one number and returns the value nearest the boundary on the passing side. The second, dp.binary_search_param, takes a function that builds a chain from one number, with d_in and d_out, and uses check as the predicate. The third, dp.binary_search_chain, does the same and returns the chain built at the value it found.
import opendp.prelude as dp

print(dp.binary_search(lambda x: x >= 5.0))  # 5.0
print(dp.binary_search(lambda x: x > 5, T=int))  # 6
print(dp.binary_search(lambda x: x <= 5, bounds=(0, None)))  # 5
The three lines show the arguments that steer a search. Without bounds, the search first looks for them by stepping outwards from zero, which is why the first call needs nothing else. The type T says whether the parameter is a float or an integer when the predicate alone does not tell, and the integer search returns the first passing integer. A pair of bounds with None on one side gives a one-sided search. The script then runs the search a context runs, on the Laplace mechanism of the first chapter with a share of \(\varepsilon/3\).
scale = dp.binary_search_param(make_laplace, d_in=1.0, d_out=share)  # the smallest scale within the share
chain = dp.binary_search_chain(make_laplace, d_in=1.0, d_out=share)  # the measurement at that scale
largest_d_in = dp.binary_search(lambda d_in: make_laplace(1.0).check(d_in, EPSILON))  # the other way round
search: scale=3.0000000000000004 chain.map(1.0)=0.3333 chain.check(1.0, share)=True
search: largest d_in at scale 1 within epsilon 1: 1.0
search: gaussian scale for rho=1 at d_in=1: 0.7071
The scale is the smallest one whose map at a sensitivity of 1 stays within a third of \(\varepsilon = 1\). It comes out a hair above 3, because the search stops on the passing side of the boundary. That is the scale param() reported in the first chapter. The chain is the Laplace measurement at that scale, and its check confirms the budget. The third call turns the question round and asks for the largest sensitivity that a scale of 1 can hide within \(\varepsilon = 1\), which is 1. The Gaussian mechanism is measured in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), which states the privacy loss as a parameter \(\rho\). For Gaussian noise that loss is half the square of the sensitivity over the scale, so the same search for \(\rho = 1\) gives a scale of 0.7071. The full edition’s chapter on the two mechanisms derives both maps.
To see what the search does, the script writes it by hand. The predicate is check, the interval starts at 0 to 100, and each step keeps the half that contains the boundary.
def search_by_hand(passes: Callable[[float], bool], low: float, high: float, tolerance: float) -> tuple[float, int]:
    """Bisection on a predicate that fails at `low` and passes at `high`: the smallest passing value, and the steps."""
    steps = 0
    while high - low > tolerance:
        middle = (low + high) / 2
        if passes(middle):
            high = middle  # the boundary is at or below the middle
        else:
            low = middle  # the boundary is above it
        steps += 1
    return high, steps
search by hand: scale=3.000000 after 27 steps
search with bounds (0, 100): 3.0000000000000004
Twenty-seven halvings of an interval of 100 bring it below a millionth, and the passing end of the last interval is the scale. The library’s search on the same bounds lands on the float just above 3, so it bisects further than that tolerance. Two things go wrong with a search, and the script shows both messages.
search with bounds (0, 1): ValueError: the decision boundary of the predicate is outside the bounds
search on a constant predicate: ValueError: unable to infer bounds
Bounds that do not contain the boundary give the first error, so widen them. A predicate that never changes gives the second, and here it is a predicate that always passes. With a real chain it means that no value of the parameter changes the answer, so look at the chain before the bounds.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.3 Serialization
A measurement is a recipe. It names the constructors it was built from and their arguments, and dp.serialize writes that recipe as a JSON string, which dp.deserialize turns back into a measurement. The use is a split deployment. An analyst builds and inspects a query on a machine without the data, and sends the text to the machine that holds them. The script serializes the first chapter’s count measurement.
measurement = count_laplace(3.0)
text = dp.serialize(measurement)  # JSON that names each constructor and its arguments
restored = dp.deserialize(text)
same_space = restored.input_space == measurement.input_space
serialized: 2152 characters, starting {"__function__": "make_chain_mt",
restored: map(1)=0.3333 same input space: True
The text begins with the outermost constructor, the chaining of a transformation and a measurement, and nests the rest inside it. The restored measurement has the same input space and the same privacy map, so a reviewer who receives the text can check the guarantee before the data are touched. The format is JSON, but the documentation does not promise that it stays the same between versions, and it asks you not to write it by hand.
Two things do not survive. The first is the param attribute that a context attaches to a measurement whose scale it searched for, which a later section explains. It is a Python attribute rather than part of the recipe, so it is gone after a round trip. The second is anything with Python state that the constructors did not set, which includes a context, a query and a plugin built from a Python function.
param before a round trip: 3.0000000000000004
param after a round trip: None
serialize a context: OpenDP JSON Encoder does not handle instances of <class 'opendp.context.Context'>
A Polars query has its own route, because its plan is a Polars LazyFrame and Polars can serialize a plan to bytes. The method Context.deserialize_polars_plan takes those bytes and wraps them in a query on a context of its own. So a client can write the plan against the survey’s schema and the server can run it against the rows.
client = lfs_context(pl.LazyFrame(schema=frame.collect_schema()))  # the schema, but no rows
plan = client.query().select(dp.len(signed=True)).polars_plan.serialize()  # bytes
server = lfs_context(frame)  # the real data
query = server.deserialize_polars_plan(plan)
summary = query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
plan: 1792 bytes
plan on the server: scale=36.0 95% accuracy=108.3429
The client’s context holds an empty frame with the survey’s schema, and the server’s holds the file. Both state the privacy unit of 36 rows per person and the budget of the chapter on the data and the context. They must, because the plan carries the query but not the guarantee. The scale of 36 is the unit’s distance over the budget, and the error bar is about 108 rows on a count of millions. The release itself is in the block at the end of the chapter.
crumbs: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.4 The compositor behind a context
The rest of the chapter rebuilds the Context API from the combinators of the previous chapter. The constructor dp.Context.compositor builds one measurement, an adaptive composition over the data’s space, and calls it on the data. Adaptive composition takes a list of per-query budgets, the d_mids, and lets you submit one measurement per share. Each may be chosen after seeing the earlier answers, and the promise is that together they stay within the sum. The full edition’s chapter on composition proves that the budgets add. The script reads the context’s accountant and builds the same one by hand.
by_hand_accountant = dp.c.make_adaptive_composition(
    input_domain=SPACE[0],
    input_metric=SPACE[1],
    output_measure=dp.max_divergence(),
    d_in=1,  # the privacy unit's distance: one row added or removed
    d_mids=[share] * QUERIES,  # the shares, which add up to the budget
)
queryable = by_hand_accountant(data)  # answers measurement queries on the data, and keeps count
context accountant: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64)) SymmetricDistance() MaxDivergence
context d_in: 1  d_mids: [0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333]
context accountant map(1): 1.0000
by hand accountant map(1): 1.0000  queryable: Queryable(Q=AnyMeasurement)
d_mids by weights [1, 2, 1]: [0.25, 0.5, 0.25]
The domain was inferred from the data, a list of floats, and the metric and the measure are the halves of unit_of and loss_of that the first chapter printed. The privacy map of the composition at the unit’s distance is the whole budget, 1, from either construction. Calling the accountant on the data returns a queryable, an object that answers one measurement at a time and refuses when the shares run out. That queryable is what the context keeps. The data are inside it and nowhere else, which is why the first chapter told you to drop your own reference.
The shares come from split_evenly_over or split_by_weights, and the context does not divide the budget itself. It hands the weights to binary_search_param and scales them until the composition’s map at d_in meets the budget, which for pure differential privacy is the proportional split you would expect. Weights of 1, 2 and 1 give a quarter, a half and a quarter of \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.5 The query behind a release
context.query() returns a Query, an object that holds a chain and the share it must fit. On plain data it is a Query, and on a LazyFrame it is the LazyFrameQuery of the Polars chapters, built on the same machinery. The chain starts as the data’s space. Each method you call, such as count or laplace, looks up the constructor of that name and chains it on. So query.count() is space >> dp.t.then_count(), with the space supplied by the context. The script watches the chain change type.
query = plain_query(context)  # the chain is the data's space: a domain and a metric
counted = query.count()  # the chain is a Transformation
noisy = counted.laplace()  # no scale: the chain is a PartialChain, waiting for one number
is_partial = isinstance(noisy._chain, dp.PartialChain)
query chain: tuple -> Transformation -> PartialChain
partial chain: True
resolve a transformation: ValueError: Query is not yet a measurement or odometer.
The interesting step is laplace() without a scale. The query counts the arguments against the constructor’s signature and finds one missing. Instead of calling the constructor, it wraps it in a partial chain, a function from the missing number to the finished chain. Only one number may be missing at a time, which is why a second noise step without a scale fails below. A query that is still a transformation cannot be resolved into a measurement, which the third line shows.
resolve is where the number is found. It calls the partial chain’s fix, which runs binary_search with the predicate “the chain at this value checks within the query’s share”. That is the search of Section 12.2, and fix stores the value it finds on the measurement as param. So param() reports the scale the search found, and None when nothing was searched for.
param of .laplace(): 3.0000000000000004
param of .laplace(scale=3.0): None
two missing parameters: ValueError: gaussian is missing 1 parameter(s).
The script now runs the same search by hand on the same chain, and releases through the by-hand queryable.
by_hand_param = dp.binary_search_param(count_laplace, d_in=1, d_out=share)  # what resolve runs on the chain
by_hand_measurement = count_laplace(by_hand_param)
dp_count_by_hand = queryable(by_hand_measurement)  # what release does: the queryable runs the measurement
resolve: context param=3.0000000000000004 by hand=3.0000000000000004 equal=True
d_mids after context(measurement): [0.3333, 0.3333]
The two scales are not just close but equal, because they are the same search on the same predicate. release does two things with the resolved measurement. It passes the measurement to the context, which hands it to the queryable and records the share as spent, so the first share leaves d_mids. The by-hand version does the same with queryable(measurement), except that nothing records the spend. That bookkeeping is what the context adds, and the reason to use it.
crumbs: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.6 Nested compositors and other measures
Two features of the Context API are easier to understand once the chain is visible. The first is Query.compositor, which nests an adaptive composition inside one share. The query’s share becomes the inner budget, split again, and releasing the query returns a new Context rather than a number.
inner = plain_query(context).compositor(split_evenly_over=2).release()  # a Context inside one share
inner_scale = plain_query(inner).count().laplace().param()
inner context: d_in=1 d_out=0.3333 d_mids=[0.1667, 0.1667]
inner count scale: 6.0000
outer d_mids after the inner compositor: [0.3333]
The inner context has the outer share, a third of \(\varepsilon\), as its whole budget, and splits it in two, so a count inside it gets a scale of 6. The outer context counts the nested compositor as one query spent, whatever happens inside it, because the composition’s guarantee covers everything its queryable answers.
The second feature is a budget stated in one measure and a mechanism proved in another. The Laplace mechanism’s measure is the max divergence of pure differential privacy, and the Gaussian mechanism’s is zCDP. When the context’s measure differs, resolve casts the measurement with the converters of the combinators chapter before it checks the budget.
approx = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=data,
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=DELTA),  # approximate differential privacy
    split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
)
laplace_cast = plain_query(approx).count().laplace().resolve()  # pure DP, cast to approximate DP
gaussian_cast = plain_query(approx).count().gaussian().resolve()  # zCDP, converted and its delta fixed
approx share: (0.3333, 3.3e-08)
laplace under (epsilon, delta): Approximate(MaxDivergence) map(1)=(0.3333, 0.0e+00)
gaussian under (epsilon, delta): Approximate(MaxDivergence) map(1)=(0.3333, 3.3e-08)
param after a cast: None
Under an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) budget the Laplace mechanism is wrapped by make_approximate, which reports its loss as the pair \((\varepsilon, 0)\). The slack goes unused, and the search fits only the \(\varepsilon\) part. The Gaussian mechanism goes through make_zCDP_to_approxDP and make_fix_delta, which spend the share’s slack to convert \(\rho\) into an \(\varepsilon\). One side effect matters. The cast returns a new measurement that wraps the old one, so the param attribute sits on the inner measurement and param() reads None. To see the scale, run binary_search_param on the chain yourself, as the previous section did.
laplace under rho: ZeroConcentratedDivergence map(1)=0.0333
gaussian under rho: scale=3.8730
gaussian under epsilon: ValueError: Unable to cast measure from ZeroConcentratedDivergence to MaxDivergence
Under a \(\rho\) budget the Laplace mechanism is cast with make_pureDP_to_zCDP, and the Gaussian mechanism needs no cast, so its param() works and reports a scale of 3.873. The one direction that cannot be cast is a Gaussian mechanism under a pure \(\varepsilon\) budget, because zCDP never implies pure differential privacy, and the context says so instead of guessing. The full edition’s chapter on concentrated differential privacy derives the conversions behind each cast.
Finally the releases of one run, read against their error bars.
released (one run):
  survey rows 3811875  (true 3811932, within 108.3 with probability 0.95)
  count by hand 94  (true 100, within 9.4 with probability 0.95)
  count through the context 101  (true 100)
All three landed within their bars. The two counts of the hundred integers came from the same measurement, once through the by-hand queryable and once through the context, and differ only by their noise.

title: Extending the library
text:
The framework is open. Anything with a stability map or a privacy map can be a transformation or a measurement, whether OpenDP wrote it or you did. This part uses that openness. Its thread is that a plugin is only as private as its map. So the work of writing one is the proof, and the library’s job is to make everything around the proof safe, from chaining to accounting.
Plugins writes a transformation and a measurement in Python and registers constructors so that they work from the Context API. It then follows the documentation’s two larger examples, a Theil-Sen regression and a private choice of grouping columns. Statistical modelling fits the two models that ship with the library. One is a differentially private linear regression, and the other a differentially private principal component analysis. The chapter reads what each guarantees. Limitations and troubleshooting says what OpenDP does not promise, from floating-point arithmetic to side channels. It explains the feature flags that gate the less vetted parts, and it decodes the error messages you will meet most often.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




Plugins
How do I add my own transformation or measurement, and what must I prove about it?


Statistical modelling
How do I fit a private regression or a private principal component analysis with the library’s estimators?


Limitations and troubleshooting
What does the library not guarantee, and what does each common error mean?






By the end of this part you will be able to extend OpenDP with a mechanism of your own and fit its built-in models. You will also be able to say which parts of a deployment the library covers and which parts remain yours.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.1 Trust and the honest-but-curious flag
Suppose the mechanism you need is not in the library, such as a new estimator from a paper or a score that only makes sense for your data. The framework of the previous part was built for this case. A transformation is any function with a stability map, and a measurement is any function with a privacy map. So you can write both in Python and hand them to the library as plugins. From then on they chain, compose and run through a context like the built-in ones.
The one idea of this chapter is that a plugin is exactly as private as its map, and the library cannot check the map. Every built-in constructor comes with a written proof of its map, and for a plugin that proof is yours. So each example below shows its calls and then says in a sentence why its map is right, or where the documentation leaves that open. You will write a measurement, a transformation, and your own domains, metrics and measures, then register a constructor for the Context API. The chapter ends with the documentation’s two larger examples, a Theil-Sen regression and a private choice of grouping columns.
The script opendp_plugins.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0. Its regression runs on the documentation’s toy data, a hundred points on a line with normal noise from a seeded generator. Its choice of grouping columns runs on the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample. Every map, check, error message, score and candidate range on this page is the same on every run. The released values are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so they appear in one block marked as one run at the end.
The documentation gives two reasons for plugins. Differential privacy is a wide and growing field, so the library cannot ship every mechanism. And an idea is easier to try in Python than in Rust, so a plugin is how a contribution usually starts. Both reasons put a Python function at the heart of a guarantee, and that changes who is responsible for it.
The library can inspect its own constructors, but it cannot read a Python function. So it cannot tell whether your privacy map is right, whether your function has side effects, or whether it raises only when the data make it. The constructors of this chapter therefore need a second feature flag next to contrib, named honest-but-curious, and the name is the trust model it describes. Whoever writes the plugin is honest, in that the map they write is one they have proved, and the library guards only against curiosity from everyone downstream. Without the flag a plugin constructor refuses to build.
Each constructor’s docstring spells out the promise. Take any two inputs in the domain that are at most d_in apart under the input metric. Then the two output distributions must be at most privacy_map(d_in) apart under the output measure, the function must have no side effects, and the map must be pure. A wrong map breaks the guarantee silently, because everything downstream believes it. The context charges what the map reports, the composition adds up the maps, and the release goes out. The snippet is the extreme case, a measurement that returns its input and claims a privacy loss of zero.
The library accepts it, and a context would release the raw data at no charge. Nothing in the rest of this chapter protects you from this. The flag records that the claim rests on your word, and the sentence that justifies each map below is the habit that makes the word worth something.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
without the flag: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled

import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance()
leak = dp.m.make_user_measurement(*space, dp.max_divergence(), function=lambda x: x, privacy_map=lambda d: 0.0, TO=list[int])
print(leak.map(1))  # 0.0
print(leak([1, 2, 3]))  # [1, 2, 3]

title: 13  Plugins
13  Plugins
text:
13.3 A transformation plugin
A transformation plugin takes one more argument than a measurement, an output domain. Its map is a stability map, which bounds how far apart two outputs can be when the inputs are a given distance apart, as Transformations introduced. The documentation’s example repeats each record a fixed number of times.
def make_repeat(multiplicity: int) -> dp.Transformation:
    """The documentation's example: a transformation that repeats each record `multiplicity` times."""

    def function(arg: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        return arg * multiplicity

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> int:
        return d_in * multiplicity  # one added record of the input is `multiplicity` added records of the output

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)),
        input_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        output_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)),
        output_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
Both metrics are the symmetric distance, the number of records added or removed between two datasets. The map multiplies that distance by the multiplicity. Every input record becomes multiplicity output records, so adding or removing one input record adds or removes that many output records. The output domain is a second claim you make. Every output must belong to it, or the function must fail in a way that does not depend on the data. Here the output is a vector of integers whenever the input is.
The documentation chains the plugin between built-in steps, a cast from strings and a clamp before a sum, and ends with Laplace noise.
repeat 2: [1, 2] -> [1, 2, 1, 2] map(1)=2 map(3)=6
cast >> repeat 2 >> clamp (1, 2) >> sum: map(1)=4 on ['0', '1', '2', '3'] = 12
... >> laplace scale 1: map(1)=4.0
domain mismatch: DomainMismatch("Intermediate domains don't match
The stability of a chain is the product of the stabilities of its links, as Combinators explains. The cast and the clamp have stability 1, and the repeat has 2. The clamp bounds every value by 2, so one added input record, repeated twice, moves the sum by at most 4. Laplace noise of scale 1 then costs that much \(\varepsilon\). The last line is what happens when the cast produces floats instead. The plugin’s input domain is a vector of integers, and the library refuses the chain, because the spaces are its objects and it can compare them.
It cannot compare the function with the output domain, and that is the second way a transformation plugin goes wrong. The snippet declares that its output lies between 0 and 1 and then returns its input unchanged.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
ints = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int))
bounded = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 1)))
claim = dp.t.make_user_transformation(ints, dp.symmetric_distance(), bounded, dp.symmetric_distance(), function=lambda x: x, stability_map=lambda d: d)
print(claim([5, 6]))  # [5, 6]
print((claim >> dp.t.then_sum()).map(1))  # 1
The sum after it trusts the bounds and reports a sensitivity of 1, while the real sum moves by the whole value of a record. A wrong output domain is a wrong map one step later, so a transformation plugin needs two justifications, one for each.

title: 13  Plugins
section: 13.4 Your own domains, metrics and measures
text:
13.4 Your own domains, metrics and measures
Sometimes a plugin works on data the library has no domain for, such as a data frame or a graph, or compares neighbours by a metric it does not define. Three constructors let you name your own, and each carries its own promise.
A user domain is built from an identifier and a membership function. Two user domains are equal when their identifiers are equal, which is how the library decides whether two steps chain. So the identifier must name one set and nothing else, or two different domains would chain and break the stability of the chain. The membership function must return true only for members. A user distance is a metric that is nothing but a name, and giving it is a promise that the distance you have in mind is a pseudo-metric. It is zero from a point to itself, never negative and symmetric, and it obeys the triangle inequality. The snippet declares a domain of even integers and an edit distance on strings, and uses the distance in a transformation that measures a string’s length.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
even = dp.user_domain("EvenInts", member=lambda x: x % 2 == 0)
print(even.member(4), even.member(3))  # True False
edits = dp.user_distance("EditDistance")
length = dp.t.make_user_transformation(dp.atom_domain(T=str), edits, dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.absolute_distance(T=int), function=len, stability_map=lambda d: d)
print(length("hello"), length.map(1))  # 5 1
print((length >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)).map(1))  # 1.0
The stability map of the length is the identity, because one edit changes the length by at most one. The output metric is the absolute distance on integers, which is what the Laplace measurement wants. So the chain closes, and a scale of 1 costs an \(\varepsilon\) of 1 per edit.
A user divergence is a privacy measure of your own. The one property a measure must have is that post-processing cannot increase it, since the promise that a release stays private under further computation rests on it. The full edition’s chapter on properties proves that for the max divergence. Two more constructors complete the set. The function new_privacy_profile turns a curve from \(\varepsilon\) to the slack \(\delta\) into a privacy profile the library can invert. And new_function wraps a Python post-processor, which Combinators did behind the scenes for a bare function after >>. The post-processor must not read global state or raise on the data, because either would open a channel from the data to the caller that no map accounts for.
import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
renyi = dp.user_divergence("RenyiDivergence(alpha=2)")
rng = np.random.default_rng()
gaussian = dp.m.make_user_measurement(*space, renyi, function=lambda x: float(x + rng.normal()), privacy_map=lambda d: d**2, TO=float)
print(gaussian.map(1.0), gaussian.output_measure)  # 1.0 RenyiDivergence(alpha=2)
try:
    dp.c.make_composition([gaussian, gaussian])
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(str(err).split(". See")[0].strip())  # Type("No match for concrete type ExtrinsicDivergence
profile = dp.new_privacy_profile(lambda eps: 1.0 if eps < 0.5 else 1e-8)
print(profile.delta(epsilon=0.499), profile.epsilon(delta=1e-8))  # 1.0 0.5
double = dp.new_function(lambda x: 2 * x, TO=float)
laplace = space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)
print((laplace >> double).map(1.0))  # 1.0
The measurement adds standard normal noise and reports its loss under the Rényi divergence of order 2. Its map is the squared sensitivity, because the Rényi divergence of order 2 between two unit Gaussians is the square of the distance between their centres. The full edition’s chapter on Rényi differential privacy derives that. The map works, but the composition does not, because the combinators add up only the measures the library defines. So a plugin measure gets map and check and nothing more. The profile answers both ways, the slack at a given \(\varepsilon\) and the smallest \(\varepsilon\) at a given slack, and its curve must be decreasing. The post-processor leaves the Laplace measurement’s map unchanged, which is the point of post-processing.

title: 13  Plugins
section: 13.5 Registering a constructor for the Context API
text:
13.5 Registering a constructor for the Context API
A plugin built with the framework API is a loose measurement, and the lesson of A first release was to put every query through a context. The function dp.register adds a constructor to the Context API, as a method of context.query(). Two rules govern it. The constructor’s name must start with make_, and the method is the name without that prefix, unless you pass a name. And if its first two parameters are named input_domain and input_metric, the context fills them in. They come from the previous step’s output space, or from its own input space for a first step. The documentation calls that partial application, and it is the convention that gives every built-in make_ constructor its then_ form.
def make_anything_constant(input_domain: dp.Domain, input_metric: dp.Metric, constant: str) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The documentation's constructor for the Context API: it accepts whatever space the previous step outputs."""

    def function(_arg: Any) -> str:
        return constant

    def privacy_map(_d_in: Any) -> float:
        return 0.0

    return dp.m.make_user_measurement(
        input_domain, input_metric, dp.max_divergence(), function=function, privacy_map=privacy_map, TO=str
    )


dp.register(make_anything_constant)  # from now on, context.query().anything_constant(...)
The script builds the documentation’s context over three integers, with a privacy unit of 36 contributions and a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) split over two queries. Then it calls the plugin through it.
anything_constant: map(36)=0.0 release=denied
budget spent by the plugin query: [0.5]
clamp >> sum >> int_constant: release=denied
register twice: 'anything_constant' is already registered in the Context API. Please choose a different name.
register without make_: constructor.__name__ must start with 'make_', found select_cols
On the second line the plugin’s map is zero, but the context charged the query its full share of the budget. A context splits the budget before it sees a query and only checks that each query fits within its share, as Utilities and the Context API inside shows. A plugin that costs less than its share does not give the difference back. The third line uses the documentation’s other style, make_int_constant, without the two leading parameters. It registers too, but its input space is fixed to integers under the absolute distance, so it works after a clamp and a sum but not elsewhere. The documentation recommends the first style, with the caution that a constructor accepting any space should check that the space suits its function. The last two lines are the errors register raises, for a name already taken and for a name without the prefix.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.6 A Theil-Sen regression
The documentation’s first larger example fits a line through noisy points. Least squares is a poor private estimator, because one far-away point can move the fitted line by any amount. The Theil-Sen estimator takes the median of the slopes through pairs of points instead, and a median is a quantile, which OpenDP already releases privately. The documentation’s variant pairs the points at random and fits a line through each pair. It records where that line crosses two fixed vertical cuts, at a quarter and three quarters of the range of \(x\). The medians of the crossings at each cut are two points on the fitted line, which give the slope and the intercept. The library ships a vetted version of this estimator, which Statistical modelling uses, so this one is for learning how plugins combine.
The first plugin is the pairing, a transformation from a two-column array to a two-column array of predictions.
def pairwise_predict(data: NDArray[np.float64], x_cuts: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
    """Pair the rows at random, fit a line through each pair, and predict y at the two cut points."""
    data = np.array(data, copy=True)[: len(data) // 2 * 2]
    np.random.shuffle(data)
    p1, p2 = np.array_split(data, 2)
    dx, dy = (p2 - p1).T
    x_bar, y_bar = (p1 + p2).T / 2
    points = dy / dx * (x_cuts[None].T - x_bar) + y_bar
    return points.T[dx != 0]
The transformation wraps that function.
def make_pairwise_predict(x_cuts: NDArray[np.float64], runs: int = 1) -> dp.Transformation:
    """A transformation from the (x, y) rows to the predictions: one row per pair and run."""

    def function(arg: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
        return np.vstack([pairwise_predict(arg, x_cuts) for _ in range(runs)])

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> int:
        return d_in * runs  # each record sits in one pair, so it changes one prediction per run

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float),
        input_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        output_domain=dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float),
        output_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
The domains come from the library’s NumPy extension, a two-dimensional array with two columns. The documentation states the map, the input distance times the number of runs, without an argument, so here is the one it relies on. Each record sits in exactly one pair, so adding or removing a record changes at most one prediction per run. Two things make that claim weaker than a built-in map. The pairing is random, so the claim is really about a coupling of two runs rather than about a function. And the function drops the last record when the count is odd, so removing one record can also change another’s pair. This is the kind of gap the flag asks you to notice.
The second plugin selects one column of the predictions, and the library’s quantile does the rest.
def make_select_column(j: int) -> dp.Transformation:
    """Column j of the predictions as a vector; one row in is one row out, so the stability is the input distance."""

    def function(arg: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
        return arg[:, j]

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> int:
        return d_in

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float),
        input_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        output_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float)),
        output_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
The library’s quantile then runs once for each cut.
def make_private_medians(output_measure: dp.Measure, y_bounds: tuple[float, float], scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The private median of the predictions at each cut, by the library's quantile, composed."""
    median = dp.m.then_private_quantile(output_measure, candidates=np.linspace(*y_bounds, 100), alpha=0.5, scale=scale)
    return dp.c.make_composition(
        [
            make_select_column(0) >> dp.t.then_drop_null() >> median,
            make_select_column(1) >> dp.t.then_drop_null() >> median,
        ]
    )
Selecting a column keeps one row per row, so its stability is the input distance. The private quantile scores a hundred candidate values between the public bounds of \(y\) and picks one by noisy max, as Measurements showed. Its map is the input distance over the scale. The composition adds the two maps, by the basic composition rule of the full edition’s chapter on composition. The third piece solves for the line, which is post-processing of two released numbers and costs nothing.
def make_private_theil_sen(
    output_measure: dp.Measure, x_bounds: tuple[float, float], y_bounds: tuple[float, float], scale: float
) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Pair and predict, release the two medians, then solve for the slope and the intercept (post-processing)."""
    x_cuts = x_bounds[0] + (x_bounds[1] - x_bounds[0]) * np.array([0.25, 0.75])
    p_inv = np.linalg.inv(np.vstack([x_cuts, np.ones_like(x_cuts)]).T)  # the line through two points

    def to_coefficients(medians: list[float]) -> tuple[float, float]:
        slope, intercept = p_inv @ np.array(medians)
        return float(slope), float(intercept)

    return make_pairwise_predict(x_cuts) >> make_private_medians(output_measure, y_bounds, scale) >> to_coefficients
The script runs it with the documentation’s bounds and a scale of 1, on the toy points. Their true line has slope 2 and intercept 1.
theil-sen: x cuts -1.5 and 1.5, 100 candidates from -10.0 to 10.0 step 0.2020
pairwise predict: map(1)=1 medians: map(1)=2.0 theil-sen: map(1)=2.0 map(2)=4.0
toy data: n=100 least-squares slope=2.0573 intercept=1.0376
pairs: 50 medians at the cuts -2.2424 and 4.2857
selection bound: 26.2 score units at noise scale 2.0
cut -1.5: best candidate -2.3232 score 2; within the bound: -2.9293 to -1.5152 (8 candidates)
cut 1.5: best candidate 4.3434 score 8; within the bound: 3.3333 to 6.3636 (16 candidates)
The pairing has stability 1 and the two medians cost 2 together, so the whole estimator costs an \(\varepsilon\) of 2 per record. The least-squares fit of the toy is close to the truth, and the exact medians of the fifty pairwise predictions are the numbers the private medians aim at.
The last three lines are the bound the released medians are read against. The private quantile adds exponential noise of scale 2 to each candidate’s score and picks the best. The difference of two such draws is a Laplace draw of the same scale. So the chance that a worse candidate wins falls exponentially in its gap to the best, measured in scales. A union bound over the other 99 candidates gives the printed bound, which a losing candidate beats at most once in ten thousand runs. The candidates within the bound span about one and a half units of \(y\) at the lower cut and about three at the upper cut. The predictions there are more spread out, so neighbouring candidates score alike.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.7 Choosing grouping columns privately
The documentation’s second larger example solves a problem you meet before any grouped release. You want to group the rows by some columns before releasing counts, but you may not look at the data to choose them. Some columns are too uniform, with most rows sharing a value, and some are too diverse, with most rows having their own. Grouping by too many columns leaves most groups too small to survive the thresholds of Grouping. The example scores each candidate set by how many of its groups reach a public minimum of rows. It then picks a set with the exponential mechanism, which chooses a candidate with probability growing exponentially in its score. The full edition’s chapter on selection derives it.
The score is a transformation plugin, and it needs a user domain because the library has no domain for a whole data frame. The documentation scores a pandas frame, and the same score runs here on a Polars frame.
def score(frame: pl.DataFrame, columns: tuple[str, ...], min_rows: int) -> float:
    """How many groups of these columns have at least `min_rows` rows."""
    return float(frame.group_by(list(columns)).len().filter(pl.col("len") >= min_rows).height)
The transformation applies it to every candidate set.
def make_grouping_cols_score(
    input_domain: dp.Domain, input_metric: dp.Metric, candidates: list[tuple[str, ...]], min_rows: int
) -> dp.Transformation:
    """A transformation from the frame to one score per candidate set of grouping columns."""
    dp.assert_features("contrib")

    def function(frame: pl.DataFrame) -> list[float]:
        return [score(frame, columns, min_rows) for columns in candidates]

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> float:
        return float(d_in)  # one row changes one group's size, so it moves each score by at most 1

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=input_domain,
        input_metric=input_metric,
        output_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)),
        output_metric=dp.linf_distance(T=float),  # not monotonic: a person's rows may be added and removed
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
The output metric is the L-infinity distance, the largest change in any one score, because noisy max compares scores rather than summing them. The map is the identity on the input distance, and the reason is that one row belongs to one group of each candidate. Adding or removing it changes that group’s size by one, so it moves each score by at most one, and d_in rows move each score by at most d_in.
The documentation declares the metric monotonic, which halves the cost of noisy max. That is right when neighbours differ by one row added or one removed, since every score then moves the same way. Here the privacy unit is a person with up to 36 rows, and a neighbouring dataset can add some of them and remove others. The scores can then move both ways, so the script keeps the metric plain and pays the factor of two. The full edition’s chapter on sensitivity is where these bounds come from.
The measurement chains the scores into noisy max and names the chosen candidate, and it is registered so that a context can run it.
def make_select_grouping_cols(
    input_domain: dp.Domain, input_metric: dp.Metric, candidates: list[tuple[str, ...]], min_rows: int, scale: float
) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Score the candidates, pick one by the exponential mechanism, and name its columns."""

    def name(index: int) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return candidates[index]  # post-processing: the index is already private

    scores = make_grouping_cols_score(input_domain, input_metric, candidates, min_rows)
    return scores >> dp.m.then_noisy_max(dp.max_divergence(), scale) >> name


dp.register(make_select_grouping_cols)


def frame_domain() -> dp.Domain:
    """A domain for a Polars DataFrame: the library has none, so membership is a Python check."""

    def member(value: object) -> bool:
        return isinstance(value, pl.DataFrame)

    return dp.user_domain("PolarsDataFrameDomain", member=member)
On the survey the candidates are every non-empty subset of six columns. Five are SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER and AGE, and the sixth is the person identifier PIDENT. This sample codes age in seven bands. A group counts when it has at least 100 rows, a public choice standing in for the smallest group worth a noisy count. The context is built over the collected frame with the user domain passed as domain, a privacy unit of 36 contributions and a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\). The registered method is called with the scale left out, so that the context searches for it against the plugin’s map.
LFS: 3,811,932 rows; candidate columns SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE, PIDENT; 63 candidate sets
distinct values: SEX 2 ILOSTAT 4 YEAR 9 QUARTER 4 AGE 7 PIDENT 1,682,306
score: groups of at least 100 rows
rank 1: SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE score 996 of 1,105 groups
rank 2: ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE score 504 of 570 groups
rank 3: SEX, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE score 432 of 470 groups
sets with PIDENT: 32, largest score 0
select scale 72: map(36)=1.0 monotonic would be 0.5
context query: param scale=72.0
within 910 of the best: 10 candidates
The scores are computed at development time, which is allowed because the survey is public, and they show the shape the documentation describes. The five columns without the identifier score best, with most of their groups above the minimum, and the next set scores about half of that. Every set that includes PIDENT scores zero, because no person has a hundred rows. The map of the selection is twice the sensitivity over the scale, so a scale of 72 costs an \(\varepsilon\) of 1, and the context’s search lands on that scale.
The bound follows the same reasoning as for the medians, with exponential noise at scale 72 and a union bound over 62 other candidates. A set that scores more than 910 below the best therefore wins at most once in ten thousand runs, and ten sets lie within that bound. The best beats the runner-up by 492, under seven noise scales, so it wins most runs, but any of the ten can appear. That spread is the price of the person-level unit on data with few, coarse columns. A person can move each score by 36, while the scores themselves are only in the hundreds. Raising the minimum group size lowers every score and brings the candidates closer together, until the choice is nearly random, and spending more budget is the only other lever.
released (one run):
  python laplace of 10.0: 9.6979  (within 6.0 with probability 0.95)
  repeated sum of ['0', '1', '2', '3'] with laplace scale 1: 13  (true 12)
  theil-sen: slope 2.1549 intercept 1.1111  (medians at the cuts -2.1212 and 4.3434)
  grouping columns: SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE
The Python Laplace landed within its error bar, and the repeated sum within one of the truth. Both private medians fell inside their candidate ranges, so the slope and the intercept land near 2 and 1. The chosen grouping columns are the five that score best, and your run can differ in each of these.
