title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.9 References

OpenDP documentation: “Plugins”, “Measurement example”, “Transformation example”, “Context API Plugins”, “Thiel-Sen Regression” and “Privately Selecting Grouping Columns” in the API user guide.
Theil (1950) and Sen, “Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall’s tau” (1968): the estimator behind the regression example.
McSherry and Talwar, “Mechanism Design via Differential Privacy” (2007): the exponential mechanism behind noisy max.
Gaboardi, Hay and Vadhan, “A Programming Framework for OpenDP” (2020): the maps a plugin must satisfy.
The full edition’s chapters on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, composition, selection and sensitivity derive the results this chapter states.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.1 A model or a table?
Every release so far has been a table of statistics, such as a count, a sum, a mean or a quantile per group. Often the question is about a relation instead. How many hours do people actually work for each hour they usually work? Which directions of a numeric table carry its variance? OpenDP ships two models for such questions, a differentially private linear regression and a differentially private principal component analysis (PCA), both with interfaces modelled on scikit-learn. The one idea of this chapter is that a fitted model is a release like any other. Behind each fit is a measurement with a privacy map, and the map, not the argument named epsilon, says what the fit costs.
You will fit the regression on the documentation’s generated points and on the Labour Force Survey (LFS), and read its privacy loss from its measurement. You will see what the estimator targets and why its sensitivity is bounded. You will fit the PCA on the documentation’s generated table and compare its release with NumPy’s exact decomposition. Then you will meet the NumPy domain and the clamp underneath both estimators, and finish with the questions a reviewer should ask about a private model.
The script opendp_statistical_modelling.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with scikit-learn 1.8.0. Its toys come from a seeded NumPy generator, and the seed also fixes how the regression pairs its rows. So the exact fits, the bounds, the cut points and every privacy map are the same on every run. The released fits are not, because the private medians and the PCA’s noise come from OpenDP’s cryptographic generator, which cannot be seeded. They appear in one block marked as one run.
The documentation’s page on statistical modelling makes one point before it shows any code. When you know which relation you need, a model tailored to it spends the whole budget on the few numbers that answer the question. A slope costs two private medians, as the next section shows. A table fine enough to read the slope off would cost a noisy count in every cell. The same holds for the PCA, which releases a handful of directions rather than a full covariance matrix.
The flexible alternative is synthetic data. A synthetic copy of the table answers any later question, including ones nobody has asked yet, and it can be handed to people who need microdata. The price is accuracy. A statistic computed from a synthetic copy is less accurate than the same statistic released directly under the same budget, because the copy had to serve every question at once. AIM and MST generates such copies. So release a table when the questions are counts, a model when the question is a relation, and synthetic data when the questions are not yet known.
The two models are narrow on purpose. The regression takes one explanatory column and one response, and the PCA takes a numeric table whose rows can be bounded in length. A model with many explanatory variables is trained by the methods of the full edition’s chapter on private empirical risk minimization, which OpenDP does not ship.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.2 Linear regression
A least-squares line is a poor thing to release directly. Its slope is a ratio of sums whose sensitivity is unbounded unless both columns are clipped, and clipping changes the line. The estimator OpenDP ships is a Theil-Sen regression, which rests on medians instead. It pairs the rows at random, fits the line through each pair, and reads each line at two fixed cut points on the x axis. At each cut point it then releases the median of those readings with a private quantile. Finally it solves the two released medians for a slope and an intercept, which is post-processing and costs nothing more.
The sensitivity is bounded because of how the private median chooses. It scores every candidate on a fixed grid by how many readings lie on either side of it. The exponential mechanism then picks a candidate with a probability that favours high scores. One person’s row sits in one pair, so it moves one reading, and that changes any candidate’s score by at most one. How far the reading moved never enters, which is why the estimator needs no clipping and survives a person who reports a thousand hours. The full edition’s chapter on selection derives the exponential mechanism and the private quantile. Its chapter on sensitivity explains why a count of readings is the right quantity to bound.
def make_regression(
    x_bounds: tuple[float, float], y_bounds: tuple[float, float], scale: float, runs: int = 1
) -> dp.sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression:
    """The private Theil-Sen regression under pure differential privacy, with public bounds on x and y."""
    return dp.sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression(
        dp.max_divergence(),  # the output measure: the privacy loss is read in epsilon
        x_bounds=[x_bounds],  # fixes the two cut points, a quarter and three quarters of the way across
        y_bounds=y_bounds,  # the range over which the candidate medians are spread
        scale=scale,  # the noise scale of each of the two private medians
        runs=runs,  # how many random pairings to pool; each multiplies the privacy loss
    )
The first argument is the output measure. Here dp.max_divergence() asks for pure differential privacy (DP), whose parameter is the privacy loss \(\varepsilon\). The bounds are public information, and they never clip the data. The x bounds only fix where the two cut points go, at the fractions fraction_bounds of the way across, a quarter and three quarters by default. The y bounds only fix the grid of candidates_count evenly spaced candidates from which each median is chosen, a hundred by default. The scale is the noise scale of each private median, and runs repeats the random pairing and pools the readings. The documentation also builds this estimator from plugins, which Plugins follows.
regression space: NPArray2Domain(num_columns=2, nan=True, T=f64) SymmetricDistance() MaxDivergence
regression map: scale=1 runs=1 -> epsilon=2.0
regression map: scale=2 runs=1 -> epsilon=1.0
regression map: scale=2 runs=3 -> epsilon=3.0
The estimator’s measurement is reachable as its measurement attribute, and it reads like any other. Its input is a two-column NumPy array under the symmetric distance, so the privacy unit is a row. Its map at distance 1 is therefore the privacy loss for adding or removing one row. Two medians at scale 1 cost \(\varepsilon = 2\), and doubling the scale halves it. Three runs at scale 2 cost \(\varepsilon = 3\), because a row then sits in three pairs and moves three readings. More runs make the median better defined, but at a fixed budget they force a larger scale, so the gain is rarely worth it on a large dataset.
The documentation’s toy is a hundred points with a true slope of 2 and an intercept of 1, drawn here by a seeded generator. The script prints the deterministic things to read a fit against.
toy: n=100 cut points=[-1.5, 1.5] candidate step=0.2020
toy least squares: slope=2.0275 intercept=0.9725
toy median line, no noise: slope=2.0379 intercept=1.0786 readings=50
The candidate step is the y range divided into 99 intervals, about 0.2 here. The cut points are 3 apart, so moving one median by one grid step changes the slope by about 0.07, before any noise is added. The median line is what the estimator would return with exact medians and the seeded pairing, from the 50 readings that 100 points give. It is close to least squares here because the noise in the toy is symmetric. The released fit is in the last section.

14.2.1 Actual hours against usual hours on the survey
The survey question is how many hours people actually worked in the reference week for each hour they usually work. The script takes the people working in the fourth quarter of 2013 whose usual and actual hours are both recorded. The survey codes hours from 0 to 98, so the bounds of both columns are public. The code 99 means “not applicable” and is dropped. A person can appear more than once in a quarter, so the script keeps each person’s first row, and the privacy unit of the fit is one person. That step and the row filter run in Polars before the array reaches the measurement, so the library does not account for them. A row filter keeps neighbouring datasets neighbouring, and keeping one row per person is the truncation of Identifier truncation. Here both are your claim rather than the library’s.
survey: working people in 2013 Q4 with hours recorded: 36,914 (one row each)
survey: of them with 0 actual hours that week: 4,109
survey: bounds=(0.0, 98.0) cut points=[24.5, 73.5] candidate step=0.9899
survey least squares: slope=0.8582 intercept=-0.1935
survey median line, no noise: slope=1.0000 intercept=0.0000 medians=[24.50, 73.50]
survey readings: 16,463 pairs; within one candidate step of the medians: 5,606 and 5,252
The two exact fits disagree, and the disagreement is the lesson. Among the 36,914 people, 4,109 worked no hours at all that week, through leave or illness. So least squares is pulled toward them, and it gives 0.86 actual hours per usual hour. The median line ignores them, because most pairs of people lie on the line where actual equals usual. So its medians at the cut points are the cut points themselves, and its slope is exactly 1. A private Theil-Sen fit therefore estimates the typical relation, not the average one, and the median line is the exact value to compare it with. The last line counts the readings, which are fewer than half the people because a pair with equal usual hours has no slope. Thousands of them lie within one grid step of each median.
model = make_regression(HOURS_BOUNDS, HOURS_BOUNDS, scale=REGRESSION_SCALE)
epsilon = model.measurement.map(1)  # the privacy loss for adding or removing one person's row
survey_slope, survey_intercept = fit_regression(model, hours, seed)
survey private fit: scale=2 epsilon=1.0
The fit at scale 2 costs \(\varepsilon = 1\) for one person. The fit method takes the explanatory column as a two-dimensional array and the response as a vector, like scikit-learn. It returns a fitted scikit-learn LinearRegression, so coef_, intercept_ and predict work as usual.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.3 Principal component analysis
A PCA finds the directions along which a table varies most. OpenDP’s version releases three things under one budget. The first is the mean of the rows, the second the singular values, which say how much variance each direction carries, and the third the components, which are the directions. The algorithm follows Amin and others (2019). It scales every row into a ball of radius row_norm, centres the rows on a privately estimated mean, and forms the matrix of sums of squares and cross-products. It releases that matrix’s eigenvalues with Laplace noise, since replacing one row moves their sum by at most twice the squared row norm. It then draws the eigenvectors one at a time from a distribution that favours directions of high variance, which is the exponential mechanism on the sphere. After each draw it projects the matrix away from the drawn direction.
That is why two facts must be public. The row norm is the sensitivity of the whole algorithm, and every map below is in units of it. The number of rows is part of the domain. It makes neighbouring tables tables of the same size with one row replaced, which is distance 2 under the symmetric distance, and it gives the mean a known divisor. Both are declared, not checked, as the reviewer’s section shows. The budget is split in three equal parts, for the mean, the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, and the eigenvectors’ part is split again over the number of eigenvectors drawn.
The table is the documentation’s. Ten thousand centred rows of four columns are drawn from a normal distribution with a random covariance, here from a seeded generator so that the exact decomposition is reproducible.
pca table: 10,000 rows x 4 columns, row length mean=8.53 max=36.56
pca table: rows longer than 1: 99.9%  longer than 40: 0.0%
pca exact, raw rows: singular values=[901.9, 278.6, 222.2, 156.9]
pca exact, rows clamped to 1: singular values=[80.48, 40.67, 34.29, 26.29]
pca exact, rows clamped to 1: first component=[-0.614, -0.534, -0.526, -0.247]
The documentation fits with row_norm=1.0, and the first line says what that means here. Almost every row is longer than 1, so the clamp scales almost every row onto the unit sphere. The singular values the algorithm can estimate are then those of the clamped table, about 80 rather than about 900 for the first. The directions survive the clamp, because scaling a row does not turn it, so the first component of the clamped table is the one to compare the release with. A row norm of 40 clamps nothing, and the script fits with it too, to show the other side of the trade.
def make_pca(epsilon: float, row_norm: float, n_components: int | None = None) -> dp.sklearn.decomposition.PCA:
    """The private PCA of the generated table, with the two public facts the algorithm needs."""
    return dp.sklearn.decomposition.PCA(
        epsilon=epsilon,
        row_norm=row_norm,  # public: every row is scaled into a ball of this radius before anything else
        n_samples=PCA_ROWS,  # public: the exact number of rows, which fixes the domain
        n_features=PCA_COLUMNS,
        n_components=n_components,  # None releases every component
    )
pca = make_pca(PCA_EPSILON, ROW_NORM)
measurement = pca.measurement()  # the measurement behind fit(), for its map and for compositors
pca.fit(table)  # the private release: the mean, the singular values and the components
pca model: PCA(epsilon=1.0, n_components=4, n_features=4, n_samples=10000, row_norm=1.0)
pca space: NPArray2Domain(size=10000, num_columns=4, nan=True, T=f64) SymmetricDistance() MaxDivergence
pca map: map(2)=2.0 map(1)=2.0 check(2, 1.0)=False check(2, 2.0)=True
make_private_pca unit_epsilon=1: map(2)=1.0 map(1)=1.0
pca n_components=2: map(2)=2.0
pca composition of epsilon 1 and 0.5: map(2)=3.0
Read the third line twice. The model was built with epsilon=1.0, but its measurement’s map at distance 2, which is one replaced row, is 2.0. The check call confirms that the fit does not stay within \(\varepsilon = 1\). The reason is in the constructor. The PCA class calls the framework’s make_private_pca with twice its epsilon, divided by n_changes, the number of rows one person may change. And make_private_pca with a unit budget of 1 has a map of 1.0 at distance 2, as the fourth line shows. So in version 0.16.0 a PCA(epsilon=1.0) fit costs \(\varepsilon = 2\) per changed row by its own map, and the map is what you should quote. The map is also flat below distance 2, because the algorithm is an adaptive composition declared at that distance, which Combinators explains.
Asking for two components leaves the total unchanged, as the fifth line shows. What changes is inside. The library draws at most one eigenvector fewer than there are columns, since the last direction is determined by the others. So the eigenvectors’ third is split over three draws for four components and over two draws for two, and each draw gets a larger share. The measurement() method exists for the compositors of the same chapter. The last line composes a fit at epsilon=1.0 with one at epsilon=0.5, and the maps add to 3.0 at distance 2. Calling the measurement on the table fits the model and returns it.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.4 The NumPy domain underneath
Both estimators live on dp.numpy.array2_domain, the domain of two-dimensional NumPy arrays. Its members are described by a number of columns, an optional number of rows and the element type. Optionally they also have a norm, its order p and an origin, which say that every row lies within that norm of the origin. A domain with a norm is a promise about the data, and make_np_clamp is the transformation that makes the promise true.
import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
rows = dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float)
clamp = dp.numpy.make_np_clamp(rows, dp.symmetric_distance(), norm=1.0, p=2, origin=np.array([1.0, 2.0]))
print(clamp(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [4.0, 6.0], [1.5, 2.0]])).tolist())  # [[1.0, 2.0], [1.6, 2.8], [1.5, 2.0]]
print(clamp.map(1))  # 1
print(clamp.output_domain)  # NPArray2Domain(origin=[1. 2.], norm=1.0, p=2, num_columns=2, nan=False, T=f64)
The clamp leaves the first and third rows alone, because they lie within distance 1 of the origin. It pulls the second row from distance 5 back to the sphere, along the line to the origin. Its stability map is the identity, since clamping each row on its own neither adds nor removes rows. Its output domain records the norm, the order and the origin, and that no value is missing. Transformations reads stability maps in general.
That output domain is what make_private_pca would rather receive. A domain built with the norm and the origin states that the rows are already bounded around a known centre. The algorithm then skips the private mean and its third of the budget.
bounded domain: NPArray2Domain(origin=[0. 0. 0. 0.], norm=1.0, p=2, size=10000, num_columns=4, nan=True, T=f64)
pca on the bounded domain: map(1)=0.50 map(2)=1.00 map(4)=2.00
The script passes an explicit split as a PCAEpsilons, with half for the eigenvalues, a sixth for each of three eigenvectors and nothing for the mean. The map is then linear in the distance rather than flat, because no compositor is declared in between. Use this route when the centre is public, for instance when the columns are scores on a known scale, and the class when it is not.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.5 What a reviewer should ask
The first question is the privacy unit. Both estimators count rows, so the claim “one person” holds only if each person has one row, which on the survey was your own Polars step. The second is the bounds. The regression’s bounds and the PCA’s row norm and row count must come from the code book or the domain, never from the data. A bound read off the data leaks it. The third is which features are on, since a feature is a statement about what you accept on trust.
regression without honest-but-curious: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled
pca without honest-but-curious: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled
pca without idealized-numerics: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "idealized-numerics", but not enabled
regression without idealized-numerics: constructed
pca with n_samples one short of the table: fitted without complaint
Both estimators need honest-but-curious, because both are built from user-defined transformations whose functions and stability maps are taken as written. The regression’s pairing step, for example, claims that one row moves runs readings, and the library records that claim rather than proving it. The PCA also needs idealized-numerics, which concedes that its proofs hold for real arithmetic and not for floating point. Every guarantee of the PCA rests on that concession. The eigenvalues, their sensitivity and the eigenvector sampler are all computed in floating point, and the library’s own source notes that it knows no floating-point-safe sampler for the eigenvector draw. The regression constructs without the flag, because its private medians run in the Rust core and only the pairing is Python.
The last line is the reviewer’s trap. The number of rows is part of the PCA’s domain, but the library does not check that the array has that many rows. A wrong n_samples is therefore a wrong guarantee that nothing reports. The row norm, by contrast, is enforced by the clamp, and the regression’s bounds need no enforcing because its sensitivity does not depend on them. Limitations and troubleshooting collects the other things the library does not check.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.6 The releases of one run
released (one run):
  toy private fit: slope=1.9529 intercept=1.0101
  survey private fit: slope=1.0101 intercept=-0.9899
  survey private fit at 35 usual hours: 34.36 actual
  pca row_norm=1: singular values=[80.48, 40.66, 34.28, 26.37]
  pca row_norm=1: |cos| with exact components=[1.000, 0.998, 0.996, 0.996]
  pca row_norm=1: mean=[0.001, 0.002, 0.001, 0.001]  explained variance ratio=[0.648, 0.165, 0.117, 0.070]
  pca row_norm=40: singular values=[906.8, 268.6, 212.6, 153.2] (exact [901.9, 278.6, 222.2, 156.9])
  pca row_norm=40: |cos| with exact components=[0.996, 0.659, 0.426, 0.086]
  pca n_components=2: returned the model: True  singular values=[80.41, 40.64]
  pca n_components=2: |cos| with exact components=[0.999, 0.999]
The toy fit is off the least-squares line by about one grid step at one cut point, which is what a private median on 50 readings at \(\varepsilon = 2\) gives. The test allows the slope within 0.3 of the least-squares slope and the intercept within 0.5. That is about three grid steps at either cut point. A candidate three steps from the best one scores lower by every reading in between, and the exponential mechanism makes such a candidate rare at this budget.
The survey fit is the same on every run. The medians sit exactly at the cut points, and the nearest candidates on the grid give a slope of 1.0101 and an intercept of about \(-1\). Thousands of readings lie within one grid step of each median, so the next candidate on the grid scores thousands of readings worse than the best one. Noise at scale 2 never overturns a gap that large. The error of the fit is therefore the grid, not the noise, and a finer candidates_count would remove it at no cost in privacy. The test allows the slope within 0.1 of the median line and the intercept within 4 hours of it, which is two grid steps at the lower cut point. The fit predicts about 34.4 actual hours for someone who usually works 35.
The PCA at row norm 1 recovers the singular values of the clamped table to within a tenth and all four directions to a cosine above 0.99. Its private mean is within a few thousandths of the true zero. The test allows each singular value within 1 of the exact one and each cosine above 0.9. Both bounds leave a wide margin, because the eigenvalues’ Laplace noise is a few units against eigenvalues in the thousands and the four directions are well separated.
At row norm 40 the singular values are the raw table’s, within a few percent, but only the first direction is right. The eigenvector sampler’s concentration falls with the square of the row norm, so a norm of 40 leaves little of it, and the last three directions are close to random. The test checks only the first singular value, within 30, and the first cosine, above 0.9. The two-component fit returns the model itself, and its two directions are as good as the four-component fit’s first two.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.1 What OpenDP does not promise
Every chapter so far has shown what OpenDP guarantees. This one shows where the guarantee stops, and what to do when the library stops you. The one idea is that the guarantee covers exactly what passes through a measurement whose proof has been checked. The arithmetic that proof assumes, the code that runs before the data reach the context, and the channels an attacker can watch besides the output are yours to account for. Most of the library’s refusals exist to keep you on the right side of that line, so an error message is usually the guarantee doing its job.
The chapter follows the documentation’s page on limitations, its feature listing and its troubleshooting page. You will read what the library does not promise and what each limit means for a deployment. Then you will switch each feature flag off and on to see what it gates. You will mark out what lies outside the guarantee, and meet the error messages of the earlier chapters again, each with its cause and its fix. By the end you will be able to read an OpenDPException, and to say what a reviewer verifies before trusting a release made with OpenDP.
The script opendp_limitations.py reproduces every message on this page with OpenDP 0.16.0 and Polars 1.36.1. It uses tiny lists for the framework calls and the France Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample behind a context for the Polars ones. The messages, the sensitivities, the scales and the error bar are the same on every run. The one released count is not, because OpenDP draws its noise from a cryptographic generator that cannot be seeded. It appears at the end in a block marked as one run.
The documentation’s limitations page names five things, and each changes something about how you deploy the library. The first is arithmetic. A privacy proof in the literature is a statement about real numbers, but a computer adds floating-point numbers, which round. Casacuberta, Shoemate, Vadhan and Wagaman studied what that does to a sum in “Widespread Underestimation of Sensitivity in Differentially Private Libraries and How to Fix It” (2022). Several libraries computed the sensitivity of a sum as if the arithmetic were exact. The rounding made the true sensitivity larger, so the noise was too small and the stated \(\varepsilon\) was wrong. The full edition’s chapter on discrete mechanisms shows the older attack on the Laplace sampler itself, where the low-order bits of a float reveal which dataset produced it.
OpenDP’s answer is to put the rounding into the proof. The script builds a float sum and an integer sum of values between 0 and 80 with the framework API of Transformations. It then asks each for its sensitivity when 36 rows are added or removed.
In exact arithmetic both would be 36 times 80. The float sum’s map adds a small term for the error of rounding floats as they are added, and the integer sum’s does not, because integers add exactly. The term is tiny here, but it grows with the number of rows. That is why a float sum on the LFS needs a public bound on that number (Essential statistics). Where a component still assumes exact arithmetic, the library puts it behind the idealized-numerics flag, which the next section tries. The rule for a deployment is to prefer integer statistics where you can. Where you cannot, read a float statistic’s scale as the library computes it rather than as the formula predicts.
The second limitation is side channels. OpenDP has not been hardened against them, so the time a query takes, the memory it uses and the cache lines it touches may depend on the data. An attacker who can time the system that runs OpenDP may learn something the output does not say, and no proof in the library covers that. The deployment question is therefore who can interact with the running system. An analyst who submits queries through a queue and reads results later is in a different position from one with a shell on the machine. Keep the second kind out, or accept that the guarantee is weaker than the \(\varepsilon\) you record.
The third is vetting. Every component of OpenDP is meant to come with a written proof and a review of that proof, and until the review is finished the component needs the contrib flag. The documentation says plainly that the process is expected to find bugs in code and in proofs. So a release made with contrib on, which is every release in this book, rests on proofs that are written but not yet checked by a second reader. Record which components a release used, so that you can revisit it if one is corrected.
The fourth is stability. OpenDP follows semantic versioning, so until 1.0.0 its interfaces may change between minor releases. When they do, the release notes say how to migrate. Pin the version, as this book pins 0.16.0, and keep a test that reruns your release code. Then an upgrade that changes a default is caught before it changes a number. The fifth is software quality. Like any project OpenDP has bugs, and its issue tracker is where to report one. But no deployment can rule out an unknown bug, so the practical answer is the one the practitioner edition gives in Release and governance. Keep a record of the run from which the guarantee can be recomputed, and a plan for what reopens a release.

text:
def sum_sensitivities(d_in: int) -> tuple[float, int]:
    """The sensitivity of a float sum and of an integer sum of values in [0, 80], at `d_in` added or removed rows."""
    float_sum = (dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=HOURS_BOUNDS)), dp.symmetric_distance()) >> dp.t.then_sum()
    int_sum = (dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 80))), dp.symmetric_distance()) >> dp.t.then_sum()
    return float_sum.map(d_in), int_sum.map(d_in)
float sum of 36 rows in [0, 80]: sensitivity 2880.0000007451
int sum of 36 rows in [0, 80]: sensitivity 2880

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.2 The feature flags
The feature flags are how the library asks for your consent to each of those limitations. There are four, plus a deprecated alias, and all are off until you call dp.enable_features. A first release switched contrib on without showing what happens otherwise. The script switches it off, tries the Laplace mechanism of that chapter, and switches it back on.
dp.disable_features("contrib")
without_contrib = refusal(lambda: space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0))
dp.enable_features("contrib")
laplace without contrib: OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("contrib")
The helper refusal runs a call and returns the exception’s type and message, and the message here names the flag and the call that enables it. The same wording appears for every flag. Running a finished script with a flag off, through disable_features, is the quickest way to find out which of its calls depend on that flag.
The second flag is honest-but-curious. It gates constructors whose guarantee depends on the arguments you pass being correct. The plugins of Plugins are the main case, because make_user_measurement takes a privacy map as a Python function, and the library cannot check that the function tells the truth. The name describes the adversary the flag assumes: one who is honest when building the measurement and only curious when reading its outputs. The script builds the smallest possible plugin, which releases its input unchanged and claims a privacy loss equal to the distance between inputs.
def plugin_measurement() -> dp.Measurement:
    """A plugin measurement whose privacy map is only a claim: the library cannot check `identity_map`."""
    return dp.m.make_user_measurement(
        dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False),
        dp.absolute_distance(T=float),
        dp.max_divergence(),
        function=identity,
        privacy_map=identity_map,
    )
plugin without honest-but-curious: OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
plugin with honest-but-curious: map(1.0)=1.0
With the flag on, the plugin reports whatever its map says, here a loss of 1 at distance 1, and nothing about that number was verified. So the flag belongs in the environment where you write and prove plugins, not in one where an untrusted analyst submits queries. Such an analyst could register a map that claims any loss they like. The same flag gates OnceFrame.lazy(), which hands back a released Polars plan that could be run twice.
The third flag is idealized-numerics, which marks components whose proof assumes exact arithmetic. In 0.16.0 none of the constructors this book uses asks for it. The float Laplace mechanism builds with the flag off, and so do the float sums above, because their proofs account for rounding. The flag’s older name floating-point still works and warns.
float laplace without idealized-numerics: no error
enable_features("floating-point"): DeprecationWarning: "floating-point" is deprecated. Use "idealized-numerics" instead.
assert_features("idealized-numerics") with the alias on: no error
assert_features("idealized-numerics") after disabling it: OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "idealized-numerics", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("idealized-numerics")
assert_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious"): OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
The last three lines use dp.assert_features, which raises the error a gated constructor would raise, without building anything. It is what every gated constructor calls first. It is also useful on its own at the top of a script, where one line then states every flag the script relies on. The fourth flag, rust-stack-trace, changes no guarantee. It adds the Rust frames to an error message, and the section on reading an exception uses it.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.3 What lies outside the guarantee
The guarantee covers what happens to the data inside a measurement. Four things happen outside it in every analysis. The first is loading the data. The documentation says that loading is not covered and should be done by a trusted curator, and gives the reason: reading a CSV infers each column’s type from its values. The script reads three two-row files that differ in one value, then a longer one whose odd value comes after the rows the inference looked at.
for raw in (b"x
1
2
", b"x
1
2.5
", b"x
1
abc
"):
    print(f"csv {raw!r}: column x inferred as {pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(raw)).schema['x']}")
late_text = b"x
" + b"1
" * 200 + b"abc
"  # a text value after 200 numbers
failed = refusal(lambda: pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(late_text), infer_schema_length=100))
print(f"csv with a text value on row 201, inferred from 100 rows: {first_line(failed)}")
as_strings = pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(late_text), infer_schema=False).schema["x"]
print(f"the same file with infer_schema=False: column x read as {as_strings}")
csv b'x
1
2
': column x inferred as Int64
csv b'x
1
2.5
': column x inferred as Float64
csv b'x
1
abc
': column x inferred as String
csv with a text value on row 201, inferred from 100 rows: ComputeError: could not parse `abc` as dtype `i64` at column 'x' (column number 1)
the same file with infer_schema=False: column x read as String
One person’s value decides whether the column is integer, float or text. When the value arrives after the rows the inference read, it decides whether the load succeeds at all. Inside a trusted environment that failure is useful, since it reveals a malformed file before anything is released. But if the success or failure of the load is visible outside, it is a release that nothing accounted for. The fixes are the documentation’s: read a format that carries its schema, as this book does with Parquet, or read every column as text with infer_schema=False and cast it yourself. The LFS loader in practitioner_datasets does the first, once, when it converts the documentation’s CSV to Parquet. That conversion is the curator’s step, and nothing on these pages claims a guarantee for it.
The second thing outside the guarantee is public information. Every bound, imputed value, key list and margin in this book was chosen from the domain or from a published source. The data and the context took its bound of 150,000 responses a quarter from Eurostat. A bound read off the private data is a release of the data, and the library cannot tell the two apart.
The third is code that runs outside the context. The same chapter told you to delete your reference to the frame once the context holds it, for the same reason. Collecting the frame itself is not a query, so nothing counts it. The fourth is the error channel. Whether a query succeeds or fails is itself an output, and a failure that depends on the data is a release. OpenDP guards against this inside a query, which is why it replaces some Polars arguments so that an expression cannot fail on one value. The loading step and your own code around the context have no such guard.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
section: 15.4 The error messages you will meet
text:
15.4 The error messages you will meet
The documentation’s troubleshooting page has one entry, the type mismatch, and the earlier chapters met several more. This section reproduces each and says what caused it and what fixes it. The first is the type mismatch. By the time you call a function, OpenDP has fixed the type of every argument from the data’s domain. It refuses an argument of another type rather than converting it. The script puts three integers behind a context and clamps them with float bounds.
float bounds on integer data: TypeError: inferred type is f64, expected i32. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/getting-started/trouble-shooting.html#inferred-type-is-xxx-expected-yyy
integer bounds on integer data: scale=10.0
The message names the type it inferred from your argument and the type the data have. The fix is to pass bounds of the data’s type, (0, 10) for integers, or to cast the data first. The documentation names one common cause: a scalar \(\varepsilon\) passed where a measurement expects an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair. The script asks an approximate measurement, built with make_approximate as in Combinators, whether it stays within a scalar budget.
check(1.0, 1.0) on an approximate measurement: TypeError: Cannot coerce a non-tuple type to a tuple
check(1.0, (1.0, 0.0)) on the same measurement: True
An approximate measurement’s privacy loss is a pair, so its budget must be one too, and a pure budget is written as the pair \((\varepsilon, 0)\). The same message comes from binary_search_param with a scalar d_out on an approximate chain (Utilities and the Context API).
Next, a domain that allows missing values. A list of Python floats is inferred as a domain that may contain NaN, and a clamp refuses such a domain. The reason is that NaN compared with a bound is neither inside nor outside it.
clamp on floats that may be nan: OpenDPException: FailedFunction("Domain contains nan")
impute, then clamp: scale=80.0
The fix is the first chapter’s: impute_constant before clamp, which maps the domain to one without NaN. The same need shows up in Polars as fill_null before a dp.sum.
Next, mismatched domains in a chain. The >> operator checks that the output domain of the left side equals the input domain of the right side, and refuses otherwise. The script clamps to one range and then chains a sum that was built for a wider one.
vectors = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
clamp = vectors >> dp.t.then_clamp((0.0, 10.0))
wide_sum = dp.t.make_sum(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0.0, 100.0))), dp.symmetric_distance())
mismatch = refusal(lambda: clamp >> wide_sum)  # the clamp's output has bounds [0, 10], the sum wants [0, 100]
chained = clamp >> dp.t.then_sum()  # a partial constructor takes the clamp's output space, so they agree
clamp to [0, 10] then a sum built for [0, 100]: OpenDPException: DomainMismatch("Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
    output_domain: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 10.0], T=f64))
    input_domain:  VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 100.0], T=f64))
")
clamp to [0, 10] then then_sum(): sensitivity 10.0
The message prints both domains, so the mismatch is there to read: the bounds differ. The fix is the partial constructor then_sum(), which takes its input space from the clamp’s output, as Transformations explained.
The remaining messages come from the Polars side, with the LFS behind a context of one query, a unit of 36 rows and a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\).
def make_context(
    frame: pl.LazyFrame, delta: float | None = None, margins: Sequence[dp.polars.Margin] | None = None
) -> dp.Context:
    """The LFS behind a unit of 36 rows and a budget of epsilon = 1, with or without a delta, for one query."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=delta) if delta else dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON),
        split_evenly_over=1,
        margins=margins,
    )
A float sum needs a margin with max_length, for the reason of the first section. Its sensitivity includes a rounding term that grows with the number of rows, and the proof needs a public bound on that number.
float sum without a margin: OpenDPException: MakeTransformation("must specify 'max_length' in a margin with by=[]")
float sum with max_length=5,400,000: scale=2,881.04
The fix is the documentation’s margin, dp.polars.Margin(max_length=150_000 * 36). The scale then comes out a little above the 2880 of the first section, which is the sensitivity of the sum over \(\varepsilon = 1\) in exact arithmetic. The extra is the rounding term at 5.4 million rows. A grouped sum needs the same bound in the margin of its grouping, which is what by=[] in the message refers to.
The next three come from one query. The script builds a count and tries to collect it before releasing it. Then it releases the count, collects the result twice, and submits another query to a context whose one share is spent.
count_query = context.query().select(dp.len(signed=True))
before_release = refusal(lambda: count_query.collect())  # the plan has no data; only a released OnceFrame does
once = count_query.release()
dp_count = int(once.collect()["len"][0])
twice = refusal(lambda: once.collect())  # a second collection would be a second release
exhausted = refusal(lambda: context.query().select(dp.len(signed=True)).release())
count: scale=36.0 95% accuracy=108.34
collect before release: ValueError: You must call `.release()` before executing a query.
collect a OnceFrame twice: OpenDPException: FailedFunction("OnceFrame has been exhausted")
query after the budget is spent: ValueError: Privacy allowance has been exhausted
A LazyFrameQuery is a plan without data, so collect on it would compute nothing private. The library refuses anyway, so that the habit of collecting a plan never meets a frame that holds data. The call to release returns a OnceFrame, which can be collected once. The noise is drawn when the plan runs, so running it twice would be two releases for one share of the budget. The third message is the one the first chapter ended on. None of the three is a bug to work around. If you need a value twice, keep the DataFrame that the first collect returned.
The last message is from Contingency tables. A contingency table whose keys or cuts cover every column has no private key set to protect, so its release spends no \(\delta\). The library refuses a budget that carries one rather than let it go unspent. The script states the slack as \(\delta = 10^{-7}\), the value the grouping chapters use.
contingency table with keys for every column under (epsilon, delta): ValueError: delta (1e-07) must be zero because keys and cuts span all columns
the same table under pure epsilon: ContingencyTableQuery
The fix is to state the budget as pure \(\varepsilon\) when the keys are all public, or as the zero-concentrated budget \(\rho\) of Utility and noise. Keep \(\delta\) for the tables whose keys the library must discover. Two more messages were decoded where they arose, but they belong in this list. One is a plain mean, which is refused as not recognized because OpenDP has no proof for it. The other is a grouping without keys or a \(\delta\), which is refused because its key set is private (Grouping). For a message that is on none of these pages, the documentation’s troubleshooting page says to ask on OpenDP’s Slack or by email. Its next-steps page points to the user guide section behind each tutorial.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.5 Reading an OpenDPException
Most of the messages above came as an OpenDPException, which is how an error in the Rust core reaches Python. It has three attributes. The variant is the kind of error, one of a fixed list such as DomainMismatch, MakeTransformation or FailedFunction, which code can match on. The message is the text. The raw_traceback is the Rust stack at the point of the error, which is recorded whether or not you display it. The script raises the domain mismatch again and reads the three, then switches on rust-stack-trace and prints the exception a second time.
try:
    _ = clamp >> wide_sum
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(f"variant: {err.variant}")
    print(f"message: {first_line(err.message or '')}")
    print(f"rust frames recorded: {err.raw_traceback is not None}")
    dp.enable_features("rust-stack-trace")
    print(str(err).strip())
    dp.disable_features("rust-stack-trace")
variant: DomainMismatch
message: Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
rust frames recorded: True
Continued Rust stack trace:
    opendp_combinators__make_chain_tt
    opendp::combinators::chain::make_chain_tt::<opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain, opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain, opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain, opendp::ffi::any::AnyMetric, opendp::ffi::any::AnyMetric, opendp::ffi::any::AnyMetric>
    opendp::combinators::chain::mismatch_error::<opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain>
  DomainMismatch("Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
    output_domain: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 10.0], T=f64))
    input_domain:  VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 100.0], T=f64))
")
The frames read from the outside in: the entry point that Python called, the chaining function, and the helper that formats the mismatch. They matter when the message alone does not say where in a long chain the library stopped. They also matter when you report a bug, since they locate it in the Rust source. The list of variants may change between versions, as the class’s own documentation warns. So match on a variant in tests you control rather than in code that must outlive an upgrade. The errors that are not an OpenDPException come from the Python layer: a TypeError from argument conversion, and a ValueError from the context and the query classes.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.6 What a reviewer verifies
A release made with OpenDP comes with a claim: this table satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy for this privacy unit. The chapters so far gave the reviewer everything needed to check it, and Table 15.1 gathers the checks. The first is the unit, because an \(\varepsilon\) means nothing until you know what it protects, and dp.unit_of(contributions=36) protects a person only if nobody has more than 36 rows. Identifier truncation is the fix when someone does. The second is the budget, read back from the context rather than from the code’s intent.
The third is the flags, because honest-but-curious means a privacy map was taken on trust, and the reviewer must then read that map. The fourth is the public information, each bound and key traced to a source outside the data. The fifth is what ran outside the context, from the load to any code that held the frame. The full edition’s chapter on the definition says what the finished claim must state, and the practitioner edition’s release chapter turns it into a record.



Table 15.1: What a reviewer verifies before trusting a release made with OpenDP.










Check
Question
Where to look




Unit
What does one privacy unit contain, and does anyone exceed it?
privacy_unit in the context; the identifier and any truncation


Budget
What was spent, under which measure, and was any release collected twice?
context.current_privacy_loss(); one collect per OnceFrame


Features
Which flags were on, and if honest-but-curious, which maps were claimed?
the enable_features line; every make_user_* call and lazy()


Public information
Where did each bound, imputed value, key list and margin come from?
the constants of the script, traced to their sources


Outside the context
What touched the data before and after the context?
the load and its schema; any code holding the frame

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.8 References

OpenDP documentation: “Limitations” and the feature listing in the API user guide; “Troubleshooting” and “Next Steps” in Getting Started; the note on data loading in “Working with Tabular Data” and the margin and float-sum notes in “Essential Statistics”.
Casacuberta, Shoemate, Vadhan and Wagaman, “Widespread Underestimation of Sensitivity in Differentially Private Libraries and How to Fix It” (2022): the finite-precision sensitivity errors in earlier libraries, and the corrected proofs that OpenDP’s sums follow.
Mironov, “On Significance of the Least Significant Bits for Differential Privacy” (2012): the floating-point attack on the Laplace sampler.
Jin, McMurtry, Rubinstein and Ohrimenko, “Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems” (2022): timing and floating-point side channels in differential privacy libraries.
The full edition’s chapters on the definition and discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms derive the results this chapter states; the practitioner edition’s Release and governance gives the record a reviewer asks for.

title: Synthetic data
text:
The last part releases not a statistic but a dataset. A synthetic dataset is a table of made-up rows whose statistics match the real table’s as closely as a privacy budget allows. An analyst who never sees the real data can still run queries on it, fit models and draw charts. OpenDP builds one in two steps. First it releases a contingency table, which holds the noisy counts of every combination of a few columns at a time. Then it fits a model to those noisy marginals and samples rows from it. The second step is post-processing, so it costs no further budget. The thread of the part is that the quality of the synthetic data is decided by which marginals are measured and how the budget is split among them.
Contingency tables releases the marginals of a fixed workload with the Fixed algorithm. It explains keys, cuts and the thresholds that handle categories the data reveals, and shows the ContingencyTable object with its projections and error estimates. Synthetic data with AIM and MST lets the library choose the marginals adaptively with the AIM algorithm, or along a spanning tree with MST, and generates the synthetic rows. Evaluating and tuning synthetic data measures the result against the real data. It checks the marginals, a query the workload did not contain and a downstream model, and shows how the budget and the workload change the answer.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




Contingency tables
How do I release the noisy counts of a set of marginals, and what does the table object hold?


Synthetic data with AIM and MST
How do I let the library choose the marginals, and how do I generate synthetic rows?


Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
How good is the synthetic data, and what changes it?






By the end of this part you will be able to generate a differentially private synthetic copy of a table and state its guarantee. You will also be able to measure how far the copy is from the original.

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.1 From grouped counts to marginals
Suppose you want to publish not one count but a whole table. It would show how many people of each age group usually work each number of hours, by employment status and sex. A contingency table is that table. It counts the records in every combination of the values of several columns. Grouping released one for two columns, and this chapter asks what changes when there are four, or forty. The answer is that you no longer release the table itself. You release a few marginals, which are the same counts for two or three columns at a time, and fit one model that agrees with all of them. The model then answers any count over those columns, consistently, from the budget already spent.
The chapter follows the documentation’s page on contingency tables. You will set up a context under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) and say which columns have known keys or cut points. Then you will release a fixed workload of marginals and read the ContingencyTable that comes back. At the end you will read a projection of the table against its error bar and add a marginal that the first release left out.
The script opendp_contingency_tables.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with mbi 1.1.0, the Private-PGM version OpenDP pins, against the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample of the earlier chapters. The budgets, scales, thresholds, keys and error bars it prints are the same on every run. The released counts are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the page shows them in one block marked as one run.
Why not release the full table with the grouped counts of Grouping? Two things go wrong as columns are added. The first is size. Each column multiplies the number of cells by its number of values, and the four raw columns of this sample already make 4,648 cells. The second is noise. The noise on a cell does not depend on how many records the cell holds. So spreading the same records over more cells makes each count smaller while its noise stays the same. Soon most cells are noise.
A marginal is the contingency table of a subset of the columns. The two-way marginal of AGE and HWUSUAL has sixteen cells once the two columns are binned as below, each with a count large enough to survive its noise. Releasing several low-order marginals keeps the relations between the columns that share a marginal and gives up the higher-order ones. The documentation’s workload has two marginals, AGE with HWUSUAL and HWUSUAL with ILOSTAT.
Noisy marginals released separately do not agree with each other. Both marginals above contain the one-way counts of HWUSUAL, and two noisy copies of the same count differ. OpenDP therefore does not hand you the noisy marginals. It fits one probability model over all the columns whose own marginals come as close as possible to the noisy ones, and every count you read comes from that model.
The method is Private-PGM, which McKenna, Sheldon and Miklau introduced in 2019 in their paper “Graphical-model based estimation and inference for differential privacy”. The model is a graphical model with one factor per measured marginal, fitted by mirror descent, a gradient method that keeps the model a valid distribution at every step. The fitting sees only the noisy marginals, so it is post-processing and costs no budget. Private-PGM is the mbi package, and the full edition’s chapter on query release covers the problem it solves, which is answering many counting queries from a few noisy measurements.
Install the contingency-table extra with pip install 'opendp[mbi]'. It brings mbi 1.1.0, the version OpenDP 0.16.0 pins, and the documentation’s code then runs as written. Every algorithm fits its model with mbi.estimation.mirror_descent at that package’s default of 1,000 steps. The check at the end of the chapter looks at whether that is enough on this data.

title: 16  Contingency tables
section: 16.2 The context under zCDP, with a delta
text:
16.2 The context under zCDP, with a delta
The context is the one of Assessing utility and choosing the noise, with a larger budget. As there, the privacy unit is 36 contributions, because a person answers at most once per quarter over nine years. The budget is a privacy parameter \(\rho\) of 0.2 under zero-concentrated differential privacy, together with a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\) for the stable keys. Of that, the two queries of the chapter take \(\rho = 0.1\) and \(\rho = 0.05\), so part of the budget stays unspent.
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dp.Context:
    """The context: 36 contributions per person, rho = 0.2 of zCDP with delta = 1e-7, spent query by query."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # a person answers in at most 36 quarters
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=RHO, delta=DELTA),  # the delta pays for the stable keys of ILOSTAT
    )
privacy unit: (SymmetricDistance(), 36)
privacy loss: (Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence), (0.2, 1e-07))
Why zCDP rather than pure differential privacy? A contingency table is many counts released together. Under zCDP the Gaussian noise on all of them composes by adding up their values of \(\rho\). That sum grows more slowly than the privacy parameters \(\varepsilon\) of pure differential privacy would add up. Combinators showed that rule, and the full edition’s chapter on concentrated differential privacy derives it. The mechanism also accepts a budget in \(\varepsilon\), with Laplace noise. The error bars below are then only approximate, because a sum of Laplace draws is not Laplace.
Why a \(\delta\)? One column, ILOSTAT, will have neither keys nor cuts. Its keys will be read from the data, which is the stable-keys release of Grouping. There a key is shown only when its noisy count clears a threshold, set so that one person alone reaches it with probability at most \(\delta\). The slack pays for that threshold and for nothing else, and the library enforces the connection in both directions. Give every column keys or cuts and also a \(\delta\), and the query is refused. Leave a column without them and set \(\delta = 0\), and it is refused too. The script provokes both refusals on this data.
delta with keys for every column: delta (1e-07) must be zero because keys and cuts span all columns
no delta with ILOSTAT unkeyed: delta (0.0) must be nonzero because keys and cuts don't span all columns
The snippet below shows the first refusal on a toy frame, together with one more fact. When every column is keyed, nothing is spent on discovering keys, and the query reports no one-way scale or threshold at all.
import opendp.prelude as dp
import polars as pl

dp.enable_features("contrib")
frame = pl.LazyFrame({"SEX": [1, 2, 1, 2]})
fixed = dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(("SEX",))])
unit = dp.unit_of(contributions=1)
pure = dp.Context.compositor(data=frame, privacy_unit=unit, privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=0.1), split_evenly_over=1)
query = pure.query().contingency_table(keys={"SEX": [1, 2]}, algorithm=fixed)
print(query.oneway_scale, query.oneway_threshold)  # None None
slack = dp.loss_of(rho=0.1, delta=1e-7)
approximate = dp.Context.compositor(data=frame, privacy_unit=unit, privacy_loss=slack, split_evenly_over=1)
try:
    approximate.query().contingency_table(keys={"SEX": [1, 2]}, algorithm=fixed)
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)  # delta (1e-07) must be zero because keys and cuts span all columns

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.3 Keys and cuts
The model needs a fixed, finite set of values for every column, because its cells are indexed by them. OpenDP takes that set from one of three places. For a categorical column you pass keys, the public list of its values, as keys={"SEX": [1, 2]} from the survey’s codebook. For a numeric column you pass cuts, the public bin edges, as cuts={"AGE": [20, 40, 60]}. The column is then binned into left-open intervals, four of them for three cuts, labelled (-inf, 20.0], (20.0, 40.0], (40.0, 60.0] and (60.0, inf]. For a column with neither, here ILOSTAT, the library spends part of the budget on stable keys, the values whose noisy counts clear the threshold.
Each of the three sources can miss values, and the library handles every miss the same way. A value outside the key list, a code 3 in SEX for instance, becomes null. A stable key with too small a count is not released and becomes null too. So null stands for “something else”, and a true null in the data joins it. If you need to tell true nulls apart, recode them to a value of their own with with_columns before the query, as the documentation advises. A cut column has no null bin, so a null AGE or HWUSUAL lands in the last bin. The check at the end of the chapter confirms that on the 255 rows without an age and the 20,819 without usual hours.
The codebook of ILOSTAT lists six codes, from 1 for working to 9 for a child under 15. Two of them, 4 for conscripts and 5 for other inactive people, do not occur in this sample at all, so the stable keys should find exactly four. The documentation describes codes 4 and 5 as absorbed into null. In this sample null is their cell, with no rows behind it, and the released key set below shows the same thing.

title: 16  Contingency tables
section: 16.4 The Fixed algorithm and its workload
text:
16.4 The Fixed algorithm and its workload
dp.mbi.Fixed releases a workload you name in advance, as a list of Count queries, one per marginal. The algorithms of the next chapter choose the marginals themselves, and a fixed workload is the right tool when you already know which relations you need. The query names the columns, the keys and cuts, and the algorithm.
def workload_query(context: dp.Context) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """The documentation's query: keys for SEX, cuts for AGE and HWUSUAL, stable keys for ILOSTAT, two counts."""
    return (
        context.query(rho=TABLE_RHO, delta=DELTA)
        .select("SEX", "AGE", "HWUSUAL", "ILOSTAT")
        .contingency_table(
            keys={"SEX": [1, 2]},  # public: the codebook's two codes
            cuts={"AGE": [20, 40, 60], "HWUSUAL": [1, 20, 40]},  # left-open bins: (-inf, 20], (20, 40], ...
            algorithm=dp.mbi.Fixed(
                queries=[dp.mbi.Count(("AGE", "HWUSUAL")), dp.mbi.Count(("HWUSUAL", "ILOSTAT"))],
                oneway_split=ONEWAY_SPLIT,  # the share of rho for the one-way marginal of ILOSTAT
            ),
        )
    )
The budget of the query is split in two parts. A share oneway_split goes to the one-way marginals of the columns without keys, which is where the stable keys of ILOSTAT come from. The rest goes to the workload, equally over its counts unless you give them weights. When you do not set the share, Fixed uses half the budget times the fraction of columns without keys, which here is a half of a quarter. The documentation sets it to one eighth explicitly, which is the same number, and the script prints the split.
oneway split: 0.125 of rho=0.1 -> rho=0.0125 one-way, rho=0.04375 per count
oneway scale: 227.68  oneway threshold: 1364
Read the two attributes before releasing. The scale is the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise on the one-way counts of ILOSTAT, and the threshold is the count a noisy key must exceed to be kept. Both follow from the privacy unit. One person’s 36 rows can all carry the same status, so adding or removing a person changes one count by up to 36. That number is the sensitivity of the one-way marginal. The Gaussian scale that spends \(\rho\) on a count of sensitivity \(\Delta\) is \(\Delta / \sqrt{2\rho}\), as Assessing utility and choosing the noise stated. The script checks the arithmetic for both parts of the budget.
scale from the formula 36 / sqrt(2 x 0.0125): 227.68
scale of each count of the workload, 36 / sqrt(2 x 0.04375): 121.70
So each cell of the two measured marginals carries Gaussian noise with standard deviation 121.70. The threshold 1364 is set as in Grouping. At scale 227.68, a key held by one person alone, in all 36 of their rows, clears it with probability at most \(\delta\). A smaller threshold needs more keys, a larger budget, or a tighter bound on how many groups one person can touch. The sensitivity 36 is the price of the privacy unit. Truncating to one row per person and year, as Identifier truncation does, would lower it. The sensitivity of each marginal is derived like that of any grouped count, in the full edition’s chapter on sensitivity.

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.5 The released table
table = query.release()
ilostat_std = table.std(("ILOSTAT",))
ilostat_accuracy = dp.gaussian_scale_to_accuracy(ilostat_std, alpha=ALPHA)
The release returns a ContingencyTable. The table holds the key sets the model was fitted on, the cuts, the thresholds that produced any stable keys, and the data type of each column’s keys.
keys: SEX=[1, 2, null]  AGE=[(-inf, 20.0], (20.0, 40.0], (40.0, 60.0], (60.0, inf]]  HWUSUAL=[(-inf, 1.0], (1.0, 20.0], (20.0, 40.0], (40.0, inf]]  ILOSTAT=[1, 2, 3, 9, null]
cuts: AGE=[20.0, 40.0, 60.0]  HWUSUAL=[1.0, 20.0, 40.0]
thresholds: {'ILOSTAT': 1364}
schema: {'SEX': Int64, 'AGE': String, 'HWUSUAL': String, 'ILOSTAT': Int64}
Every key set that is not a cut set ends in null, the cell for values outside the keys. SEX has one although the data hold only 1 and 2. The stable keys of ILOSTAT are the four codes with rows, plus null. The schema shows that a cut column now holds strings, the bin labels, so a query on the table names bins and not numbers.
The method project sums the model over every column but the ones you name and returns the counts as an array, in the order of the keys. The method project_melted returns the same counts as a data frame with one row per combination of keys. Both are post-processing. You can project onto any set of columns, including ones no marginal measured, which the next section shows is a mixed blessing.
std estimates the standard deviation of a projection, and dp.gaussian_scale_to_accuracy turns it into an error bar, as for any Gaussian release. Projecting a two-way marginal onto one of its columns sums four noisy cells, so the standard deviation doubles, from 121.70 to 243.40. With probability 0.95, each count of ILOSTAT is therefore within 477.06 of the truth. That estimate leaves out the one-way marginal of ILOSTAT itself. It was measured only over the keys that were released, a prefix of the marginal rather than the whole of it. OpenDP counts no cell-wise precision for such a measurement. The column HWUSUAL sits in both measured marginals, and the two estimates combine by their inverse variances to 181.42.
std ILOSTAT: 243.40  95% accuracy: 477.06
std AGE x HWUSUAL: 121.70  95% accuracy: 238.53
std HWUSUAL: 181.42  95% accuracy: 355.58

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.6 Adaptive estimation
SEX has keys, but no marginal of the workload contains it. The model has an estimate of the total number of rows and nothing about how they split by sex. So it spreads the total evenly over the three keys, and std refuses to put a bar on that.
std SEX: attrs (('SEX',)) are not covered by the query set
A second query repairs this without starting over. Passing the released table as table= tells the library to keep its keys, cuts, marginals and model, measure the new marginals, and refit. Every column now has keys, the ones found by the first release included, so this query must carry \(\delta = 0\) and spends nothing on key discovery.
def sex_query(context: dp.Context, table: dp.mbi.ContingencyTable) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """A second query that adds the marginal of SEX to the released table's model; every key is known, so delta = 0."""
    return (
        context.query(rho=SEX_RHO, delta=0.0)
        .select("SEX")
        .contingency_table(
            table=table,  # keep the keys, cuts, marginals and model of the first release
            algorithm=dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(("SEX",))]),
        )
    )
The new marginal is a one-way count at \(\rho = 0.05\) with the same sensitivity as before, so its scale is 113.84. The three cells of SEX now have an error bar of 223.13. The model has four marginals, and the context has spent \(\rho = 0.15\) of its 0.2. The second query’s budget was chosen after seeing the first query’s table, which is the adaptive composition that Combinators described. The refit starts from the first model’s potentials, a warm start, and runs its own 1,000 steps of mirror descent from there.
std SEX after the second query: 113.84  95% accuracy: 223.13
marginals in the model: [('ILOSTAT',), ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL'), ('HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT'), ('SEX',)]
privacy loss spent: (0.15, 1e-07)

text:

  last bin of both, the nulls' cell: 1,038,588  (true 1,039,109, off by -521)
  SEX before the second query: 1,270,525 1,270,525 1,270,525  (uniform)
  SEX after: 1: 1,828,537  (true 1,828,992)  2: 1,982,506  (true 1,982,940)  null: 610  (true 0)
  ILOSTAT after the second query:
    ILOSTAT 1: 1,516,288  (true 1,517,011, off by -723)
    ILOSTAT 2: 155,608  (true 155,661, off by -53)
    ILOSTAT 3: 1,450,301  (true 1,450,283, off by +18)
    ILOSTAT 9: 688,867  (true 688,977, off by -110)
    ILOSTAT null: 590  (true 0, off by +590)
Start with the cells the noise alone explains. The largest of the sixteen two-way errors is 521 rows, past twice the per-cell bar of 238.53 but inside three times it. That largest error sits in the last bin of both columns, which holds the 20,819 rows without usual hours and the 255 without an age. A null placed in any other bin would have left this cell some 20,000 rows short, so the run still confirms where the library puts a null. The null keys of ILOSTAT and SEX have no rows behind them, and their estimates are positive, because a fitted distribution cannot go negative. Read a cell whose truth may be zero with that in mind.
Now the counts that the noise does not explain. The working code 1 of ILOSTAT came out 1,422 rows short, past twice its bar of 477.06. The empty null key holds 1,142 rows. Both are the fit, not the noise. The fit starts from the uniform model, the one that spread SEX evenly above, so null begins with a fifth of all rows. A key with no rows is the slowest cell to fit, because the model can empty it only in the limit. One thousand steps bring it down to about a thousand rows and no further, and the rows it keeps are missing from the other keys.
The second query shows the same thing in SEX. Its fit starts from the first model, in which the null key of SEX holds a third of all rows. After its own thousand steps that key still holds 610 rows, more than twice its bar. The two real keys are short by 455 and 434 rows. Those steps also carried on fitting ILOSTAT, so its working code is now 723 rows short and its null holds 590.
A refit settles it. The script refits the four released marginals of the second table from scratch, with 10,000 steps of mirror descent instead of the default 1,000, by calling mbi.estimation.mirror_descent on them. That touches no data, so it is post-processing and a dev-time check, never part of a release.
  the same marginals refitted at 10,000 steps (dev time, post-processing):
    ILOSTAT 1: 1,516,829  (true 1,517,011, off by -182)
    ILOSTAT 2: 155,587  (true 155,661, off by -74)
    ILOSTAT 3: 1,450,277  (true 1,450,283, off by -6)
    ILOSTAT 9: 688,859  (true 688,977, off by -118)
    ILOSTAT null: 103  (true 0, off by +103)
    SEX: 1: 1,828,829  (true 1,828,992)  2: 1,982,798  (true 1,982,940)  null: 27  (true 0)
    AGE x HWUSUAL largest |refit - true|: 295  (accuracy 238.53)
The refit leaves 103 rows in the null key of ILOSTAT and 27 in that of SEX, inside their bars. Code 1 is within 182 rows of the truth, and each real key of SEX is within 163. The largest two-way error is 295 rows, inside three times its bar. A fit that stops early biases the empty cells upward and the largest ones downward, and nothing in the release warns you. A dev-time check against public or historical data is how you notice it.
The test behind the script holds each two-way cell and each refitted count of ILOSTAT and SEX within three times its bar. A correct run leaves that band less than once in a thousand. The released counts of the default fit it checks as this section describes. Each null holds fewer than a tenth of a percent of the rows and more than the refit leaves there. Each real key is within three times its bar plus the rows left in null, because those rows were taken from the real keys.

16.8 Summary



Table 16.1: The calls and concepts of a contingency-table release, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb

A zCDP budget with a slack for stable keys
Gaussian noise composes tightly over many marginals; the \(\delta\) is needed exactly when a column has neither keys nor cuts


keys={"SEX": [1, 2]}

Values outside the list become null


cuts={"AGE": [20, 40, 60]}
Left-open bins of a numeric column
Three cuts make four bins; a null lands in the last one


A column with neither
Stable keys, bought with oneway_split of the budget
Rare values fall below the threshold and join null


dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(...)], oneway_split=1/8)
A workload named in advance
The rest of the budget is shared equally over the counts, or by their weights


query.oneway_scale, query.oneway_threshold
The noise and the cut-off of the key discovery
Read them before releasing; both are None when every column is keyed

What the model was fitted on
Cut columns come back as bin labels, not numbers

Post-processing; a column no marginal covers comes back uniform

Raises for an uncovered projection; a cell near zero is biased upward

Adds marginals to an existing model
Every key is then known, so \(\delta = 0\)

16.9 References

OpenDP documentation: “Contingency Tables” in Getting Started, and the opening of “Synthetic Data”, which lists the algorithms and the rules for null values.
McKenna, Sheldon and Miklau, “Graphical-model based estimation and inference for differential privacy” (2019): Private-PGM, the model that one consistent table is fitted from, and the mirror-descent fit.
Bun and Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (2016): zCDP and the Gaussian mechanism under it.
The full edition’s chapters on query release, sensitivity and concentrated differential privacy derive the results this chapter states.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.1 When you do not know the questions
Contingency tables released the marginals you asked for, which works when you know the questions in advance. The analyst who will use a synthetic dataset usually does not, and a workload that guesses wrong leaves the relationships they care about to chance. This chapter hands the choice to the library. The AIM algorithm picks the marginals it measures one round at a time, going each time for the one its current model gets most wrong. The MST algorithm picks a spanning tree of column pairs in one go. Both fit a model to the noisy marginals, and synthesize() turns the model into rows. Only the measurements and the choices touch the data. Fitting the model and drawing rows post-process released values, so they cost nothing.
The chapter follows the documentation’s synthetic-data page and the docstrings of dp.mbi.AIM, dp.mbi.MST, dp.mbi.Sequential and ContingencyTable.synthesize. You will release three tables over the same four survey columns and read which marginals each algorithm chose, at what noise scale. You will generate a synthetic frame of 3.8 million rows, state the guarantee of the whole release, and compare the synthetic marginals with the real ones. That comparison turns up a problem with nulls that the documentation warns about, and you will fix it. Keys, cuts, Fixed and the ContingencyTable object are the previous chapter’s, used here without re-teaching them.
The script opendp_aim_and_mst.py runs everything on the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample with OpenDP 0.16.0 and mbi 1.1.0, the Private-PGM version OpenDP pins. It runs JAX, which mbi uses to fit the models, on the CPU, and filters the warnings mbi may print when it imports JAX. The noise scales, the threshold, the budget arithmetic, the conversion to \(\varepsilon\) and the facts about the data are the same on every run. The marginals the algorithms choose, the noisy counts, the synthetic rows, the run times and the distances to the real data are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded. The page shows them in blocks marked as one run. The whole script takes about 75 seconds on this machine.
A fixed workload spends the budget on the marginals you name and on nothing else. If the analyst later asks about a pair of columns you did not name, the model answers from the one-way marginals alone, as if the two columns were independent. The documentation’s contingency-table page shows this on SEX, which comes out uniform over its keys because no measured marginal contains it. With four columns you could name every pair and every triple. But the budget would then be spread over ten marginals, most of which the model would have fitted well anyway. The question is how to spend it where the model is wrong.
AIM answers it adaptively. It first measures the one-way marginal of every column with half the budget, which also releases the keys of a column that has none, as the previous chapter explained. Then it fits a model to those marginals and runs rounds. In each round it scores every candidate marginal, by default every marginal of up to three columns. The score is the distance between the model’s version of the marginal and the true one, as a sum of absolute cell differences, minus what measuring it would cost in noise. Candidates are weighted by how much they overlap the workload, so the three-way marginals, which are the workload itself, weigh most.
A noisy selection then picks one candidate with a tenth of the round’s budget. The pick is differentially private because Gaussian noise is added to the scores, the report-noisy-max form of the exponential mechanism that the full edition’s chapter on selection derives. The chosen marginal is measured with Gaussian noise with the other nine tenths, and the model is refitted.
The adaptive part is in the budget per round. AIM starts with a small share per round, the budget divided by the number of rounds. A measurement may change the model’s version of that marginal by less than the noise it carried. Then the round taught little, and the next round gets four times the share. The rounds stop when the budget is spent, which a privacy filter enforces. The rounds argument sets the number of planned rounds and so the starting share. Its default is sixteen per column, which is 64 here, and the script uses 10 so that a release takes seconds. The max_size argument caps the memory of the model in megabytes, and a candidate that would push the model past the cap is skipped. With four small columns the cap never binds.
The queries argument is either the largest number of columns a candidate may have, 3 by default, or an explicit workload. A workload is a list of dp.mbi.Count objects, each a set of columns with a weight, and AIM then favours the candidates that overlap the heavy ones. The measure_split of 0.9 is the share of each round that goes to measuring rather than selecting. MST has the same split and one argument of its own, num_selections, which Section 17.3 explains.
