import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
aim = dp.mbi.AIM()
print(aim.queries, aim.measure_split, aim.max_size, aim.rounds)  # 3 0.9 80.0 None
print(dp.mbi.MST().num_selections, dp.mbi.MST().measure_split)  # None 0.9

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.2 The AIM release
The context is the documentation’s, with three times the budget because this chapter releases three tables. The privacy unit is 36 contributions, the most quarters one person can answer over nine years, as the data and the context explained. The budget is \(\rho = 0.3\) under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), where \(\rho\) bounds the privacy loss on average rather than in the worst case and the noise is Gaussian. Assessing utility and choosing the noise introduced it, and the full edition’s chapter on concentrated differential privacy (DP) derives its composition and conversion rules. The slack \(\delta\) of \(3 \times 10^{-7}\) is the small failure probability that pays for releasing the keys of ILOSTAT, which the query does not name.
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dp.Context:
    """The context: a privacy unit of 36 rows, a budget of rho = 0.3 with delta = 3e-7, one share per release."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # neighbours add or remove one person's 36 rows
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=RHO, delta=DELTA),  # zCDP with Gaussian noise; delta pays for ILOSTAT's keys
    )
Every release goes through one function, because the three queries differ only in the algorithm plugged in. The query takes a third of the budget, \(\rho = 0.1\) with \(\delta = 10^{-7}\). It selects the documentation’s four columns, gives the keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL, and leaves ILOSTAT to the threshold. The fill argument is for later.
def table_query(context: dp.Context, algorithm: Algorithm, fill: bool = False) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """The documentation's contingency-table query at rho = 0.1 and delta = 1e-7, with the algorithm plugged in."""
    query = context.query(rho=RHO_QUERY, delta=DELTA_QUERY)
    if fill:
        query = query.with_columns(fill_nulls())  # a row-by-row transformation before the table
    return query.select(*COLUMNS).contingency_table(
        keys=KEYS,  # public categories of SEX; ILOSTAT's are released with the threshold
        cuts=CUTS,  # bins for the two numeric columns
        algorithm=algorithm,
    )
The first release plugs in AIM with ten rounds. Before releasing, the query reports the scale and the threshold of its one-way step, which cost nothing to read.
aim_query = table_query(context, dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS))
oneway_scale, oneway_threshold = aim_query.oneway_scale, aim_query.oneway_threshold
table_aim, seconds_aim = timed_release(aim_query)
privacy unit: (SymmetricDistance(), 36)
privacy loss: (Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence), (0.3, 3e-07))
query budget: rho=0.1 delta=1e-07
aim: oneway scale=227.6840 threshold=1364
aim: rho per one-way marginal=0.0125  scale 36/sqrt(2 rho)=227.6840
aim: rounds=10  rho per round=0.0050  measure=0.0045  select=0.0005  scale of a round's marginal=379.4733
aim keys ILOSTAT: [1, 2, 3, 9, None]  thresholds: {'ILOSTAT': 1364}
The scales follow from the budget split. Half of the query’s \(\rho\) goes to the one-way step, and AIM measures all four one-way marginals there, so each gets 0.0125. Adding or removing one person changes the cells of a marginal by at most 36 rows in all, and in the worst case all in one cell, so the sensitivity in the Euclidean norm is 36. Write \(\Delta_2\) for that sensitivity and \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise. The mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2}{\sqrt{2\rho}}, \tag{17.1}\] and that formula gives the 227.68 the query reports.
The other half of the share is divided over the ten rounds. Nine tenths of a round’s 0.005 goes to measuring, and the formula gives 379.47 for a round’s marginal. The threshold of 1364 is the noisy count a category of ILOSTAT must clear to be released. The keys came out as the four codes in the data plus the null that stands for anything else.
aim release (one run): 13.4 s
aim measured: ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=189.74
aim measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'ILOSTAT') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL') std=379.47
aim measured: ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=379.47
The release took 13 seconds in this run. The table’s marginals attribute holds every measurement with its clique, the columns it spans, and its noise. The script lists them grouped by clique, in the order the cliques were first measured. In this run AIM measured all four three-way marginals before any pair, as the weights predict. One of them appears twice, the second time at half the scale, which is the adaptive rule at work. A round had moved the model by less than its noise, so the next round took four times the share, which was all that was left, and measured that marginal again. So there were seven measurements rather than ten. Another run chooses differently, which is why you read this list after every release.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
section: 17.3 A spanning tree of pairs with MST
text:
17.3 A spanning tree of pairs with MST
MST is the mechanism that won the 2018 NIST synthetic-data contest, and it is simpler than AIM. After the same one-way step it considers only pairs of columns. Each pair is scored by how far the model’s version is from the true one, again as a sum of absolute cell differences. MST then selects pairs one at a time with a noisy maximum, each time among the pairs that join two columns not yet connected by an earlier pick. With four columns that gives three pairs, and they form a tree that spans every column, which is where the name comes from. The num_selections argument sets how many pairs to pick and defaults to one fewer than the number of columns. Then all selected pairs are measured at once with nine tenths of the remaining budget, and the model is fitted.
mst_query = table_query(context, dp.mbi.MST())
table_mst, seconds_mst = timed_release(mst_query)
mst: oneway scale=227.6840 threshold=1364
mst: pairs=3  rho per pair=0.0150  scale of a pair=207.8461
mst release (one run): 3.3 s
mst measured: ('HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=207.85
mst measured: ('AGE', 'ILOSTAT') std=207.85
mst measured: ('SEX', 'ILOSTAT') std=207.85
mst pairs form a spanning tree: True
The one-way step is identical, so its scale and threshold are the same. The three pairs share nine tenths of the remaining budget, 0.015 each, and the formula gives 207.85. Each pair is therefore measured more precisely than one of AIM’s rounds, because MST commits to three measurements where AIM keeps budget back for rounds it may need. In this run the tree is a star on ILOSTAT, the column most related to the other three. The script checks that the pairs connect all four columns without a cycle, which the selection guarantees. The release took three seconds.

section: 17.4 A first look at the one-way marginals
text:
17.4 A first look at the one-way marginals
The data are public, so the releases can be compared with the truth, which no real release allows. The script draws the synthetic rows of each table, puts their numeric columns back into their bins, and compares each one-way marginal with the real one. The distance it reports is the total variation distance between the two marginals read as distributions, which is half the sum of the absolute differences of their shares. It also reports the largest error of any cell in rows, and the table’s own standard deviation for that marginal from std.
The last column is a bound. Write \(k\) for the number of cells of the marginal and \(n\) for the number of rows. If every cell were off by three standard deviations at once, the distance would be \[\frac{3 k \sigma}{2 n}. \tag{17.2}\] A well-fitted marginal stays far under that, because the cell errors have different signs and few reach three standard deviations.

one-way AGE (aim): tv=0.00015 largest cell error=1,547 rows  std=201.1 bound=0.00032
one-way HWUSUAL (aim): tv=0.00200 largest cell error=11,310 rows  std=192.3 bound=0.00030
one-way ILOSTAT (aim): tv=0.00039 largest cell error=1,670 rows  std=792.7 bound=0.00156
one-way SEX (mst): tv=0.00004 largest cell error=2,779 rows  std=204.5 bound=0.00024
one-way AGE (mst): tv=0.00017 largest cell error=1,981 rows  std=204.5 bound=0.00032
one-way HWUSUAL (mst): tv=0.00257 largest cell error=13,620 rows  std=204.5 bound=0.00032
one-way ILOSTAT (mst): tv=0.00040 largest cell error=1,963 rows  std=227.7 bound=0.00045
SEX and AGE are right as shares, with distances below their bounds. Their largest cell errors of two or three thousand rows are more than the noise explains, and the next section traces them to the model’s total. HWUSUAL is wrong even as shares. Its distance is many times its bound in both releases, and one cell is off by more than eleven thousand rows, over fifty standard deviations. Both algorithms measured that marginal at the same scale as the others, so noise cannot explain it. Something systematic is wrong with the column.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.5 Nulls and the key set
The model behind every table needs a fixed set of keys for every column, which the documentation’s section on nulls explains. The keys come from you, through keys and cuts, or from the stable-key release with the threshold. Either way the set need not cover the data, and every value outside it is replaced by null before counting. For a cut column there is no null key. The four bins of HWUSUAL are its whole key set, and the column has 20,819 real nulls, hours that were not recorded.
rows: 3,811,932  AGE nulls: 255  HWUSUAL nulls: 20,819
HWUSUAL = 99 (not applicable): 2,294,921
In version 0.16.0 those nulls take two different paths. The one-way step counts a cut column by joining its counts onto the bin labels, so a null row is not counted at all. The multi-way step indexes every row into a bin before it counts, and a row whose bin is null gets the last index, so the same row is counted in the bin above 40 hours. The model is then fitted to measurements that disagree about how many rows there are, and it compromises. The script shows the compromise on the fitted one-way marginal of HWUSUAL, against the real counts with the nulls in the last bin.
aim model total (one run): 3,806,638.8  real rows 3,811,932
HWUSUAL bins (aim, one run): fitted count against the real count with nulls in the last bin
  (-inf, 1.0]: fitted 8,953  real 6,961  difference +1,992
  (1.0, 20.0]: fitted 121,660  real 119,893  difference +1,767
  (20.0, 40.0]: fitted 1,028,785  real 1,026,527  difference +2,258
  (40.0, inf]: fitted 2,647,240  real 2,658,551  difference -11,311
The last bin is eleven thousand rows short and every other bin is two thousand rows over. The model’s total, which it estimates from the one-way marginals, is five thousand rows below the real count. Those are the missing nulls, spread by the fit. The smallest bin suffers most in relative terms, since two thousand extra rows on seven thousand is more than a quarter.
The documentation’s remedy is to turn true nulls into a key before the table, with select or with_columns, and that is what the fill argument of the query does. It is a row-by-row transformation inside the query, so it changes nothing about the privacy unit. The script sends the nulls of HWUSUAL to 99, the survey’s own code for not applicable, which already accounts for most of the last bin. It sends the 255 nulls of AGE to zero, the youngest bin. Which code a null gets is a modelling decision. What matters for the fit is that every row lands in a key, the same way in both steps.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.6 Guaranteeing marginals with Sequential
Adaptive selection has a cost. If a particular marginal must be in the release, AIM may or may not measure it. Sequential runs a list of algorithms one after another on the same table, each starting from the model the previous one left, and splits the budget evenly between them unless weights says otherwise. A Fixed workload first and AIM second gives you both. The named marginals are measured whatever happens, and AIM spends the rest where the model is still wrong. The third release does this with the pairs of ILOSTAT with SEX and with AGE, and it fills the nulls.
sequential = dp.mbi.Sequential(
    algorithms=[
        dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(by) for by in GUARANTEED]),  # these two marginals, whatever happens
        dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS),  # then AIM chooses the rest
    ],
)
sequential_query = table_query(context, sequential, fill=True)
table_seq, seconds_seq = timed_release(sequential_query)

sequential: rho per AIM round=0.0025  scale of a round's marginal=536.6563

sequential measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=536.66

The one-way step again takes half, and the rest is split evenly between the two algorithms. Fixed divides its quarter between its two marginals, which come out at the familiar 227.68. AIM runs its ten rounds on the other quarter, so each round’s marginal is noisier than in the first release, 536.66 against 379.47. That is the price of the guarantee, and weights can shift it either way. The oneway and oneway_split arguments belong to the outer algorithm here, Sequential, which measures all four one-way marginals as AIM does. The model’s total is now 219 rows from the truth, within one standard deviation of a one-way measurement. The nulls were the problem, and the one-way marginals confirm it.

Every distance is under its bound by a factor of three or more, and no cell is more than 360 rows off, which is under two standard deviations. HWUSUAL went from eleven thousand rows of error to 273.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.7 Generating the rows
A ContingencyTable is a model, and synthesize() turns it into a frame. The model is a graphical model over the four columns whose marginals match the noisy measurements as closely as they can be matched at once, fitted by Private-PGM with mirror descent. The full edition’s chapter on query release explains why answering many queries through one consistent model beats answering them separately. Drawing rows from the model looks only at released values, so it is post-processing and spends nothing, however often you call it.

synthetic AGE from 19.00 to 61.00  HWUSUAL from 0.00 to 41.00
synthetic dtypes: {'SEX': Int64, 'AGE': Float64, 'HWUSUAL': Float64, 'ILOSTAT': Int64}
synthetic SEX values: [1, 2]  ILOSTAT values: [1, 2, 3, 9]
Without a rows argument the frame has as many rows as the model’s total, which is the noisy estimate of the row count and not the true one. The frame has the four columns with their original types, and SEX and ILOSTAT take values from their keys, the null key included. The default method="round" scales the model’s expected counts to the number of rows and rounds them at random, so the synthetic marginals match the model’s to within a row per cell. The alternative, method="sample", draws each row independently from the model. That adds sampling noise of the order of the square root of each count, and it is the right choice when the rows should behave like a sample.
sample = table_aim.synthesize(rows=SAMPLE_ROWS, method="sample")  # draws rows independently from the model
synthesize rows=100,000 method=sample: shape (100000, 4)
The numeric columns deserve a second look, because the first rows all show an AGE just under 20. The model knows only which bin a row is in. For a cut column, synthesize() draws a value uniformly inside the bin, and for the two open-ended bins it draws within one unit of the edge. So every synthetic age lies between 19 and 61, whatever the real range was, and the rows coded 99 in the real data all become hours just above 40. An analyst who computes a mean age from this frame gets a number that reflects the bins and the sampling rule, not the data. The ages are right as bins and wrong as numbers. If the numbers matter, give finer cuts, at the cost of more cells per marginal and more noise per cell, which Evaluating and tuning synthetic data weighs.
The script seeds NumPy’s global generator, which the rounding and the within-bin draws use, so the frame is a function of the released table.

text:
17.8 The privacy statement
The context has spent its three shares, and the statement of the whole release is written from the variables of the script, not typed in.
budget spent: (0.3, 3e-07)
rho=0.3 at delta=1e-07: epsilon=4.2709
whole context converted: epsilon=4.2709 delta=4e-07
A budget in \(\rho\) is stated to readers in \(\varepsilon\), and the conversion is the one Assessing utility and choosing the noise used. A Gaussian measurement whose scale makes a sensitivity of 1 cost exactly \(\rho = 0.3\) is converted with make_zCDP_to_approxDP and make_fix_delta at a further \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\). That gives \(\varepsilon = 4.27\). The same two combinators applied to the context’s accountant give the same \(\varepsilon\) with the total \(\delta\), three parts for the keys and one for the conversion. So three adaptive releases cost \(\varepsilon = 4.27\), which is a loose guarantee.
print(
    f"This release of three contingency tables and the synthetic rows drawn from them satisfies "
    f"(rho = {RHO:g}, delta = {DELTA:g})-zero-concentrated differential privacy, which is "
    f"(epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {total_delta:g})-differential privacy, "
    f"for adding or removing all of one person's survey responses, at most {CONTRIBUTIONS} of them, "
    f"under the central model, using OpenDP {dp.__version__} with Gaussian noise. "
    f"The keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL were fixed in advance; the keys of ILOSTAT were released "
    f"with a threshold of {oneway_threshold}. Generating the rows is post-processing and spent nothing."
)
The statement covers the synthetic rows without a separate term, because post-processing adds nothing to the loss. It names what was public, since a cut chosen by looking at the data would leak it. The unit of 36 contributions is the expensive part of this guarantee. Every scale above carries the factor 36, and Identifier truncation and bounds showed that hardly anyone in the file answers more than a few times. The same query runs under the identifier unit with a truncation to four rows per person. The script builds it to read the scale and does not release it.
context_id = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=frame,
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT"),  # neighbours add or remove one person
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=RHO_QUERY, delta=DELTA_QUERY),
)
query_id = (
    context_id.query(rho=RHO_QUERY, delta=DELTA_QUERY)
    .truncate_per_group(TRUNCATE)  # at most 4 rows per person, so a person moves a count by at most 4
    .select(*COLUMNS)
    .contingency_table(keys=KEYS, cuts=CUTS, algorithm=dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS))
)
identifier unit, 4 rows per person: oneway scale=25.2982 threshold=142
identifier unit: scale ratio 9.00 = 36/4
The one-way scale falls nine-fold, to 25.30, because a person now moves a count by at most 4 rows rather than 36. The threshold falls from 1364 to 142, and every other scale of the release carries the same factor. The cost is the truncation, which drops every row beyond the fourth of anyone who answered more often, before anything is counted.

Two things stand out. First, in the two releases that left the nulls alone, every marginal containing HWUSUAL breaks its bound, and the pairs without it are further from the truth than in the third release, because the wrong total leaks into every marginal. Second, in the release that filled the nulls, every measured marginal is under its bound by a factor of four or more. The bound counts three standard deviations in every cell at once, which never happens, so a three-way marginal with a distance of one thousandth is a good fit.
What this check does not say is how the synthetic data answers a question nobody measured, or how a model trained on it compares with one trained on the real rows. Those are the questions of Evaluating and tuning synthetic data, which also shows what changes when the budget, the cuts or the number of rounds change.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.1 What good means
Synthetic data with AIM and MST ended with a synthetic table and a privacy statement. The statement says how little the table reveals about any one person, but it says nothing about whether the table is any good. This chapter measures that. The one idea is that “good” is three separate questions, and only the first has an answer that the release itself can give. You will compare an AIM release with the real data on the marginals it measured, on a table it never measured, and through a classifier trained on its rows. Then you will repeat the comparison at three budgets and for MST, and write down what to publish alongside the rows.
The documentation stops once the rows are generated, so this chapter goes beyond it. Its methods come from the paper that introduced AIM and from a benchmark of private synthetic-data generators, both cited at the end. The Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample is public, and that is what makes the comparison possible. On private data you would run the same comparison on a public or historical stand-in before the release, never on the data you protect.
The script opendp_evaluating_synthetic_data.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with mbi 1.1.0, and it imports the previous chapter’s script for the functions the two share. The budgets, noise scales, thresholds, conversions to the privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the classifier trained on real rows are the same on every run. The releases, the fitted models and every distance to the truth are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded. So the page shows them in blocks and tables marked as one run. The whole script, with four releases, took 55 seconds in one run.
A synthetic table can be judged by three questions. The first is whether the marginals the algorithm measured match the real ones. The second is whether queries it never measured come out right, such as a count over all four columns or a share within a small group. The third is whether a model trained on the synthetic rows works on real rows. These are the checks of the benchmark by Tao and coauthors, and each one catches failures that the other two miss.
Only the first question has an error bar that comes from the release. Every measured marginal carried Gaussian noise of a known scale. So the table’s std method can say how far its fitted counts should be from the truth, as Contingency tables showed. A table that no measurement covers has no such bar, and std refuses it. A downstream model has no bar either. The second and third questions can therefore be answered only against real data. On a real release that means public or historical data of the same kind, which the full edition’s chapter on public data discusses.
The release under evaluation is the previous chapter’s AIM release with its nulls filled. It uses the same privacy unit of 36 contributions, the same four columns with their keys and cuts, and ten rounds. The budget is \(\rho = 0.1\) under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), where \(\rho\) bounds the privacy loss on average and the noise is Gaussian. A slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\) pays for releasing the keys of ILOSTAT. Two functions build the context and the query from a budget, so that later sections can change it.
The release itself is one line, and the next one prepares the comparison. It puts the real rows through the same steps as the query, filling the nulls, cutting the numbers into bins and mapping codes outside the keys to null. So every real marginal has exactly the cells of the synthetic one.
The scales are the previous chapter’s, since the query is the same. The one-way marginals carry noise of scale 227.68 and each round’s marginal 379.47. Converted at a further \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\), the budget is \(\varepsilon = 2.35\). In this run AIM measured all four three-way marginals and then a pair at half the scale.

def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, rho: float) -> dp.Context:
    """A context for one release at budget rho, with the previous chapter's unit and slack."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # neighbours add or remove one person's 36 rows
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=DELTA),  # zCDP with Gaussian noise; delta pays for ILOSTAT's keys
    )


def table_query(context: dp.Context, rho: float, algorithm: Algorithm) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """The previous chapter's query with its nulls filled, at the budget rho, with the algorithm plugged in."""
    return (
        context.query(rho=rho, delta=DELTA)
        .with_columns(synth.fill_nulls())  # every null lands in a public key before anything is counted
        .select(*COLUMNS)
        .contingency_table(keys=synth.KEYS, cuts=synth.CUTS, algorithm=algorithm)
    )

aim_query = table_query(make_context(frame, RHO), RHO, dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS))
table_aim, seconds_aim = synth.timed_release(aim_query)
real = synth.binned(frame, table_aim.keys, fill=True).collect()  # the real rows in the table's keys and bins

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.2 The workload error
The first question asks how far each measured marginal of the model is from the real one. The AIM paper calls the average of that distance over a workload the workload error, and it is the number AIM itself tries to make small. The distance here is the total variation distance of the previous chapter, half the sum over cells of the absolute differences between the two tables’ shares. It is the largest difference between the shares that the two tables give to any set of cells. So the worst distance below, 0.00102, means that no question about those columns gets a share that is off by more than that.
The function below computes it for a list of cliques, the sets of columns each marginal spans. It reads the model’s own counts with project_melted rather than drawing rows, because drawing rows adds noise of its own, which Section 18.6 measures. Next to each distance it puts the bound of the previous chapter. That bound is the distance the marginal would have if every one of its cells were off by three of its standard deviations at once.
def marginal_errors(
    table: ContingencyTable, real: pl.DataFrame, cliques: Sequence[tuple[str, ...]]
) -> list[MarginalError]:
    """Each clique's distance between the fitted model's marginal and the real one, with the table's own standard
    deviation for it and the bound that three standard deviations in every cell would give."""
    errors: list[MarginalError] = []
    for clique in cliques:
        fitted = table.project_melted(clique)  # the model's counts: no rows are drawn
        tv, worst = distance(synth.marginal(real, clique), fitted, clique)
        std = table.std(clique)
        bound = synth.tv_bound(synth.cells(table, clique), std, real.height)
        errors.append(MarginalError(clique, tv, worst, std, bound))
    return errors

Every distance is under its bound by a factor of three or more. The worst measured marginal, the triple of AGE, HWUSUAL and ILOSTAT, is under it by a factor of 11.7. No cell is off by more than a few hundred rows out of 3.8 million. The one-way standard deviations are not the one-way scale of 227.68, because the model combines each one-way measurement with every measured marginal that contains the column. That is why ILOSTAT, which sits in four marginals, gets 201.0. The triples have larger distances than the one-way marginals although their largest cell errors are similar, since they spread the same noise over many more cells.
Read the table as a check of the pipeline, not only of the noise. A distance that breaks its bound means something systematic, and the previous chapter traced one such break to nulls that the two steps of the release counted differently. On private data you cannot fill this table in, because it needs the real marginals. You can fill in the std column, which comes from the release, and that is the error bar you publish.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.3 A query nobody measured
The second question asks about a table that no measurement covers. AIM’s candidates have at most three columns, so it never measures the four-way table of SEX, AGE, HWUSUAL and ILOSTAT, whose 240 cells hold every combination at once. The model still answers it. It fills those cells with the distribution that agrees with the measured marginals and assumes nothing else. The full edition’s chapter on query release explains why many queries are best answered through one such model. But the table can no longer put a bar on the answer.
try:
    four_std = f"{table_aim.std(COLUMNS):.1f}"
except ValueError as err:
    four_std = str(err)  # no measured marginal covers all four columns, so the table has no error bar for it

std of the four-way table: attrs (('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT')) are not covered by the query set
four-way (aim rho=0.1, one run): tv=0.00141 largest cell error=450 rows  best measured (SEX, ILOSTAT) tv=0.00022  worst measured tv=0.00102

share working by SEX, AGE, HWUSUAL (aim rho=0.1, one run): largest error=2.05 points at {'SEX': 1, 'AGE': '(-inf, 20.0]', 'HWUSUAL': '(1.0, 20.0]'}  real=100.00%  model=97.95%
In this run the four-way table is further from the truth than every measured marginal. Its errors add up from two sources. One is the noise of the overlapping triples it is assembled from. The other is any dependence among all four columns that no triple shows, which the model cannot know about. Here the four measured triples overlap so much that little is left to guess, and the distance stays near the worst measured one. A release that measured fewer marginals would leave more to the model’s assumptions, as Section 18.5 shows for MST.
A conditional share is a harder test, because it divides one small count by another. The script reads the share of people working in each combination of SEX, AGE band and HWUSUAL band off the four-way table. It compares the 26 cells with at least a thousand real rows. The largest error in this run was two points, in the cell of men under 20 who usually work 1 to 20 hours. Everyone in that cell works, since a usual number of hours implies a job, but the model gave the cell a share of 97.95%. Noise is added per count, not per person, so a small group gets the largest relative error. When an analyst will ask about small groups, measure them, for instance with Fixed inside Sequential as the previous chapter did.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
section: 18.4 Train on synthetic, test on real
text:
18.4 Train on synthetic, test on real
The third question is whether a model trained on the synthetic rows works on real rows. The benchmark calls this “train on synthetic, test on real”. The task here is to predict whether a person works, ILOSTAT equal to 1, from SEX, the AGE band and the HWUSUAL band. The model is a logistic regression from scikit-learn on eleven indicator columns, one per key of each feature.
The script draws 200,000 synthetic rows with method="sample", which draws each row independently from the model, as a sample from the population would be. It also takes 400,000 real rows in one seeded Polars shuffle. The first 200,000 train the yardstick, a model on real rows, and the rest are held out to score both models.
rows = synth.synthesize(table, seed, rows=ROWS, method="sample")  # independent draws from the model
rows = synth.binned(rows.lazy(), table.keys, fill=False).collect()  # the numbers back in their bins
model = classifier(rows, table.keys, seed)  # train on synthetic
def classifier(train: pl.DataFrame, keys: dict[str, Any], seed: int) -> LogisticRegression:
    """A logistic regression that predicts ILOSTAT == 1 from SEX, the AGE band and the HWUSUAL band, fitted on
    `train`, which is either synthetic rows or real rows."""
    return LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=seed).fit(design(train, keys), labels(train))


def accuracy(model: LogisticRegression, test: pl.DataFrame, keys: dict[str, Any]) -> float:
    """The share of the held-out real rows the model labels correctly."""
    return float((model.predict(design(test, keys)) == labels(test)).mean())
held-out real rows: 200,000  real training rows: 200,000  synthetic training rows: 200,000
features: 11 indicators
share working in the held-out rows: 0.3976
train on real, test on real: accuracy=0.9313
standard error of an accuracy on 200,000 rows: 0.0006
train on synthetic (aim rho=0.1, one run), test on real: accuracy=0.9313  gap=+0.0000  mean probability difference=0.0015
The model trained on real rows labels 93.13% of the held-out rows correctly, against 39.76% working. The model trained on synthetic rows scored the same in this run, so the gap is zero, well inside the standard error of 0.0006. The test allows a gap of one percentage point. That is generous against the standard error, and it is the size of gap a model would show if it got a few small cells wrong.
Accuracy is a coarse check, though. Two models that put every cell’s probability on the same side of one half make the same predictions, whatever the probabilities are. So the script also reports the mean difference between the two models’ predicted probabilities, 0.0015 in this run, which sees changes that accuracy cannot. A richer model, one with interactions between the features, would also depend on the parts of the table that are hardest to get right. Statistical modelling fits private models directly, and for a single model that is often better than training on synthetic rows.

section: 18.5 What the budget and the algorithm buy
text:
18.5 What the budget and the algorithm buy
Tuning means running the evaluation under different settings and choosing between them. The script repeats it with AIM at a fifth of the budget, \(\rho = 0.02\), and at five times it, \(\rho = 0.5\). Then it runs MST at the original budget. Each release gets a context of its own, because the comparison is between alternatives and you would publish only one of them. Released from the same private data, the four would compose to \(\rho = 0.72\), and so tuning on the private data spends budget too. Tune on a public stand-in, and release once.

budget the four contexts add up to if all were released from the same data: rho=0.72
The scales follow the formula of the previous chapter, the sensitivity of 36 over the square root of twice the budget. Twenty-five times the budget therefore divides every scale by five, from 509.12 to 101.82 for the one-way marginals. Converted to \(\varepsilon\), the smallest budget is 1.00 and the largest 5.67. The full edition’s chapter on choosing epsilon discusses which of them a release can defend.

The budget buys accuracy everywhere, but not evenly. Across the three budgets, the worst measured marginal and the four-way table improve steadily, though by less than the scales shrink. The one-way marginals, already close at \(\rho = 0.1\), improve least. The share error falls fastest at the low end, from 15.64 points to 2.05, because small groups are the first to drown in noise. A larger budget also lets AIM measure more marginals in its rounds, and in this run it measured four, five and six. All four classifiers scored the same accuracy of 0.9313, so for this task the budget makes no visible difference.
The algorithm changes more than the budget does. MST measures three pairs, all of them with ILOSTAT in this run, and so treats SEX, AGE and HWUSUAL as independent once employment status is known. That assumption is false, since hours depend on sex and age among those who work. The four-way table comes out tens of times further from the truth than AIM’s at the same budget. The share error reaches 24 points, in the cell of women under 20 who report at most one usual hour. The predicted probabilities move by 0.028 on average, while the accuracy still does not change. MST is the better choice when the questions are about pairs and the release must be fast, since in this run it took 3.3 seconds against 13.7 for AIM.
The cuts and the number of rounds are the other two settings. Finer cuts multiply the cells of every marginal, and since every cell carries noise of the same scale, the bound on each marginal grows with them. More rounds give each round a smaller share, so AIM measures more marginals, each less precisely. Evaluate either change on a public stand-in in the same way.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
section: 18.6 How many rows, and how to draw them
text:
18.6 How many rows, and how to draw them
The evaluation of the marginals read the model, not the rows, and this section shows why. Drawing a fixed number of rows independently adds a sampling error on top of the model’s error. The script computes its expected size for each one-way marginal from the table’s own shares, at 200,000 rows and at the size of the real table.
sampling noise on one-way SEX: expected tv at 200,000 rows=0.00090  at 3,811,932 rows=0.00021
sampling noise on one-way AGE: expected tv at 200,000 rows=0.00152  at 3,811,932 rows=0.00035
sampling noise on one-way HWUSUAL: expected tv at 200,000 rows=0.00100  at 3,811,932 rows=0.00023
sampling noise on one-way ILOSTAT: expected tv at 200,000 rows=0.00140  at 3,811,932 rows=0.00032
aim rho=0.1 one-way tv summed (one run): model=0.00029  round=0.00028  sample=0.00745
aim rho=0.1 four-way tv (one run): model=0.00141  round=0.00139  sample=0.00483
mst rho=0.1 four-way tv (one run): model=0.05610  round=0.18410  sample=0.05791
mst rho=0.1 pair ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL') tv (one run): model=0.01504  round=0.12370  sample=0.01261
At 200,000 sampled rows the sampling error of SEX is many times the model’s error in Table 18.1, so the rows are much worse than the release. Even at the real table’s size the sampling error stays above the model’s, because the privacy noise at this budget is small against 3.8 million rows. More rows than the model’s total add no information, since they only sample the same model more finely.
The default method="round" avoids the sampling error, and for AIM its marginals matched the model’s in this run. But in mbi 1.1.0 it draws each column by the rank of a row within the group of its parent columns. Two columns drawn from the same parents are then sorted together, which ties them. MST’s star makes AGE and HWUSUAL such a pair, and rounding moved their marginal from 0.01504 to 0.12370 while sampling left it near the model. So sample when the joint distribution of the rows matters, and draw as many rows as the model’s total if the marginals must be close. Check the pairs before you trust rounded rows.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.7 What to publish
A synthetic dataset needs a statement of its guarantee and enough description for a user to judge what it can answer. The practitioner edition’s chapter on release and governance builds such a statement for a trained model, and the same rules apply. The numbers come from the variables of the script, never typed in, and the statement names what was public.
print(
    f"This synthetic dataset of {ROWS:,} rows was generated by AIM (OpenDP {dp.__version__}, mbi "
    f"{importlib.metadata.version('mbi')}, rounds={ROUNDS}, queries up to 3 columns) from one contingency table "
    f"over {', '.join(COLUMNS)} released under (rho = {RHO:g}, delta = {DELTA:g})-zero-concentrated differential "
    f"privacy, which is (epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {2 * DELTA:g})-differential privacy, for adding or "
    f"removing all of one person's survey responses, at most {CONTRIBUTIONS} of them, under the central model. "
    f"The keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL were fixed in advance; nulls were recoded to "
    f"{synth.FILL}; the keys of ILOSTAT were released with a threshold of {aim_query.oneway_threshold}. "
    f"Drawing the rows by independent sampling is post-processing and spent nothing."
)
This synthetic dataset of 200,000 rows was generated by AIM (OpenDP 0.16.0, mbi 1.1.0, rounds=10, queries up to 3 columns) from one contingency table over SEX, AGE, HWUSUAL, ILOSTAT released under (rho = 0.1, delta = 1e-07)-zero-concentrated differential privacy, which is (epsilon = 2.35, delta = 2e-07)-differential privacy, for adding or removing all of one person's survey responses, at most 36 of them, under the central model. The keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL were fixed in advance; nulls were recoded to {'AGE': 0.0, 'HWUSUAL': 99.0}; the keys of ILOSTAT were released with a threshold of 1364. Drawing the rows by independent sampling is post-processing and spent nothing.
The statement covers the rows without a further term, because drawing rows from a released model is post-processing, which the full edition’s chapter on properties proves cannot weaken the guarantee. It covers this one table only. The other releases of this chapter, made from the same people, would add to it.



Table 18.3: What to publish with a synthetic dataset, and where this chapter found each item.










Item
What to publish
In this chapter




The guarantee

The columns

The algorithm

The error bars
The measured marginals and their std, which come from the release and cost nothing
Table 18.1, the std column


The utility
The marginal errors and the downstream check, measured on public or historical data
Never on the private data itself






The last row is the one most often done wrong. A distance computed on the private data depends on that data, so publishing it is a new release that the statement does not cover. Limitations and troubleshooting put it as a rule: the guarantee covers what passes through a measurement and nothing computed beside it. The error bars from std are safe to publish. The distances in this chapter’s tables were safe only because the data are public.
This is the last chapter of the book. You can now state a privacy unit and a budget, release statistics, tables and models through a context, and read every scale and threshold before spending anything. You can build the framework’s pieces by hand when the context is not enough, and turn a contingency table into synthetic rows. You can also measure how good those rows are, on data you are allowed to look at, and publish them with a guarantee that says exactly what it covers.

18.9 References

OpenDP documentation: “Synthetic Data” in the statistical modelling guide, “Contingency Tables” in the tabular data guide, and the API reference for opendp.extras.mbi.ContingencyTable (std, project_melted, synthesize). The documentation gives no evaluation; this chapter’s is its own.
McKenna, Mullins, Sheldon and Miklau, “AIM: An Adaptive and Iterative Mechanism for Differentially Private Synthetic Data” (2022): the workload error and the selection that minimizes it.
Tao, McKenna, Hay, Machanavajjhala and Miklau, “Benchmarking Differentially Private Synthetic Data Generation Algorithms” (2021): marginal errors and downstream tasks as the measures of quality.
The practitioner edition’s chapter on release and governance: the statement of a guarantee and the evidence that goes with it.
The full edition’s chapters on post-processing and composition, query release, public data and choosing epsilon derive the results this chapter states.
